THE FIRST SNOWFALL. The snow had begun in the gloaming, And busily all the night Had,been heaping field and highway With a silence deep and white. Every pine and fir and hemlock Wore ermine too dear for an earl, And the poorest twig on the elm-tree Was ridged inch deep with pearl. From sheds new-roof'd with Carrara • C-ame Chanticleer's muffled crow: The stiff rails were softened to svran's-down, And still fluttered down the snow. I stood and watch'd by theyindow The noiseless work of the sky, And the sudden flurries of snow-birds, Like brown leaves whirling,by. I thought of a mound in sweet Auburn Where a little headstone stood; How the flakes were folding it gently. As did robins the babes in the wood. Up spoke our own little Mabel, Saying—" Father ! who -makes it snow?" And I told of the good All-Father Who cares for us here below. - Again I looked at the snowfall, And thought of the leaden sky That arch'd o'er our first great sorrow, When that mound was heap'd so high. I r- —embered the gradual patience That ftll .N-o-n that cloudlike snow, Flake by flake, healing and hiding The scar of our deep-plunged woe. And again to the child I whisper'd, "The snow that husheth all, Darling! the merciful Father, Alone! can make it fall !" Then, with eyes that saw not, I kiss'd her; And she, kissing back, could not know That my kiss was given to her sister, Folded close under deepening snow. - JAMES RTISSELL LOWELL.

"'So as to know where his head begins," peplied the master. None but the dissolute among the poor look upon the rich as their natural enemies, or desire to pillage their houses and divide their property None but the dissolute among the rich speak in opprobrious terms of the vices and follies of the poor.—Ruskin. A young lady, reading in a newspaper the other day of a girl having been made crazy by a sudden kies, called the at- tention of her uncle, who was in the room, to this singular occurrence, whereupon the old gentleman gruffly demanded what the fool had gone crazy for. "What did she go crazy for ? " archly returned the ingenious maiden, "Why, for more I suppose." "In my airly days," said the old man as he shovelled the coal into an np-town, schoolhouse basement "they didn't depend on no coal to keep us school young 'uns warm, I kin tell you." "What did they use?" asked a boy near by. A dreamy, retrospective look passed over the aged man's wrinkled face, and he sighed as he responded, "They used birch my boy—birch." The proverbial wit of the Irish jarvy is oftentimes mixed with an under-current of stern reality that is as touching as it is eloquent. Driving through Dublin on an outside car, the wretched appearance of the horse suddenly struck me. I said," Pat, you're sure to be taken up for cruelty to ani- mals, driving such an old screw as that." " Begor, stir," was the quick reply, " if I didn't dhrive that I'd be taken up for cruelty to a wife and six children." - . THE QUEEN AND THE HERD LADDIE. One day some years ago, when the Queen was standing on the public road rear Balmoral, sketching the Castle from a particular point, a flock of sheep approached. The Queen, being intent on her work, took little notice of the flock, and merely moved a little nearer the side of the road. A boy in charge of the sheep shouted at the top of a stentorian voice, " Stan' oot o' the read, 'onaan, an' let the sheep gae by !" The Queen not moving out of the road quite so fast as the shepherd wished, he again shouted," Fat are ye stan'in there for? Gang oot o' that, an' let the sheep pass!" One of the Queen's atten- dants, who had been at a distance, on hearing his Royal mistress thus rudely assailed, went up to the shepherd, and thus addressed him :—" Do you know whom it is you have been speaking so rudely to boy ?" " No; I neither ken nor care; but, be she fa' she likes, she sudna be i' the sheep's road." "That's the Queen," said the official. The boy looked astonished, and, after recovering his senses, said, with great simplicity, "The Queen! Od, fat way disna pit on claee that foulk can ken her ?" MR. J. S. MILL, M.P.—lt was almost the first time, per- haps the very first time, in English history that a philosirs phicel and economical writer of the first rank had come forward to ask for the vote of a constituency solely on the ground of his writings. Hence it was that Mr. Mill's candi- dature was looked upon with such intense interest by so many persons. A. large committee was' formed, including moo:, of the leading Liberal names in England, to carry him Into Parliament at no expense to himself—in accordance with the principle which he had laid down in his book on "Repeesentative Government," that a man ought to look upen the representation of his fellow-citizens in Parliament rather as a duty to be underaken under certain circum- stances than as a duty to be paid for. The exertions of his admirers, the novelty of the experience, and the influence of Mr. Mill's own dignified presence, seen as it was by so many for the first time, carried him to his seat, and gave him for three years to the service of his country and his party in Parliament and of those who had voted for him, few regretted his success when they saw how his clear luminous speeches tended to enlighten difficult questions, and how his lofty character seemed sometimes to raise the very character of debate and of legislation itself. But en- thusiasm for an idea does not hold its ground for very long in England. • When we come to tell the story of the Gene- ral Election of 1868, we shall have to record the defeat of Mr. Mill.—Cessell's Illustrated History of England. - A DU3I7kIY TRONCLAD.—The following incident occurred in February, 1863. An old coal barge adrift had been picked up in the James River, and the brilliant idea seized some of Admiral Porter's men to convert her into a " moni- tor." The whole scheme was carried out in twelve hours. In fact, her construction was hardly more solid than the "paper forts" lonilt of canvas and boards by the Chinese during our war with them, and which collapsed after a shot or two as readily as would the "Rock of Gibraltar" or "Mount Vesuvius" at a firework display. The barge was built up high with boards, while funnels and turrets e-eletrneted of pork barrels reared above, and two old canoes did duty for quarter-boats. A small house, taken from the back yard of a planter's dwelling, stood for the pilot-house. Her furnaces were built of mud or clay: they were only in- tended to make smoke, not steam. Then a good coat of black paint or pitch; her furnaces were filled with pitch and other inedammalele materials, and she wee ready. As soon as the "dummy" turned adrift on the Mississippi came in range of the Vicksburg batteries, the alarmed garrison opened fire upon it. The black monitor glided down the stream, belching out fire and smoke, bat gave not a shot in return. With amazement the Vicksburg soldiers found that they could not make the slightest impreseion7on the tur- reted monster. They did not know that it was full of water, and had not a man on board! In ominous and silent disdain she seemed to be making for the Confederate iron- clads; one of them, the Queen of the West, leevinn part nf her crew ashore, incontinently fled, with all her steam power, making the best of her way to the Red River. The Indian- ola, a vessel previously captured from the Northerners, was lying aground, and rot to be taken by this ruthless monster of a monitor, was ordered to be blown up, which was ac- coeingly done. Thus was this bloodless victory gained by the dummy ironclad. It is not impossible that we may hear of similar tricks in future warfare, as all IS fair therein. ...ph The AS'ea," for December. COLLECTING ANTS' EGGS IN vrE Trot.—The ant-egg collectors, amei sen or amas-hexen (ant-witches), as they ~.are called, because they put on the most shabby and ragged articles of clothing they possess for this occapation are seen principally in the neighbourhood of ~Seefeld. There the woods and forests are thick with underwood, and the soil bituminous, conditions very favourable to the well- doing of ants. The Formica rufa (brown-red forest ant) is the one the girls look for, as ants of this species live to- gether in great numbers, and have larger eggs than other kinds. The way the eggs are collected is singular. First of all the girls seek a sunny place where a brook or some Dale runnel flows. At the edge of the stream they make a kind of island by scooping out a small ditch round about two feet of sail, and leading the water of the runnel into it, let it flow off below into its natural bed. In the little island this formed theensceop a few hogs, which are covered over with green leaves and twiei to keep them shady. After these arrangements the gins go into the woods in all directions and look for ant-hins. They have a kind of small spade or trowel with them and a ban; now and then also a pair of coarse gloves to protect their hands from stings. The ant-hill discovered, they remove the soil gently with their spade till the white eggs are laid bare. If the ezgs be much scattered they do not waste time, but shovel the whole ant-hill into their bag, and proceed on Thee, search for more. After they have filled the bag they re- turn to their island, and empty the contents of the bag, ante, eggs, and soil, on to it, taking care to leave the shaded 1 holes free. Then they go a little aside and eat their frugal meal by the brook's side, perhaps, too, take a nap, for they know that the ants will do the rest of their work for them. And so it is. The little creatures set to work without delay to remove all their eggs into the ehady holes provided for them. At the approach of evening the girls can collect the eggs without difficulty, and turning the water off so that the poor deluded ants can leave the island at their leisure, they march off with their booty. These eggs sell well for Mae food of birds.—Little Folks Magazine.

div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES,

The Lacaze prize of £4OO for discoveries in science has been awarded by a commission of the French Academy of Sciences to M. Balbiani for his important inquiries into the anatomy and physiology of insects. hi. Balbiani's compe- titor was M. Colin, of Alfort, for whom three votes were given, against five for M. Balbiani. At the last meeting of the French Academy of Sciences, M. Barg presented a resume of inquiries amongst the manu- facturers of Paris concerning the influence of copper work- ing as protection against cholera. The testimony is un- animously in favour of the alleged immunity of workers in copper from cholera and infectious diseases in general. A NEW SYSTEM OF ELECTRIC LIGHTING.—An electric arc lamp on a new principle, which has been invented and patented by Messrs. Clark and Bowman, was publicly exhi- bited for the first time on Tuesday night at 411, Brixton- road, London. The main feature of the lamp consists of an improved form of clutch, in which the carbons are fed by very small impulses, and the length of the feed is deter- mined by the clutch. The feed can be regulated at will while the lamp is burning. As the length of the arc in- creases it immediately feeds its prearranged length, and then locks itself until the arc has again increased. Among other advantages the inventors claim that the lamp contains less moving parts than any other, while the whole of its moving parts can be removed or replaced while the lamp is burning without shutting off the current. The lamp is not affected by dust, heat, or atmosphere, and will burn from six to 24 hours with one pair of carbons, and will moreover run in any position. The inventors also state that it will run off almost any current, having in fact been successfully tried on the Brush, Gramme, and other dynamo machines. INOCULAT/ON.—PROTECTION AGAINST YELLOW FEVER.— We learn from Rio de Janeiro that up to the end of October 48 persons, chiefly foreigners, had been vaccinated by Dr. Domingos Freire with attenuated cultures of the yellow fever microbe, In the expectation, according to his experi ments, of obtaining immunity from attacks of yellow fever. A regular service of the vaccination has been opened at the Instituto Vaccinico by authorisation of the Junta Central de Hygiene Publica. In a recent discourse on Thuillier, M. Pasteur called the attention of the French Academy of Sciences to some curious results obtained from inoculation experiments performed by himself and Thuillier with the microbe of " rouget," an epidemic which afflicts pigs. Cul- tivated through the bodies of a series of pigeons, the microbe in question acquires increased virulence and becomes more rapidly fatal to pigs; cultivated through the bodies of rab- bits, it increases in size, assumes a figure of eight form, and, though still fatal to rabbits, when re-inoculated into the pig it is no longer fatal to that animal, but, on the contrary, acts as a protective vaccine against the original virus. The Lancet points out the analogy between the latter process and the view extensively adopted by English physicians that va.ccinia is " attenuated " rariola. Just as the " ronget " of pigs, when passed through the rabbit, becomes a " vaccine " against " rouget " in the pig, so, it is inferred, the virus of smallpox passes through the cow and becomes vaccinia. The cow-pox reproduced in the human subject by vaccination is, according to this view, simply attenuated smallpox. Thuillier was the discoverer of the microbe of " ronget," but M. Pasteur mentioned that it-was indepen- dently discovered, and at an earlier date, by Professor Det- mers, of Chicago. THE DIGESTIBILITY OF RAW AND COOKED MEAT.—E. Jessen has recently completed some interesting investiga- tions regarding the time required to digest meat and milk prepared in different ways. His first experiments were made with artificial gastric juice. Twenty-five grammes of beef were placed in it for 24 hours, and the undissolved portion weighed at the end of that time. Of the raw beef about 51 grammes only remained, of the half cooked 91 to 91 grammes, while that which was well done left from 17 to 18 grammes. The next experiments were made on a dog with an opening in the stomach. Here, too, the raw meat digested more quickly than boiled or roasted meat. The time for raw beef was 5.3 to 55 hours. Experiments were also made upon men by introducing 100 grammes of meat and 300 cc. of water into an empty stomach. After a certain time the contents of the stomach were pumped out, and if the microscope detected no muscle fibres, the digestion was considered finished. The time required was as follows : Raw beef, shaved fine, 2 hours; half done boiled beef, shaved fine, 2-1 hours; well done boiled beef, shaved fine, 3 hours; half done roasted, shaved fine, 3 hours; well done roasted, shaved fine, 4 hours; raw mutton, 2 hours; raw veal, two and a half hours; raw pork, 3 hours. In the experiments with milk such a quantity was given as to correspond in the quantity of nitrogen it contained to 100 grannies of beef. The time was as follows: 602 cc. raw cow's milk, 31 hours; 602 cc. boiled cow's milk, 4 hours; 602 cc. sour cow's milk, 3 hours; 675 cc. skimmed cow's milk, 31 hours; 655 cc. raw goat's milk, 31 hours. A NEW ELECTRIC RAILWAY.-150 MILES AN HOUR.—A light railway system, driven by electricity, and running at high speeds, has been devised by Mr. F. Hahn Dauchell, C.E., whose object is to effect the rapid transit of letters and parcels by electrical means. The distinguishing fea- ture in its construction is that it has only one rail for the train to run on, instead of two, and that it is balanced by another rail overhead, which at the same time performs the function of conducting the electric current, and also pre- vents the train leaving the metals, as it is embraced by side friction pulleys, placed in pairs and connected with the roofs of the carriages. We have recently examined a working model of this invention at the offices of Messrs. Bauer and Co., 6, Union Court Chambers, Old Broadstreet, London, which gave very high rates of speed. The railway is circular, and about_ eight lea in diameter, the motor being about 12 inches long, eight inches high, and deriving its current from an ordinary bichronaate battery. This mo- tor, or engine, has a pair of grooved driving wheels of large diameter, and placed in line with each other. The object
of this construction is to reduce the friction to a minim-um,
and thus facilitate the production of high speed. Mr. Dauchell proposes a speed of from 150 to 200 miles per hour, the railway being specially designed for the transit of

, . .. . . .. letters, parcels, and light goods, thus appealing to the necesqities of our postal system. Experiments on a larger scale have, we understand, been carried out by Mr. Dauchell at Maidstone, which have demonstrated the practicability of the invention for its intenied purpose.—lron.

Oa, ABRAUAM !—On the night previous to the meeting of the Convention of Chicago, Mr. Lincoln did not get home until eleven o'clock at night. In the morning MrsoLincoln, who was of a most amiable disposition, remonstrated with her good man at breakfast. She kindly but firmly informed him that politics were leading him into bad habits—keeping late hours and drinking at the rum shops; that she did not like it—she had to sit and keep the children up; and— " Now, Abraham, let me tell you that to-night I will go to bed at ten o'clock. If you come before that hour, well and good; if not, I will not get up and let you in." Ten o'clock came that night, and, true to her wo:d, Mrs. Lincoln went to bed with her children. About an hoar later, Mr. Lincoln knocked at the door. He knocked once, twice, and even three times, before an upper window was raised and the nightcap of a female looked out. " Who is there ?" "Me." You know what I told you, Abraham ?" " Yes ; but, wife, I have got something very particular to tell you. Let me in." "1 do'nt want to hear. It is some political stuff." "Wife, it is very important. There is a telegraphic de- spatch, and I have been nominated for the Presidency." "Oh, Abraham, this is awful! Now I know you have been drinking. I only suspected it before; and you may just go and sleep where you got your liquor ;" and down descended the window with a slam. True enough, the next day con- firmed the news that the best anecdote teller of the village had redly been nominated to rule over millions.

RATM.—Various theories have been advanced to account for the formation of rain drops, but the most satisfactory explanation is that proposed by Professor Osborne Rey- nolds. The minute particles of which clouds are composed are moving downwards in consequence of the attraction of gravity; but, by reason of the resistance which the air sffers to their descent, they are only moving very slowly. Since, however, the resistance offered to the passage of large drops is much smaller in proportion to their weight than that offered to small drops it follows that the large drops will descend faster than the smaller ones, and will overtake them, coming into collision with any which are in the direct line of their descent. When two drops collide they will unite to form a larger drop, which will descend with in- creased velocity, sweeping up all smaller drops in its path, and thus increasing in size until it emerges from the cloud. Since many clouds are several miles in thickness it is- easy to see that a particle desoending from the upper part of the cloud may become a rain drop of considerable size before it emerges from the cloud. In their passage from the cloud to the earth the large rain drops will overtake the small ones in a precisely similar way; at the same time, the size of the drops may be slightly increased by the condensation of water from the air through which they are falling, or may be slightly diminished by partial evaporation from the sur- faces of the drops. A falling rain-drop descends with a velocity which increases until the acceleration is balanced by the resistance of the air, after which the drop descends with uniform velocity. It is, of course, well known that large clouds may exist without any rain falling from them. In some cases rain is actually formed, but evaporates and is again converted into vapour before it can reach the ground; in many cases the non-formation of rain is. possibly due to the fact that under certain unknown atmospheric or other' coniitions the particles forming the clouds do not unite when they collide. As an agent of geological change, rain is of the greatest importance. It plays a large part in the disintegration of rocks and the formation of soils, washes the smaller particles into streams and rivers, and is, in fact, one of the most important of the various denuding agents. Indeed, since rain is the ultimate source of all our brooks, rivers. &c. it may be said to be the principal agent of geo- logical, ch;nge on the earth's surface. The amount of the rainfall varies very considerably in different countries, and in different parts of the same country, depending on geo- graphical 130sition, the conformation of the surface of the ground, thepioximity of large lakes and the sea, tic. The heaviest annual fall of rain occurs in the zone of calms over the equatorial region of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and on the west coasts of the British Isles, India, Norway, North and South America, and New Zealand. In all these latter districts the west wind blows over a large tract of ocean and becomes heavily charged with moisture, which it deposits when forced upwards by the action of the mountains on the coasts. The driest districts in the world are the desert regions of Africa and Asia. The amount of rain which falls in single showers is sometimes enormous, especially in the Tropics. In the British Isles one of the heaviest falls on record is a fall of 5.36 inches in twenty- four hours in Monmouthshire, July 14th, 1875. On Octo- ber 25,1836, at 4ibraltar, there was a fall of 30.11 inches. —"Cassell's Concise Cycloperdia" for Deceniber. THE UNDERLEY HEnt..—The following births have taken place in the herd of *Earl Bective :—Nov. 14: Darlington' 26th, a white heifer calf, by Grand Duke 31st (38,374). Nov. 16: Maplewell Darling, a red and white bull calf, by Grand Duke 31st (38,374). Nov. 22: Grand Duchess 23rd, a white bull calf, by Grand Duke 31st (38,374). Nov. 23: Red Rose of Fairburne' a roan heifer calf, by Underley Prince (45,710). Nov. 24: Underley Darling Bth, a roan heifer calf, by Underley Prince (45,710). THE ALLEGED FABRICATION OF CLYDESDALE HORSES' PEDIGREES.—The two young men named Wm. M'Kinlay, clerk to a well-known horse dealer, and David Raeside, farmer, Craigton, Bishopton, agent in Scotland for an American horse dealing firm, have been fully committed for trial by Sheriff Balfour on a charge of forging and uttering several false schedules of Clydesdale horses, signed by breeders, purporting to contain the true lineage of the dams of certain colts. The men, it will be remembered, were ap- prehended some days ago. LABOURERS' ASSOCIATION.—It has been resolved at a meeting held at Birmingham to form an association to assist labourers to obtain their rights under the Allotment Extension Act. Speaking at a subsequent meeting at the Town Hall, Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., said Mr. Collings' mo- tion for assisting the establishment of a peasant proprietary was kindred to the extension of the Allotment Act, and would be fraught with the greatest possible advantage to the nation. He hoped that the motion would tend to the restoration of charity lands to labourers.—Mr. Jesse Col- lings said that trustees must be shown that labourers had a powerful organisation, to which they could loak for assist- ance to overcome difficulties and vindicate their rights. SHORTHORNS IN IRELAND.—The Irish Farmers' Gazette has published its usual annual analysis of auction sales of Shorthorns in Ireland daring the past season. The mean average is 2s. 9d. less than that of last year. Altogether 291 animals were sold, and the average was £33 18s. 2id. Of the number sold 198 were bulls, at an average of £34 2s. ed., and 93 were cows and heifers, at an average of £33 Bs. 3id. In 1882, the number of Shorthorns sold in Ireland was 238, which brought an average of £34 Os. ; and in 1881, 370 animals were sold, at an average of £25 4s. qd. Last year the average for bulls was £35 2s. Sid., and for cows and heifers, £32 18s. 91d. The average for bulls this year was thus about £1 less per head than last year, while for cows and heifers the average was about 10s. per head more. In 1881, the average for bulls was £2B 14s. nd., and for cows and heifers, £22 13s. 2d. HOUSEHOLD EssiLZE.—" E.," writing to the Standard, says it may be interesting to some to know that the farmer's wife, in the Netherlands, has her silo. This is an earthen- ware jar about two feet high: Into one such in summer time she shreds kidney beans; into another she puts shelled green peas; into another broad beans say; and having thus formed a six-inch layer she sprinkles on the top a little salt, and presses the whole firmly down. Then comes another layer, with another sprinkling and so on, until she has come to the end of her vegetables. Leaving a light weight on the top, which serves to keep all firmly pressed and exclude the air, when more vegetables are ripe she repeats the process until the jar is filled. A good substan- tial weight is then placed on the top and the opening covered with brown paper; and her object is attained, viz., ensilage for her family, i.e., vegetables preserved green for winter use, more or less good, according to taste, when brought to table. AGRICULTURAL RETURNS.—The agricultural returns of Great Britain for the present year have been published. In Great Britain the area reported to be under all kinds of

crops, bare, follow, and grais amounts to 32,385,000 acres, an increase of 72,000 acres, compared with last year. The increase is almost exclusively in permanent pasture, the area in tillage still tending to diminish. In Ireland there are 15,151,000 acres under the same heading—a decrease of 61,000 acres. The gross total of 47,667,000 acres under crops, bare, fallow, and grass, in the United Kingdom, in- cluding the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, is divided as follows :—Corn crops, 10,326,000; green crops, 4,708,000;

clover, sanfoin, and grasses under rotation, 6,311,000; per- manent pasture or grass not broken up in rotation (exclu- sive of heath or mountain land), 25,288,000; flax, 100,000; hops, 68,000; bare, fallow, or nncropped arable land, 803,000. The numbers of live stock as returned upon the sth of June were—ln Great Britain: Horses, 1,410,000; cattle, 5,692,000; sheep, 25,068,000; pigs 2,617,000. In Ireland : Horses, 478,000; cattle,-4,096,000 ; sheep, 3,219,000; pigs, 1,351,000. There were imported into the United Kingdom in 1882 the following :-343,699 live cattle, 1,124,391 sheep, and 15,670 swine, of the total value of £9,271,956. The imports of fresh and salted beef and pork were 4,649,270 cwts. A JERSEY Cuoss.—With regard' to crosses with the Jer- sey, a Cheshire gentleman, who a year ago purchased a number of Jersey crosses upon _local breeds—the best he could obtain at the time for his cold land—reports that his first season has been most satisfactory considering that in

each case the animals were obtained without lineage or any record of their performances other than farmers give when they sell an animal. One cow (and all were young) gave twelve pounds of butter a week while on grass, and the others averaged between eight and ten pounds. Now the most sceptical farmers will allow that a cow giving any- thing like this quantity of butter pays very well indeed, but how many animals of pare race, if we except Channel Island cattle, do it Absolutely none. The isolated cases in other breeds are no guide to the value of the. _breed in . _

, general. It must be remembered that the above instance is , not a lair ersampis, betaase,the animals were ordinary ones, ' not selected, and of no special milking breed. What, then, might be expected of a cross between two deep milking ' races such as the Jersey and the polled Suffolk or the Ayr- shire, where the sire and dam are especially good examples? ' What is wanted by the farmer is milk or butter, good vigo- rous constitution, and some capacity to lay on flesh; and to obtain these he should not mind how he crosses, in spite of the rage for purity of breed which has been preached to ; him until he has almost begun to believe that the exhibi- tion shorthorn is a paragon of animals. AN INTERNATIONAL AGRICULTURAL EXHIBITION has been suggested by a contemporary. "The harvest of the sea" has been well housed in the Fisheries Exhibition, which has just closed. The time is opportune; agriculture wants a lift; husbandry is languishing; and farmers require some practical instruction in dairying. The Royal Agricultural Society is the chief body among farmers, and should have something to say on this matter. The patrons of the late Fisheries Exhibition were noblemen and gentlemen, and were also connected with stock-rearing and arable xarming. They are also members of the Royal Agricultural So- ciety, or of county associations; and therefore it only re- quires the initiative to be taken by influential patrons of agriculture, in conjunction with the officials of the Royal Society, to make next year's show, on the site of the Fisheries Exhibition, a thoroughly influential one, and un- like anything ever attempted before in Britain. If this sug- gestion were adopted, it would do more to popularise Eng- lish farming and educate the public as to the patience and skill of husbandmen than all the commissions of inquiry which have ever sat, or all the facts ever narrated in Blue Books. Were specimens of the agricultural produce of the earth exhibited and illustrated on the same lines as the Fisheries Exhibition, it would, interest all who have at heart the development of the productive power of the earth. The buildings are ready to hand; it only requires a little , exertion and some influence to make an Ir ternational Agri- cultural Show in London an unqualified success.—Farmer. SMALL TENANCIES.—Mr. C. H. Fox, of Gloucester, in a contemporary, gives the following Instances of successful small tenancies :—A—, a middle aged'aran with six chil- dren, has lived for nearly twenty years on the profits de- rived from 7 acres of land.VHe has regularly paid £3O a , year in rent, and the soil is of precisely the same value as his neighbour's Mr. Y., who pays £4OO for his farm of 400 acres. The children are decently clad, and his wife a tidy, respectable woman. Suppose this worthy man had been only charged a fair agricultural rental of £lO a year for his land, and had invested the £2O his landlord has received at 5 per cent, through these past years, a sum of over £650 would be awaiting the time when old age required providing for. No stinting of food has taken place in the household, and the head of the family has often wasted a few odd shillings on market days in unnecessary liquor. There is no reason to believe that security of tenure would make him any less inclined to improve the farm and work harder. The eldest son, a strong intelligent lad who can read and write capitally, would start with better chances than his father, who begun on the savings from 10s. a week, and he wonld be as well off on the fertile holding as in the shop- man's situation he covets. Poor old B— is, alas, nearly worn out with severe work, and his few pounds in the Savings Bank will not be sufficient to make him indepen- dent of parish relief, yet that man has toiled nobly and perseveringly all his life' and fed many of the community on the produce grown. During the last eight years, since he started farming on his own account, no less than £320 has been paid over to his landlord for less than 11 acres of ground. The difference between accommodation and agri- cultural rental would here again have provided something worth toiling for, would perhaps have saved the life of his overworked and care-worn wife, and the aged couple would have been able to hold up their heads to the last, free from the despised lot of a pauper. A strong horse, used by his master in hauling, ploughing, and other *field work on the farms of his fellows, has materially helped to provide the heavy annual pay- ments, and has at the same time been an important assist- ant on his own labd. C— is a young, sturdy fellow, the descendant of a yeoman family, known to the country-side for generations. The son of a younger branch of the tree, he had no inheritance but a stalwart frame, and thorough knowledge of his difficult trade. He and his strong, healthy young wife are at work early and late on their few acres, and keep a pretty cottage home with comparative ease; now both are active, and there are no children to absorb the woman's time. They grow about an acre of wheat, to pro- vide the wholesome home-made bread; an acre or two of potatoes, and other crops, such as barley, beans, and carrots, Ito feed the half-dozen pigs usually found in the sties. 1 These lively grunters are sold to be converted into the famous Wiltshire hams and bacon, while three-fourths of the cash received is paid for the right to cultivate this tiny spot of ground. The last case I will mention is that of the village tailor, who has saved enough money to make it pos- sible to farm 10 acres with his son's help, and a few pounds spent occasionally in labour. His crops were chiefly vegeo tables, such as peas and beans, which find their way long miles across country to the Bath and Trowbridge markets, and if exorbitant rent had not hampered this artisan's exer- tions, he would be, for his station, a wealthy man. Within a radius of three miles I could find twenty families living entirely, or almost entirely, from the profits of such farms as thee; and far from the system of spade husbandry , having been proved in England a failure, I consider these .

facts entitle one to say that, with security of tenure and a rental such as larger farmers are charged, they would ac- complish wonders. If Mr. Y., who finds it well•nigh im- possible to make both ends meet, could, by a judicious out- lay in labour and manure, and the most skilful,use of the best machinery, produce such a gross value per acre as hi despised competitors, £3,000 a year would represent his income.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Lord Mftyor is said to be writing an article on the Transvaal for one of the monthly reviews. At Hall, on Saturday, police-constable Gritnshaw, a detec- tive in the borough force, was sent to prison for 30 days for having stolen a bottle of claret from the cellar of premises while they were on fire.

A meeting of ironworkers at Stockton on Monday resolved that the sliding scale should be refused if the minimum rate of wages with an advance of 10 per cant, in poundage al- lowance were not conceded.

At a conference of Yorkshire miners, at Barnsley, on Monday, it was resolved that an application for a ten per cent, advance in wages should be made at once to every col- liery proprietor in the county. A boat containing six seamen was on Sunday coming ashore from the Royal yacht Royal George, in Portsmouth Harbour, when the boat was caught in a squall, an! cap- sized. Two of the men were drowned. _

At Birmingham, on Tuesday, a young man who gave his name as Henry Smith, but who would not state his place of residence, was committed for trial charged with stealing a nuraberof postal orders at suburban post offices. A MITNIFICINT GIFT.—It is announced that the late Mr. R. Newshans has bequeathed to the Corporation of Preston his fine collection of pictures, statuary and other works of art, the value of which is said to be ever .£60,000. In deciding an appeal from the County Court judge at Shoreditch. in which the General Omnibus Company were defendants, Mr. Justice Day and Mr. Justice A. L. Smith held that an omnibus conductor is not a " workman" within the meaning of the Employers' Liability Act. A man named James Wilson, aged 58, employed at the works of Messrs. W. Edelsten and Co., dyers, Sowerby Bridge, on Tuesday, fell into a vat of boiling dye. He was immediately rescued from his terrible position, but suc- cumbed to the injury received in about half an hour. On Tuesday, in the Queen's Bench Division, a motion was made for a mandamus calling upon the Justices of Bradford to hear a charge of assault against the master of a Board school who had detained a child for not having learned her "home lessons." A rule nisi was granted. At Croydon, on Wednesday, two Irishmen, named Connor and Sheaham, were fined £3B Bs. fot driving calves suffering from foot-and-mouth disease through the streets of Croydon, on the sth and 6th lusts. The calves were 75 in number, had been travelling from Cork, and had been all over the south of England.

510110175 ACCIDENT AT A FIRE.—An " escape " which was being taken to a fire at Oldham, on Wednesday morn- ing, struck a telegraph wire fixed across the street. The strain brought down a quantity of brickwork, which fell upon the people congregated to watch the fire. • Two men received dangerous injuries to the head and several others were cut by the dislodged masonry. CONFERENCE OF "CARDIES."—The cab trade had its con- ference in London last week. According to the statement of the chairman, the cabdrivers of the country are labouring under serious grievances, and it was decided to ask the Government to introduce next session a measure of oab law reform. Among other things the drivers seek protection against being cheated by "fares." DYNAMITE EXPLOSION.—A fatal dynamite explosion oc- eurred on Monday night at a pit connected with the Town- hill Coal Company, near Durnferline, under singular circum- stances. Four men werb employed in blastinc, operations, when one of them, lifting some charges of dynamite. for the purpose of using it, found it was frozen. He thereupon put the dynamite in a canister containing hot water. The result was that one man named Edward Hutcheson was blown to atoms, while others were knocked down and injured. An accident of such a nature has never been experienced in any mine working in the district. MINERS ENTOMBED.—On Tuesday evening a fire was dis- covered in one of the roadways of the Neville Hill Colliery, near Leeds. The miners had left their work, but four men were engaged in arranging the pit for the next day. They attempted to reach the fire, but were met by choke-damp and dense smoke. Two retreated, but the other men, named Hall and Roebuck, persisted in their attempt. Some time later their dead bodies were found in the roadway by an ex- ploring party, some members of which also suffered greatly from the damp. It is not known how the fire originated,. as the mine is a " safe " one, in which naked lights are used. LORD ABERDEEN AS Mn. GLADSTONE'S CAAORMAN.—A novel incident occurred at Hawarden Castle on Monday evening. The Premier, Mrs. Gladstone, and the Misses Gladstone were going to dine with Mr. and Mrs. Scott Bankes, Loughton Hall, Mold, where they were meeting the Duke and Duchess of Westminster. The Premier's coach- man was unable to drive owing to indisposition' but an able substitute was found in Lord Aberdeen. His lordship put on the coachman's attire, and drove the distinguished party to their destination, returning with the carriage to the Castle. The incident caused great amusement both at Lough ton Hall and Hawarden Castle.

1 EXECUTION OF OTONNELL.—OTOiIIieII, the murderer of James Ca- ey, was executed within Newgate Prison on Monday morning. Except that the doomed man's brother was in attendance outside the gaol, and that the crowd was somewhat larger than usual, the execution was similar in all respects to those that have preceded it. Binns was the executioner, and he did his duty efficiently, death being instantaneous. With the death of the misguided man, O'Donnell, it is to be hoped that the Phoenix Park tragedy has now passed into the region of history. Carey's fate has al least diverted attention from the other wtnesses in the trial of the Invincibles,"and these, being less obnoxious to Irishmen than Carey was, may be assumed to have suc- ceeded in hiding their identity in places wnere they are not likely to be traced by those hostile to them. THE Canis IN THE COTTON TRADE. An adjourned meeting of the Central Committee of the North and North- East Lancashire Cotton Spinners' and Manufacturers' As- sociation was held on Tuesday at Manchester. It was re- ported that since the last meeting of the committee the em- ployers in certain districts had met and pledged themselves to support the manufacturers of Blackburn, Darwen, and Padiham, by running their mills short•time. The Central Committee then passed a resolution affirming that the em- ployers of Blackburn, Darwen, and Padiham are entitled to the support of the trade, and recommending that short time be immediately adopted. The struggle now going on in the cotton trade affects 26,500 looms at Blackburn, 6,500 at Padiham, 4,500 at Darwen, 1,990 at Rarusbottom, and 5,830 at Oswaldtwistle. An appeal has been made by the Opera- tives' Central Committee for a subscription of 6d per loom per week from those working full time, and of 2d per loom from those working either three or four days per week. A TRAGIC AFFAIR.—A tragic affair occurred at Deptford the other day. A man named Walter John Waters, aged 28, of John-street, Battersea New Road, who had been living apart from his wife for about 18 months, wrote making an appointment to meet her in the New Cross Road for the pur- pose of effecting a reconciliation. After they met they visited a public-house, and then walked to the market gardens, through which the South-Eastern Railway passes. Waters seems to have drawn a pistol from his pocket and shot the woman in the neck. A man who happened to be passing heard the shot fired, and saw Waters making off. The in- jured woman was taken to the Seaman's Hospi al. At about 20 minutes past 10 o'clock the driver of an up train saw a man lying on the railway near the junction of the Greenwich and main South-Eastern lines. He reported the case to a signalman, who went to the spot, and found Waters lying bleeding from a terrible wound in the head, the result of a shot. He was conveyed to Gay's Hospital. It is believed that the wife will survive her injuries. Waters has been employed as n platelayer by the South-Western Railway Company. _ _

RENEWED POLICE PRECAUTIONS AT HAWARDEN.—Some startling rumours were created at Hawarslen on Tuesday by the renewal of the police precautions at the castle, which for some time past have been almost wholly suspended. Mr. Aplin, chief clerk of the Flintshire constabulary, accom- panied by two police officers, arrived at Queensferry by the 4-41 train on Monday afternoon, and at once drove up to the castle. They were followed by other officers who reached Queensferry by the 6-57 train, while the 9-27 train brought the chief constable of the county (Mr. P. Browne). Monday being the day of the execution of O'Donnell, the theory was soon got up that the Scotland-yard authorities had received information to the effect that the Invincibles had threatened to have their revenge on Mr. Gladstone or the Home Secretary. A little colour was lent to the sup- position by two facts—the first being that Sir William Har- court was daily expected at the castle; and the second, that Mr. Gladstone did not sleep at Hawarden on Monday night. As to the latter, the Premier was at Soughton Hall, en a visit to Mr. J. Scott-Bankes, chairman of the Flintshire Quarter Sessions, which did not terminate until about coon on Tuesday. Mr. Gladstone drove back from Soughton Hall in nn open phaeton, which was closely followed by a carriage containing Mr. Aplin, chief clerk of the Flintshire constabulary, and Police-officer Wright. 'Domino ON A SCOTCH MOOR.—lntelligence has reached Stornoway of the deaths, through exposure, of the three young men belonging to the township of Lionel, near the Butt of Lewis. on the moor between Stornoway and Ness. The deceased, whose names are Allan Campbell, James M'ltitchie, and Angus Morrison, went into Stornoway in connection with the purchasing of their discharge from the Rossshire Militia, of which they were members. On Tues- day afternoon in last week they left Stornoway to return home, and each carried a bottle of whisky. Accompanying them was a lad from Ness, named Alexander Gunn. When the four arrived at the Black Water Bridge on the road to Barras, about four miles from Stornoway, the deceased men made up their minds to proceed home by the moor, a dis- tance of about twenty miles, instead of round by the road, which was five miles longer. Gunn refused to accompany them, and returned to Stornoway. The night turned out very stormy, accompanied by hail showers and snow, and no more was heard of the three men. On Wednesday Gann returned home by the road, and on his arrival at Ness he ascertained that the other three had not returned. On Sunday the male population of the various villages at Ness turned out to search for the missing men. About two o'clock the searchers came upon the bodies of Campbell and Morrison, lying face downwards on the moor near a summer shealing about five miles south of Lionel. About three- quarters of a mile nearer Lionel the body of James M‘Ritchie was found. The deceased were from 1S to 20 years of age, and were unmarried.

--- WARRINGTON SAVI3ZITBANK, ANNUAL MEETING. • The 66th annLial meeting of the trustees and managers of the above instill:. lion was held at the Bank on Tuesday. Alderman Pickmere (Gitairman of the Trustees) presided, there being also present the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), Aldermen Holmes, Kean, WebstCr, Councillors Broadbent, Monks, Wallington, Woolfall, Messr.. Cruickshank, Darby- shire, Dobson, Finney, Hatton, H. N. Houghton, Jolley, Morris, J. R. Young, the Revs. J. G. Richards, J. Yonge, and Mr. John E. Davies (actuary). The Chairman read a letter of apology for non-attendance from Mr. Wm. Long, vice-chairman of the Trustees. THE COMMITTEE'S REPORT. The ACTUARY read the annual report of the Committes of Mabagement, as. follows : The Committee of Management have pleasure in submitting the general statement of the funds of the bank for the year ending 20th November, 1883. The total funds now amount to £2•81,642 Os. as under : With National Debt Commissioners— £ s. d. On General Account 278,864 14 8 On Separate Surplus Fund Account 7OO 0 0 And the Balance in the hands of the Trea- surer 2,077 14 4

2281,642 9 0 £7,293 7s 9d interest, and £l5 3s dividends on stock have been credited depositors during the year, and the total amount due to them is £279,560 15s sd, showing an increase of £5,939 12s sd. 735 new accounts have been opened, and 589 closed, showing an increase for the year of 146, The total number of depositors, including friendly and charitable societies and penny banks now is 9,058. 7,937 deposit; have been made during the year, and 5,437 payments. At the monthig meeting of the committee the accounts of the insti- iution have teen examined and found correct It is a pleasure to present so satisfactory a report, especially as to the number of a, ceunts ; the total number now being over nine thousand, showing that the institution is doing good work. No one knows better than those who have experienced it, how pleasant and easy it is to lead provident lives and save up for a rainy day; and the committee hope that the depositors will read this report and hand it over to some friend or neighbour with a word of encouragement to make a beginning. The money deposited is theirs, but in safe keeping, and always ready for them when wanted. T'oere are many now with large sums to their credit, who bless the day they started to save with a few pounds or a few shillings. Sums as low as one shilling are received, and children over seven years of age may themselves come to the bank and open ' accounts. Parents should encourage their children in provi- dent habits, and they cannot do better than send, and assist them, to deposit the:r savings. 4t becomes a habit to many ' and a pleasure to come to the bank, and no one can make a commencement too early in life. For those who oannot attend in the workint; hours of the day, the bank is open on Matufday evenings, and it is gratifying to see that the number availing themselves of this privilege are incressing.—F n. the Committee of Management.—JouN RICHARD PICKMERE, Chairman; WIL- LLAM LoNG, Vice-Chairman. 4th December, 18S3. The CHAIRMAN said he thought the meeting would agree with him that the report was a very satisfactory one and they were glad to see that the Bank went on encouragiegly to all parties connected with it. The amount of deposits seemed to increaee and the people who deposited appeared to have a great amount of confidence in the management of the Bank, and therefore it went on increasing. There was nothing new connected with the management to report, the business of the Bank going on as it was that time last year, and consequently he had nothing else to say on that subject, although he would be glad to answer any question that the gentlemen present might wish to ask concerning the affairs. He moved that the statement of accounts pre- prepared by the Actuary and examined by the accountant be approved; one copy of the accounts being transmitted to the National Debt Commissioners, and a duplicate copy be affixed in the Savings Bank.—Councillor MONKS seconded, and the report was unanimously adopted. SCHOOL CHILDREN AND THEIR SAVINGS: IMPORTANT TO PARENTS. Mr. JOLLEY said that as a member of the Finance Com- mittee he should like to make a remark with reference to a matter which had often been brought forward, viz., as to getting collectione from schools. He was glad to see a schoolmaster present that morning. He had been reading an account of what had been done in Manchester, where he found between 40 and 50 per cent. of the scholars sub- scribed to the Penny Savings Bank fund.—The CHAIRMAN supposed Mr. Jolley alluded to the pupils attending the Board Schools?—Mr. JOLLEY said that he did. The aver- age amount this year was 33 6d per head; last year he be- lieved it was 3s, showing that the matter was well taken up and was growing. He thought the present was a good oppor- tunity to ventilate the question; as he had said, it had often been discussed, but hitherto it had not borne any fruit, but perhaps by means of what he had stated it would be taken up in Warrington. He should ba glad if it could be. (Hear, hear.) They knew that the schools in their town were as well worked as any School Board establishments could possibly be, and if they undertook to rrork with the Bank they would be encouraging those saving habite among children, which they all wished to see. (Hear, hear.)—Councillor Monies observed that the same question had been brought under their notice before, but the great difficulty had been with the masters who did not care about the trouble such an undertaking would involve. They Warrington were in a different position to Manchester, which had a School Board who took the question up as a matter of thrift, but here it must of necessity be left to the individual school manager or master.—Mr. JOLLEY remarked that he was a school manager, and would not wish to force any- thing oil the master which would cause the latter greater trouble than he could well manage, but he thought there would be no harm in considering and discussing the subject. —The ClIA.uniAN We have no School Board, thank good- ness.—Alderman WEBSTER : I don't think the School Board have anything to do with it.—The CHAIRMAN continuing, observed he meant to say that probably a School Board would have better means of collecting the money than they in the voluntary schools in Warring Con. The masters had told them that what with new codes and so many changes being made in the work of education they had enough to do without entering Into a matter like the present. When everything was a little more ship-shape they might see their way to fall in with the suggestion—Aid. WEBSTER _remarked that with reference to Councillor Monks' observa- tions it was not that the masters objected to any trouble in the matter, but there were so many difficulties in the way. He had read the article in the Manchester Guardian on the subject, and it struck him as being a very useful thing, but he conceived at once that there were so many difficulties in the way of the Warrington schools carrying out the plan.— Councillor MONKS said there could be no doubt the question rested with the school-masters. Of course if the managers of schools took the matter up he was sure the committee of the Bank would do all they could to facilitate the collection of the money because after all they were constantly making a profit. This year they made a profit of £2OO on the working of the Bank, and they might as well spend that for the benefit of their own people of Warrington as to hand it over to the Commissioners.—The .CHAIRMAN said that as far as he could see the subject had been discussed fre- quently, and there was no doubt it rested with the masters of the schools to carry it out, and they would not be put to any considerable trouble thereby. Probably the master would collect the pence once a week, and the committee would send someone from that bank to the schoolmaster, and he would then have nothing to do but to count it over and get a receipt for it.—Rev. J. YONGE suggested that the matter should be referred from that meeting to the school managers of the town, as he thought by:that means Mr. Jolley's idea would have a practical solution. Ho would move a resolution to that effect.—Mr. D. W. FINNEY would be glad to second the proposition. He thought that was a most important discussion, and one which had occupied his mind considerably. He had often thought it over, and had felt sorry when he had seen children going with their pence to the sweet shop that there were no means—at least, no ready means—by which those children coulii, go and de- posit their pennies in some place where they could be taken care of instead of spending them at the sweet slop. He hoped he might be allowed te say on behalf of the teachers of the town that he was quite sure there was no disposition on the part of the teachers to shirk any responsibility that might be put upon them in this direction. (Hear, hear.) He considered that one of the most important things in the profession of a schoolmaster was to train up children to be thrifty, because they knew that if the founda- tion was laid they might expect trait hereafter. It was said "Train up a child in the way he should go, and he will not depart from it." He believed in that to a certain extent, for if they promoted such habits among children while they were young they would be thrifty when they became older ; and they would, then have less distress than at present among persons of advanced age. (Hear, hear.) He hoped any discussion of that kind might go forth to the public, and, if possible, be read by the poor people themselves, as it was that class they wanted to get at. He assured the meet- ing on behalf 'of the teachers, that they would be quite ready and willing to help as fa e as they could to carry out the objects of that important institution. He knew there were difficulties in the way, and he might say that in their con- nection with the Committee of Council on Education, in consequence of the frequent change of codes, Sm., they were often called upon to make returns to the Council and pre- pare them after school hours, and which prevented teachers taking up these subjects as they ought to do and as they would wish to do. (Hear, hear.)—Councillor MONKS thought if they entertained the matter that there should be a conference of school managers with the Com- mittee of the Bank, and try to establish some system upon which to work.—Mr. FINNEY considered it would be very easy if the school teachers col- lected the pence from the scholars and an officer of the bank came to collect it.—Alderman KEAN suggested that the Sunday schools should be included.—The MAYOR pointed , out that the Board schools had no Sunday schools. Chil- dren attending a Sunday school had, generally speaking,l some little gift presented by their parent for good conduct or something of the kind, and those pence they might have, on Sunday would then be more easily collected than on a week-day. It was therefore important that they should in- clude Sunday schools. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. J. Yonge's resolution, which was subsequently carried, was as follows: —" That this meeting recommends the Committee of Management to take into early consideration the subject of making arrangements with the managers and teachers of day and Sunday schools in this town for the collection of pence from the scholars in order further to encourage the practice of thrift amongst the young." VOTES OF THANKS AND ELECTION OF COMMITTEE, &O. The MAYOR had great pleasure in moving "That the report of the committee of management is approved, and 'this meeting acknowledges the valuable services rendered to the institution by the gentlemen on the committee duringl the past year, and 'tenders its best thanks to them." As a , former member of the committee he could testify to the attention and care displayed in the preparation of the accounts, and the voluminous figures which bad been read by the actuary must show that the duties of the Committee of Accounts were by no means of a light character. (Hear,

hear.)— Alderman HOLMES seconded the resolution, which I was carried unanimously.—Councillor BROADBENT then proposed "That J. R. Pickmere, Eq., be elected chairman, and William Long, Esq., vice-chairman for next year.;'— This was seconded by Alderman KEAN, and carried nem ;con.—The CHAIRMAN said that as far as he was concerned , what little duties he had to perform—they were very im- portant certainly—he did with a great deal of pleasure. He , always kept his eyes on the affairs of the bank as much as he possibly could. He thought they had some very good ' officers connected with the bank, and the public might thoroughly put their trust in whatever was done there. Mr. Long also took a very great interest in the institution, and would have said the same if he had been present. (Hear, hear.)—Alderman WEBSTER moved that the following gentlemen be requested to become the Committee of Management for the ensuing year :—Trustee: the chairman, vice-chairman, and Messrs. S. Rigby, F. Monks, John White, Joseph Davies; managers: The Mayor of Warrington, Messrs. Jolley, Woolfall, IV, Owen, junr., S. Lees, J. Smethurst, J. R. Young, J. Morris, Darbyshire, Rev. J. Yonge, and the Rev. J. Kenworthy.—On the proposition, of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman WEBSTER, the name of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., was aided to the list of tills- tees.—A hearty vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding. that day and for his assistance to the bank having been accorded on the proposition of Councillor WOOLFALL, seconded by the MAYOR, the meeting separated.

POLEFICAL. MR. JOSEPH ARCH AT NOTTINGRAM.—Mr. Joseph Arch, speaking at Nottingham on Tuesday night, said he had collected £2,000 to teach the agricultural labourers to hISISt upon compulsory cultivation of land. He said that if ever the people came into collision with the Throne, it would be through the madness and inconsistency of the House of Lords.

THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.—A meeting of the General Committee of the National Liberal Federation was held at Birmingham on Monday. A resolution was adopted in favour of the appointment of a special committee to consider and report upon the question of rediatribution, with regard to the principle upon which a measure for that purpose should be based. The mooting also passed a resolu- tion in favour of the extension of the Corrupt Practices Act, and, having regard to the approach of another general elec- tion, expressed the opinion that such extension should take place in the coming session. A third resolution was adopted declaring that the present arrangements with regard to the hours of polling both at Parliamentary and municipal elec- tions tend- to deprive large numbers of electors of the oppor- tunity of exercising their electoral rights; that the injustice thus inflicted upon the working classes will be greatly in- creased by the operation of the new law with regard to con- veyance of voters; and that the hours of polling should be extended until at least eight pm., such extension to be fixed by legislation and not determined by the returning officer or the local authorities.

LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL ON EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS.—.- Lord Randolph Churchill, addressing the Edinburgh Con- servative Association on Tuesday night, made a long speech on Egyptian affairs. He accused the Government of having given false information to the people of this coun`ry about our interference in Egypt, and said that we had flung back the Egyptians to the toils of their Jewish taskmasters. He held that the Govermatent by taking the side of Tewfik against Arabi had committed a great crime. Tewfik was one of the most despicable wretches who ever occupied an eastern throne, and was personally responsible for the mas- sacres at Alexandria; while* Arabi was the leader of the national movement and the exponent of a nation's wrongs. Mr. Gladstone by his action had given three fatal blows' to commerce between Europe and the East. All that we hasl done for the Egyptians was to present them with a dozen doctors and a dozen Dutch judges and increased the Egyp- tian debt by six millions. What he (Lord Randolph) would advocate was the expulsion of Tewfik, the recall of the exiles from Ceylon, the restitution of the national party, and the institution of a government with a prince at its head who should ba enlightened and just. The question of, Conservative and Liberal finance is dealt with by Sir Stafford Northcote in an article which is to appear in the forthcoming number of the National Review. The right hon. gentleman examines the points in dispute at great length, and he lays down these propositions, that the assertion that expenditure is always high under a Conservative, and low under a Liberal Government, is not true; that in some of its most important branches the in- crease in our expenditure has been inevitable, and must have taken place under any administration; that where the increase has been optional it has been incurred for adequate objects, and has been productive of substantial results well worth the cost incurred ; and finally he challenges com- parison between the. optional expenditure of the Conserva- tives and that ortheir Liberal successors. Sir Stafford, at the close of his arguments, claims to have proved that the Conservatives spent less than the Liberals; that if there was any extravagance on the part of the Conservative Government there has been at least equal extravagance on the part of the Liberal Government; and that, if the ex penditure of the latter has been no more than was reason- able, it is fair to claim a similar admission with regard to he earlier.

SIR CHARLES DILKE AT BIRMINGHAM. Sir Charles Dilke on Monday night delivered to a crowded audience, in the Birmingham Town Hall, his address as President of the Junior Liberal Association. He said that Parliament might be expected next session to deal with the extension of the franchise, the reform of London gcvernment and county government, as well as with minor measures for ex- tending the hours of polling and dealing with the City guilds, which latter measure might be introduced in the House of Lords. The passing of an equal franchise for England and Scotland, if coupled with the retention of the present high frauchise in Ireland, would give fresh life to the sep tratist agitation. This Parliament might before its dissolutien do good work, after th,e passing of the franchise bill, in reforming local government. Not only county councils should be appointed, but •also district councils to remove overlapping and conflicting jurisdictions. He in- tended, in the hope of improving the homes of the poor, to put the tenement provisions of the Act of last year in force. He did not know whether the Tories proposed to op- pose the Government's three great measures on principle, or to encourage Lord Salisbury to destroy them in the Upper House; but if the Liberals stood firm, not only these, but smaller measures which would call the householders of the three kingdoms into full citizenship, would pass during the life of the present Government.—Mr. Chamberlain also spoke. MR. BRIGHT AND Mn. CHILDERS ON POLITICAL AFFAIRS.—Mr. Bright and the Chancellor of the Exchequer (Mr. Childers) addressed a large assemblage in front of Gawthorpe Hall, the residence of Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttle- worth, on Tuesday morning. Mr. Bright claimed that during the last 40 years he htd been actuated by a desire to pro- mote what he believed to be justice and right. Since the last R2form Bill he believed there had been more done in this country in the direction of justice and right than had been done in any other country in the same time. This was done without shedding a drop of the country's blood, and it tended to uniteiclass and class in a manner unknown before. Referring taf the corn laws, the right lion, gentle- man said it was amazing that in a country like this there should have been a law that denied the great mass the right to import food from any part of the world where Providence had allowed it to be grown. With regard to the franchise, he expressed the belief that every householder within the next twelve months would be a voter. He believed the present Govern- ment was the most intelligent and most conscientious and honest Administration the country had ever known. Not- withstanding the commercial depression now prevailing in the country he looked ,hopefully to the future.—Mr. Chil- ders said he knew of no greater honour than to be attached, as he had been for many years, in the bonds of political hard work to such a man as Mr. Gladstone. He believed the franchise would be extended to the whole of the work- ing classes during the coming session. There was a great deal before them to be done, but the Govenment hoped to receive the support of the people in doing it.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

WALKS.—These, when well made, add beauty to a garden as well as yielding pleasure and comfort to the owner. An essential condition of a walk is that it should be dry enough to walk upon in the rainiest of weather, and to secure this the drainage must be perfect. The bed of the walk should be taken out 9in, deep, leaving the foundation slightly con- vex, so that the water may fail to either side and ensure a dry centre, for it is obvious that if water laid under the middle it would act mischievously on its surface and at a j point where there is the most traffic. Every ten yards in length there should be a receptacle for the water made by placing three or four courses of bricks (without mortar) in the form of a square, drawing each course inward, so that there may be an aperture of 4in. to 6in. at the top to place a grating upon, to prevent solid substances flowing in and obstructing the free passage of water. It is not absolutely necessary that these ." traps," as they are usually termed, should be wider at the base than at the apex, and it is only resorted to where the subsoil is tenacious or the walk on a declivity, for the purpose of securing more capacious lodge- ment for the water as' well as a more extensive area to escape. In large,gardens these traps are connected with a row of land drain pipes on either side, and the traps are made on opposite sides and connected by ,pipes across the walks; but as the cottager is nnt likely to require any drains, we will not enter into any further details. The first layer of six inches forming the walk should consist of stones, broken bricks, or clinkers, the largest pieces being placed at the bottom and graduating till the uppermost are not larger than a bantam's egg. The remaining three inches may be either gravel or cinders, whichever is most accessible. The width of a walk should be taken into con- sideration ; if too wide much ground is wasted, and if too narrow considerable inconvenience is frequently experienced, especially when one is proceeding with a wheelbarrow and another person coming from the opposite direction; to pass by necessitates the placing of the feet on the soil by one or the other. A width of 2ft. 6in. would obviate that. Where the garden is so small as not to allow this width, we would make a recess about midway. This may appear a small matter, but we feel sure it will save many a footmark on the soil, and maybe on a batch of emerging tender seedlings. For the purpose of defining the outline of walks, sundry materials are in use, which may be classified as living and dead edging. Of the first, box is mostly used, and occa- sionally the thrift plant, and the only objection to them is that the first requires replacing frequently in the neigh- bourhood of towns or smoky districts, and both form a harbour for vermin, which is not the case with dead edging or such things as the blue Staffordshire tiles, stones, bricks on edge slightly sloping to the walk, large clinkers, or 6in. boards nailed to supports driven into the ground the depth of one foot. The boards should be nailed on the side next the walk, and appear about four inches above its level, and if fixed before the walk is completed, the remaining two inches can be hid more readily. The first of these materials is decidedly the best, but their cost places them beyond the reach of many cottagers. They shopld therefore select the most comeatable of the others.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Why the Chrysanthemum is not oftener seen in the front garden we cannot .understand. They have flowered well with us this season, and some pre- sentable blooms could be culled at the present time, and by making a selection of varieties they may be had in flower as early as August. They are adapted to plant against the dwelling or a fence having a south aspect, and give very little trouble to keep in order. A couple of nails—one on each side,—with a piece of string attached from one to the other, is generally found sufficient to prevent injury from winds. In such a position they can be protected from early frosts by suspending some protecting material in front, for it occurs occasionally that a night or two of frost during October or early in November will work more mischief than all the frost from that time to Christmas.

CREEPEns.—Resumineour notes on the representatives of this class of plants, such as are suitable for covering our dwellings, we would draw our readers' attention to the Vir- ginian Creepers, as well as a small variety called Veitch's, or Ampelopsis Veitchii. They are both deciduous, but the colour of their foliage in early autumn reminds one of the beautiful hues we have recently witnessed in the skies. There is a nice plant of Veitchii to be seen growing against the residence of the Superintendent of the Parks in this town. It is interesting to watch the tenacity with which this clings to the walls of buildings, surpassing the ivy in this respect. THE WINDONV.—Musk: This is frequently left in the window for weeks after the tops have entirely died down. It requires no such harbour, for the plant is perfectly hardy, and should, therefore, be turned out into the garden, and the pot plunged in the ground three or four inches ; and, as many have windows but no gardens, they can adopt the lat- ter method in a corner of the back yard, and, for the sake of neatness, they can use a box or an old hamper to hold the plants and ashes. When we advise plants that are hardy to be thus protected, the object is to protect them from fluctuations of temperature, for it is evident that a plant in a pot above-ground is more liable to these than a plant that has its roots buried in the soil. In frosty weather the soil in a pot expands if unprotected, and the pot bursts, rhich is another reason why-gardeners plunge their pots.
WINSFORD SALT TRADE AND . SUBSIDENCES.

Considerable interest is attached to the production of salt just now, since the brine supply- in the Weaver Valley has so sensibly decreased, owing to the vast amount used up to this year. For months back the yield has been greatly below the average at many of the works ; or, to put it another way, the demand for salt has risen now, and its production has not kept pace with the markets, or even been ahead of them, as last year, till the latter were getting glutted. One result of this was to lower the price of salt, and a tendercy in the salt proprietors to meet this and make the best bargains they could, to the neglect of the Union or Salt Chamber; which has in consequence been bwken up. The fair average demand for the past month has kept stocks at the low point, which they have main- tained during the whole summer end autumn, eepecially as there is no alteration yet in the brine supply, if we except what is thought to be an accidental rise, of which notice will be taken further on. Hence many pans still remain stopped for the want of brine, and many of tha salt boilers have nothing to do, or very little at best. There is no material alteration to notice in the price quotations, if any- thing they are easier, as will be seen by the annexed list : Runcorn and Weston shipments are is per ton less than at Liverpool. Total from Mersey 82723 76179 The rise referred to above, which took place in several of the shafts at the works during the preceding week, and which has maintained itself at three feet or so, may be traced to the subsidence at Marton, where the great land- slip took place several years ago, and at which other smaller subsiderces have continued occurring from time to time. Last week a much greater one took place. What at first seemed an awful chasm now looks much more so. And the many thousands of tons which fell in last had the effect of sensibly stirring the brine in most shafts, indicating the probable flow of brine from the west or Delamere Forest way. If the rock head is there, and the outcrop of the salt is toward Etldisbury Hills, the flow may come from Oak- mere, which receives but never seems the fuller for what it gets. Indeed there has been a surface diversion of the brine, for the will at Bradford, near Winsford, has been grinding corn with brine instead of water, as if the ordinary channel was insufficient for the augmented supply caused by the fall of such a volume of earth. It must, however, be something like a safety valve to Winsford and Northwich, the depres- sions or landslips which eceur so freely between New Bridge, the northerly works of Winsford, and Oakmere, or to limit it to a smaller area, say between New Bridge and New Church Common. Anyhow we have seen fewer of the changes in the houses and streets while these landslips have been progressing so largely. It may be that a more uniform depression has been going on at the same period if only levellings had been taken.
The heart causes us to do stupid things; the head makes us avoid them.

div.head: LANCASHIRE-IRON AND COAL
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE-IRON AND COAL
TRADE.

There has been very--lit-t-l-e—d—oing in the iron market ; prices have been scarcely tested, but nominally they are without quotable alteration. The downward movement in outside brands of pig iron, such as Scotch and Middles- borough, does not appear to have any material effect upon the local and district makers. North country iron can now be bought at about 44s 101 net cash for foundry brands de- livered equal to Manchester, and Scotch iron continues to be offered at under makers' prices; but for Lancashire and Lincolnshire brands makers still bold firmly for late ratcs. Except for forge iron there is little or no inquiry, but busi- ness could be done in forge at about Oct under makers' rates. For local branda, however, makers hold to 455; Lincolnshire makers still decline to take under 44s 10d to' 45s 10d. less 2/, for forge and foundry delivered equal to Manchester, and it is only in very exceptional cases that buyers are able to place orders at under nese figures. The finished iron trade is quiet, with prices for delivery into the Manchester dis- trict averaging £6 to £6 23 61 for bars, £6 78 61 to £6 108 for hoops, and £7 15s per ton for sheets.— The pressure brought upon the coal market by the recent threatened strike has not entirely disappeared, but there is still a fair trade doing for the time of the year. The present output of the pits is going away., with stocks in some cases still being filled up to meet requirements. The better classes of round coal are moving off freely for house-fire purposes, and common round coals suitable. for furnace purposes, are in good demand. Engine fuel, however, shows rather a tendency to hang in the market, with supplies of slack again getting somewhat plentiful. This, to some extent, may be due to the unsettled state of the cotton trade; but it is pro- bably chiefly owing to consumers of this class of fuel hav- ing bought in largely in anticipation of the strike. Some giving way has been necessary upon the full extent of the advance in pit prices put on in the West Lancashire dis- tricts at the commencement of the month, but generally pit prices are steady at about lOs 61 for best coals; fis 6d for seconds; 7s to 7s 61 for common house-fire coals; Os to 6s 61 for steam coals; 4s ed to 58 for burgy ; 3s 9d to 4531 for good qualities of slack; and about 38 to 3s 6d.for inferior sorts. For shipment there is a moderate business doing, with Lancashire steam coal averaging about 88 61 per ton delivered at Garaton or Liverpool.
