"Every moment." "I wish f had lots of gold," said Minnie, biting a piece of "Oh, Minnie !" cried the young man bitterly, as he paced thread in two. "If I had I'd take my dear old father down up and down. to the sea-side, and he should have a carriage, and be driven "Why, Frank," she cried, looking up, "you're jealous." about, and get well and strong again; that's what I'd do "Jealous !" he sail, in a tone of contempt. "Not I." with gold." "Oh, Frank !" she said, crossly. "No geld would make me well and strong again, my dar- "Well, then, I am," he said. "Isn't it enough to make a ling," said the old man sadly. "The machine's nearly worn man jealous, to know that that fellow—l can't call him a not, and I sometimes think that if it weren't for you, my gentleman—has been here talking to you?" dear, I should be bett r put away altogether." ' "No! Not nearly enough," she said, stitching away "Oh, father, father!" cried Minnie, throwing her work rapidly, her needle keeping pace with her emotions. "Why, aside and running to clasp her soft little arms round his Frank, if I saw you talking to Miss Lofty Morris, I shouldn't neck, "don't, don't, pray don't talk like that," be jealous in the least." "Well, well, well, my darling, I won't if it troubles "Miss Lotty is a sweet, good, young lady." you; bat it mast come some day, Minnie • and if I could "Well, isn't Mr. Ezra a sweet, good young gentleman ? " see you happily married and comfortable, I'm in that state Frank Lawrence stooped and gazed down at Minnie, half uf misery sometimes that I think I should be glad to go to wonderingly; and as she looked up at him with her pretty, sleep." provokingly arch face, his anger passed away, and he dropped upon his knees beside her, catching her hands in his, and saying— " Minnie, darling, I wish I could say he was ; and it hurts me to know that he is here with you. If it had been his brother, I should not have said a word. Mr. Ned's a true, frank, honest gentleman. Don't be hard, upon me, Minnie, for it hurts me more than I can tell you." "My own Frank," she cried, with a sob; and she flung her arms ro'und his neck; "what a dear, good, loving, doubting fellow it is. There,. that'll do, for I must work, and work bard, at Miss Lotty's dress. Get up." "One kiss more, then, and I will," he whispered. "Just one, then," said Minnie; and "Just one" was taken before Frank leaped up once more. " Now,l'm going to lecture you, sir," said Minnie, making threatening motions with the needle, as she went on worli- ing. "As I said before, I should not have been cross if I had seen you talking to Miss Lotty, or any young lady, and I'll tell you, Frank, it hurts me, too, to think that you have not more confidence and trust in me." "Forgive me, darling," he said; "and in future I always will have. "Please do, Frank," she said ; and her bright, merry way passed off to leave her eyes suffused with tears. " You may, Frank, you may trust me, indeed. If lam to be your little wife—and a very poor, helpless little wife I shall make." "Not you Minnie." " Ah, butl shall," she said sadly. "A good daughter makes a good wife," he said tenderly.; "and I know what a good daughter you have been?' "Say, 'tried to be,' Frank, dear. But you must have con- fidence in me, please, and trust me." "Yes, yes, and I will," be said, bending over the back of her chair, so that he could rest his cheek upon her glossy little head. "I can't help Mr. Ezra coming here, and more than once he has tried to talk nonsense to me." "He has!" cried Frank, starting up furiously; "a scoun- drel!

"Father ! " "Well, well, I won't go. I'll stop and worry you as long ae I can. Is Frank coining to-night ? " "Yes, dear," said Minnie, blushing, as she went back to her seat, and resumel her work. Ah, he's a nice lad. I like Frank. When's it going to be, Minnie ? " "When's what going to be, father?" said Minnie, pouting, as she turned away her head. "When are you going to be married? There, you needn't "turn red. There's nothing to be ashamed of in marrying, my dear, I wish I'd married when I was thirty, instead of waiting till I was fifty." "Oh, I don't know, father. Some day, perhaps." "I should like it to be soon, my dear," said the old man —" soon. I should like to feel that you'd got some one to take care of you when—when I'm gone.' " Ah, father dear, don't talk like that," cried Minnie. "No, no: I won't, I won't. And so you don't think there's any harm in Ned's young lady ? " " Harm ! No, father. She's one of the sweetest and nicest of girls." "But she seems giddy for a young lady, Minnie." "Yes, father; that's it ; she seems giddy, but you know it's like this—her aunt—Miss Mosterly, is so hard and cold and strict with her, that after being kept down so long, bent like a piece of whalebone in a drese, she springs up directly she is let loose, and seems giddy." "Oh, that's it, is it? said the old man, nodding his head. "Yes, that's it, dear." " Humph ! I'm glad of it. You'd know, Minnie; be- cause you are such a clever one at seeing things. Well, I'm glad of it, for Mr. Ned's sake. I'm very fond of Mr. Ned, Minnie." "I know you are father; and he is very nice and merry always. Do you know, though he is engaged to be married to Miss Lotty, her aunt will only let him see her once a week."

"Nonsense, Frank." "How dare he!" said the young man. "I hate him and his overbearing ways. It makes me half mad. What did he say?" Nothing worth repeating, Frank, dear—nothing that need trouble you, for I look upon it as what I say—Non- sense, not worth a thought. And now I'm sure you ought to be back. Oh, how ,silly we are. You came for the pocket-book." She leaped up and took it from out of an old coat hang- ing behind the door. "Yes, I'll run back with it," he said. "I shall come in again this evening to ask pardon again." "No, Frank, dear," she said softly; "please don't." "Not come ?" he sad, his countenance falling. "No, I don't mean that; don't ask pardon again. Why should you ask pardon for leaving me so early ?" "Not for that, dear, hut for doubting you," he said humbly. "That's all forgotten now," she said, placing her,little white hand in his. "Now, goodbye." Frank Laavrence raised the little hand to his lips, and kissed it reverently, lowered it, and raised it again, kissed it once more, and then hurried away. "Dear Frank," said Minnie, softly. "What a brave, true fellow he is; and how proud I ought to be to have won his love." She worked on diligently for the next hour, thinking very deeply about Ezra Anson and what it was her duty to do under the circumstances. Little, light-hearted lady as she was, self-reliant from her long battle with the world as her father's housekeeper, she felt not the slightest fear of the Tonna.b fellow or his advances; but they troubled her a great deal on Frank's account. Certainly Ezra Anson was not Frank's master, but the Young man was beginning to have a great deal of influence in the business; and the possibility of a quarrel between them was always to the fore. This would be most serious, for a post in Anson's firm meant a post for life, with steady increase ef remuneration, and good treatment to the end. "I must laugh it off," said Minnie at last with a sigh. "I won't bother psor father about it. Yes, I'll laugh at if. all, and he'll fancy some one else soon, and forget all abon poor little me."

"Why not ?" "Because she says it is not proper. Miss Lottie told me so herself, and cried about it when I tried on this dress." Ah, gentle-people's ways ain't our ways, Minnie. and I daresay Miss Mosterly's right. I shall only let Frank come and see you once a week." "Oh, father dear !" cried Minnie, dropping her work. "What a shame! You're teasing me," she continued, taking up the work again, as she heard the Old man chuckling. "There, if I talk so I shall never get done." "That's a pretty dress, though, my dear." " Yes, isn't it, father? and it's to have a great wreath of holly leaves and berries sloped right acrosss the front." "Be very prickly, wona it, Minnie ?" "Why, nt, of course not; it will all be artificial. And I say, father, this dress is all being made on the sly." "On the sly ?" "Well, I didn't like to refuse to make it when Miss Lotty came with Mr. Ned; bat she said her aant mustn't know, • and I was not to send it homi." "But why not?" "Because it's a ball dress, don't you see, and her aunt don't approve ef dancing." Ah ?" said the old man, "I see. Come in!" he added, as there was a sharp tapping at the door, which was opened on the instant, and a tall, dark, handsome young fellow came doffing his glossy hat in rathera n impressive manner to Minnie, who rose quickly, curtysed clumsily, and then sat down again and blushed warmly as she hurried on with her work. "How do, Walters?".., "How do, Mr. Ezra? Nice day, sir." " Lovely ; bat look hero; my father says can you make it convenient to go on, as he wants to go out." "Yes, sir; of course, of course," said the old man rising slowly. "He wants you to see to the packing of those things for India. He don't like to leave it to the other men." "No, sir, of course not. I'll go on at once. Coming, Mr. Ezra ?" "No, Walters, I'm going on to the Park. I'll just light my cigar, though, first." "Yes, '• do sir, do. Give Mr. Ezra the matches, my dear," i the old man, gqing out. " I'll get back, my dear, as soo y can." As iler.r closed an uneasy look came over Minnie's face, but B: rose with alacrity, took a box of matches from the chim&Ley-piece, and prepared to strike a light. " WhyWou're not ready, sir," she said, gently. " Not ready, Ninnie," he cried, catching her hand in his. " Oh, yes, lam ready to tell you how I love you—to run away with you—to buy you horses and carriages and jewels, and everything you like. What a beautiful little witch you are." "I'm not a witch, Mr. Ezra," said Minnie, extricating her hand; "and I don't want to be run away with;' and horses and carriages and jewels would be' no use to me." Don't talk like that, Minnie," he cried," when you know how I love you. What a cruel little thing it is. Ah ! What are you doing?" "Did it barn you, Mr. Ezra? Oh, I am sorry," cried Minnie; for as the young man tried again to seize her hand she struck a match afresh, and turned it so that it touched his fingers. "Bum me? Why you know it did. You did it on pur- pose. Ah, Minnie, Minnie, why do you play with me like this?" "Why do you talk nonsense to me, sir, like this ?" "Because I love you." ".Then you ought not to, sir. your equal." CHAPTER 111. NED'S MESSAGE. " Get's very cold, Minnie, my girl, or else it's my poor old bones," said old Tom Walters, as he sat cowering near the tire. "I can't keep warm, my dear." "You must be extravagant, father, and poke and stoke," said Minnie merrily. "Young bones feel it, and fingers too. Look at my hands." She held out her red fingers towards him. " It't setting in cold as cold," she said; " and we're going to have a very sharp Christmas." " Ah, yes, a regular nipper," ha said, nodding, as he cowered over the fire. "Hard times for the poor folks out of work. Frank been to-day, my dear ?" "No, father, not yet. He's coming in this afternoon, he

said." " liah, yes. I shan't go down to the house to-day. They don't want me. Nearly done Miss Lotty's dress ?" "Very nearly father." " Ah, I suppose it's for Christmas parties and junket- tinge." "I don't think it will be worn much, father, unless Miss Lotty goes away." "Goes away? Ah, yes, Mr. Ned goes away directly. Sails on Boxing Day, I suppose. Rough life a sailor's, Minnie, very rough life; but he seems to like it. I'm glad Frank isn't a sailor." "So am I dear." " Ah, yes ; Christmas again," said the old man • "this makes seventy-one Christmases I've seen, Minnie, and lately I've always been wandering whether I should see any more. We must have Frank to dinner on Christmas Day, my dear, if he'll come. Think he will ?" The old man looked smilingly round at Minnie, who was busily sewing artificial sprigs of dark green holly upon the dress, and holding them out at arm's length from time to time to watch the effect. "Oh, yes, father, he'll came," she said, nodding her head, with her lips full of pins. "Yes, yes, he'll come, 4.1 d we mit hive a bit of a feast Minnie. I'll give you something extra, my dear—some- thino., I've saved up." "No, father," said Minnie, importantly, "I'm going to provide the feast myself, out of my own savings, so I shall not come to you." " Well, well," said the old man, "just as you like, my dear; just as you like ;" and he sat thoughtfully by the fire, hour after hour, till evening, when he rose. "To-morrow's Christmas Eve, Minnie, and I shan't go out then; so I think I'll go out for an hour to-night, and smoke a pipe with old Sam Kerridge. I shan't be very long, my dear. You won't mind being alone ?" "Oh, no, dear; and besides, I want to be alone; Frank is sure to come in." "Yes, yes, to be sure," said the old man. " Of course ;" and stooping down to kiss Minnie, he tied his wrapper round his neck, his child being ready directly after to help him on with his great coat. "I won't he late, Minnie; I won't be late." T le old man had hardly been gone five minutes' when theo was a sharp rap at the door, and Minnie started in her sear, turning red and white in turn. "It's that Mr. Ezra," she exclaimed, trembling. "Pooh ! what a little coward I am to be afraiii ol him. What should

this." • "But it must be of use." No, sir, it must not," stid Minnie, striking another match. "Then there is a reason," cried the young man, stamping his foot angrily. "You think you love somebody else." "Do I, sir ?" said Minnie quietly, striking another match, letting it burn, and then throwing it in the fire. "Yes. I tee through it all. It is that scoundrel of a brother of mine." "I don't think Mr. Edward would like to bear you call him a scoundrel, Mr. Ezra; and he always behaved to me with the greatest respect." " Respect? why I offer you love." "What some men call love, Mr. Ezra, air," said Minnie, with quiet good tempered firmness. "Ain't you ready for a light ?" 'Light! no, you beautiful little thing. Why, Minnie, I've loved you over since I was quite a boy. How can you be so cruel to me?" "I'm not cruel to you, sir. You're cruel to yourself. \I ill you please take a light, sir? I want to go on with my work." As she ipcke she mtde a movement towards the table. Is that pretty dress for you, Minnie ?" he said eagerly. "For me? No, sir. What nonsense! Why it is for-- a young litdy." "I thought it was for you, Minnie," he exclaimed. "Listen to me, and you shall lrave better dresses than that —as many as you like." "Please, sir, I don't want any," slid Minnie. "Then what is the reason that you treat rue like this ?" he said bitterly. "There is reason, is there not?" Minnie did not answer, for just then there came a qaick tap at the door; the handle was turned, and a sturdy, curly- haired young man, with dark-grey eyes and thorough Eng.

I be?" and rising Iron her sect, she trossed the room and opened the der. "Ship ahoy, there! What cheer ?" cried the visitor, com- ing into the room with a rush, his brown face full of anima- tion, eted his whole manner breezy of the sea. " Hilli-ho, little Minnie. Why, how pretty you look. Here give ale a "Oh Mr. Ned," cried Minnie, drawing back. "Quite right, little one ; quite right. I always forget myself. I'm engaged and mustn't do such things. I say, how's Franky ?" "Quite well, Mr. Ned; he is coming presently." "Is ? ,Then I must be off. I say, don't be offended. It's a way Sailors have." "And a very rude way, too," said Minnie, laughing. "So it is, little one; but it's the salt water does it. Now I say—let me see—l musn't forget! Ah, all right; I've come about Miss Morris's dress." "Here it is, Mr. Ned," cried Minnie, taking it up deftly, as only dressmakers and lady's-maids can, and holding it before her, so as to display its sheeny folds. "Phee-ew ! " whistled Ned Anson, junior lieutenant in Her Majesty's Navy. "What a spanker; just the thing for the ball. Look here, Minnie, this is the style." Before Minnie knew what he was going to do, he had caught her•round the waist, and whisked her about the room in a waltz, to which his lips were the orchestra. "Mr. Ned—Mr. Ned! Pray pray!" cried Minnie. "The dress—the dress." " Murder ! " he cried; "have I done any harm?" and he loosed her to gather up the dreiss and examine it. "Only knocked one holly spray off," said Minnie, pasting with the exercise. "Tot, tut, tut? What a pity! Here, I'd better give my message and go. Been here five minutes, and in mischief twice.' "Have you a message for me, then, Mr. Ned ? " "To be sure I have; from Miss Morria—Lotty, you know." "Anything about the drew, Mr. Ned ?" " Yes; she wants it to-morrow night." "To-morrow night, Mr. Ned?" cried Minnie. "Yee, without fail. She's going with me to a bell. Christmas Eve, you know." " Well, I'll get it done, Mr. Ned." "That's right. And look here. She wants yoa to take the frock and dress her, so as to get her quite taut." "Down to Clapham, Mr. Ned? Well, yes, I'll do that. I could go by rail." "No' no, not to Clapham ; to Richmond. To the Thistle, where the ball is. you know." " Ah," said Minnie, "I see." ale" Look here; Lotter has planned it all. You are to be ready with all the fal-de-rals in a box. Then I'm going to drive you down to Clapham, pick up Lotty, and drive you both down to Richmond. There you'll dress her, and I've arrangea that you can see the ball and the cempany. See the dresses, you know." "But how, Mr. Ned? I can't go to a ball." "You're to be in the tea-room till the dance is over. Then you help Lotty to change her dress again, and I drive you both back, drop her at Clapham, and bring you home. That's all. Good idea, isn't it ?" "Oh, but, Mr. Ned, I should be out all night." "Of course you would; but what of that? I'm often up all night at sea, when I have the watch." "Oh, but, Mr. Ned, I couldn't go." "Nonsense, little one! Why not ?" "I don't think I should like to do such a thing." "Why what stuff! Look here; I'll take all the care of you that I would of my own sister, if I'd got one." "Yee, Mr. Ned,'l know you would, bat----" "Oh, lor ! now she's beginning to but. I say, Minnie, little one, don't spoil our fun. You know how seldom Lottie gets out." "Yes, Mr. Ned, buf—M" "But again, you wicked little spell-sport. Oh, holv can such a pretty little girl be so hard ? ' "Pm not afraid, Mr. Ned; but I want to do what's eight." "Of course yore do, and so you shall. Now, look here, little Minnie, I think you like me." "Indeed, I do, Mr. Ned; you were always kind to me when I was quite a child." "Well, I think you like my darling Lottie. I know she likes you." "She's the best and kindest of young ladies, sir." "That she is, my dear; and now, look here, I sail on Boxing-day on a cruise round the world. Perhaps we shall be away for two years, and I did hope to have one jolly good evening with my darling before I went away. I say, Minnie, she's just like as if she was in prison." "ladeed, Mt. Ned, I don't like to disappoint you." "You'll disappoint Lottie, too, you know. I say, what's the good of a dress like that if it isn't to be danced in. Please, say yes." "I don't like to promise, Mr. Ned; I must speak to my father." • "Oh, he will let you go, my dear, if it's to oblige us; I know he will." " But—but—" "Here, I know what you're going to say, Minnie—that you will go." "I don't like to refuse Miss Lottie, sir; and I should like to see the ball dresses," said Minnie thoughtfully. "Of course you would, and you'll come." "And bring the dress, sir; and you'll drive me to Clap- ham, and take Miss Lottie on with me ?" "To be sure; and as soon As the dance is over, and Lotty has got rid of her ball dress, I'll drive you both back, leave Lotty at Clapham, and bring you here." "Really, Mr. Ned, I hardly like to say yes." "But you will, to oblige us," said the young sailor. "And look here, Minnie, directly I come back Lotty and I are going to be married; and, mind, you are to make all her wedding toga." "Thank you, sir." "And now this is a bargain. I, Edward, commonly called Ned, Anson, promise that I'll stand the whole of your rig- ging when you are married to Frank Lawrence. There, now, it's yes, isn't it? " " Well, then—yes, Mr. Ned," said Minnie, unwillingly. " Hurrah ! Be quite ready, with all the ball tackle in a bag, and I'll call for you with a cab at ten o'clock to-morrow night." "So late as that, Mr. Ned?" "No use to go sooner, my dear; and now here's off. Good-bye. Never fail, little • one, and—oh, stay just a moment; I've forgot half my message. Lotty says you are to keep it secret." "Keep it secret ?" "Yes; for if Miss Mosterley knew there'd be no ball. You promise ?" "Oh, yes, Mr. Ned, I'll keep it secret if it is necessary ; but I must tell my father." "Of course, my dear; but no one else. You promiee ?" "Yes, sir," Slid Minnie, laughing; "I will promise." "At ten o'clock to-morrow night, then, punttually. Good-bye. Hello ! Frank, you there? Didn't hear you come in. Bye-bye I" ile.nodded lightly to the young men and hurried off, leav- ing Frank Lawrence standing by the door, looking white, and with a curious expression in his eyes.

"Come at last, then, Frank 2" said. Minnie. "Yes, I've come at last," he replied ; and there vas some- thing in the tone of his voice that made Minnie start. " thy, Frank," she cried; "why --" She stopped short, as the recollection of her promise flashed across her mind, and gazed at Frank, with the colour gathering in her cheeks, and then leaving her very pale. "What did Mr. Edward want here?" said Frank, sternly. "lie came to—Oh, Frank, what is the matter ? " faltered Minnie. "I gay, why did he come here? " "To ask me something about Miss Lotty's dress." "What about it ?" "Why, Frank, how can you?" she said, forcing a laugh. "Did it take half an hour to say ?" "No. Why, what nonsense. Don't be so foolish.* "I ask you what Mr. Edward came for. It was something more than about that dress." "Well—yes," said Minnie, hesitatingly. "What was it, then ?" "Don't ask me now, Frank. I'll tell you another time." "I do ask you now," he said, angrily; "and I wish to know. What did Mr. Ned Anson want here 2" "Really Frank, dear, I can't tell you. I'll tell you every- thing in a day or two, but not now." "Not now," he said bitterly; and the angry look in his face intensified. "I would tell you if I could, Frank, dear," she said, im- ploringly. "Wait a little while, and I will toll you every- thing." " 'jou need not trouble yourself," he cried, more angrily. "I was not listening, but it was impossible to help hearing what he said while I waited till he had gone." "And what did you hear ?" cried Miante, angrily. "Your promise to meet him at ten o'clock to-morrow night." "Then it was cowardly and unmanly of you to listen," said Minnie, with spirit. "I cannot tell you now, Frank, for it is Miss Lotty's secret; but I will tell you after- wards." "Tell me now," he said, with a contemptuous look in his eyes; but she shook her head. "As you like," he said, bitterly; "as you like ;" and he turned to go. "You are not going, dear ?" she said, excitedly. "Not going !" he replied, bitterly. "Why not ?" "Bat, Frank." "Tell me what all this means," he cried. you going with Mr. Edward ?" "Not now, Frank; in two or three days I will." "Thank you," he said, with a mocking laugh; and turn- ing on his heel, he left the room, where Minnie stood look. ing stupefied at the turn matters had taken. Recovering herself the next minute, she ran to the door.. "Frank! Frank !" she cried.' "All, he has gone. Was ever girl so unlucky What could I do? It would have been oreaking my word to tell him. How foolish of me to promise. I—l--" She sank into a chair, covered her face with her hands, and sobbed bitterly for some minutes. till a feeling of pride came to her help, and she hastily dashed away tho tears fro.n her pretty eyes. And he slid he'd trust me." she said bitterly. " Oh, ho.v can he be so foolishly jealous. It is too bald. I'll never forgive him more." CHAPTER V. IN THE EARLY MORNING. Christmas Eve in Chelsea—in old Chelsea, with the snow falling fast in narrow, quiet little Bury-place,=where the houses were built a hundred years ago, and a small cottage- home could be obtained at a moderate rent. In the neighbouring thoroughfare, in spite of the wintry weather, business had been brisk, the butchers had made a fine display of white and red behind the flaming gas jets, and the pieces of holly that had been stuck in different joints at the beginning of the day were changed into many others as the joints were sold. Brisk trades had been done at the poulterers' and grocers', but by degrees the shops were closed, the gas jets were turned off, and at last the main street, save for the muffled rattle of a cab here and there, was as still as Bury-place, where a brass plate on a door told of Minnie Walters, dressmaker, &c.—the latter being in a very large and flourishing character. It had been freezing earlier in the night, and consequent- ly instead of turning as it fell into black mud the snow covered the pavement more and more thickly, and in place of Frank Lawrence's footmarks standing out clearly in the gaslight, the flakes rapidly filled them up till as he paced to and fro it was in silence. How the snow fell that night! lying thickly upon the tops of the lamps, in deep patches upon the window-sills, and covering the roofs, while as it fell silently, softly down it seemed to thing with it a deadly stillness as if all the world were in its wintry sleep. During the early part of his watch Frank had heard the rolling of the wheels. Now all was still, and the lights bhat had shone out here and there had one by one disappeared, while so thick was the cloud of snow which fell that a dozen yards from the lamp-post close by old Walter's door, the gas lamp that shone as a rule so brilliantly upon the well-pol- ished brass plate was only visible as a dull haze. How still it was in the little street, a stillness that seemed to increase, as the young man tramped up and down—up and down as if fatigue were impossible. . For he had seen, as he stood aside, Minnie start off a little before ten, to ba mat and handed quickly into a cab; her light box was placed upon the roof, and as, half-mad with agony he ex- psrienced, Frank stood back in a doorway, the cab was driven off. _ _ _

The next moment the desire had come upon him like a wave of rage to follow that cab, to insist 'von Minnie re- turning with him, as she was his by right. For the moment there had been the natural shrinking of a servant before one who was almost his master, but that had passed away now, and he started to follow, fiercely angry with himself for what he called his cowardice. But it was too late. He }hurried after the vehicle some distance, as he thought; but it provdd to be theiwrong cab, and panting for breath he stood in the snow, feeling that he had allowed the chance to go by, and that nothing re- m ained for him to do but wait for Minnie's return. As he tramped back it was with the full intention of. going straight to the house and asking old Walters wha tt meant; but he felt that he could not do that, and hesitating and wretched, he began his weary tramp up and down. At times the idea came upon him that perhaps Minnie would not return She had taken a hex and gone with Mr. Ned—for it was her plain enough. She was not coming back that night! And to help out this idea, he saw a light appear over the front door, where there was a pane of glass, and then disappear, to be seen directly after in the front bedroom. "She will not come back," he muttered; "the old man has gone to bed." He stood as if fascinated for the next few minutes, watch- ing the light—watching that light till it was put out, when immediately the desire to speak with old Walters, and ask him about Minnie's absence, came upon him strongly. But it was now too late; his hesitation had again lost him the opportunity. "She is nothing to me now," he muttered, as he walked up and down in the snow; "but I will see her come back; I will stand face to face with her, and tell her that I sin not the weak boy she thinks. Fool, fool, fool !" With brew knit and teeth set he paced to and fro, mak- ing at last quite a hard, trampled, and worn course in the snow, which at times grew slippery; but still the flakes fell rapidly down, softening the outline of his footprints, and anon filling them up. One o'clock, two, three, four had struck by the neighbour- ing church, the strokes of the great hammer upon the bell sounding strange and mused, as if coming from some vast distance ; but still no Minnie. Five o'clock, and still she did not come; and it was Christmas morning. What a beginning of the festive day! Frank Lawrence uttered a low, harsh rangh as he thought of the holiday and what a time of pleasure it was to be for him. Here was the end of all his aspirations! The woman he loved so well, and whom he meant to make his wife, playing with him, trifling with him, and proving to be utterly unworthy of his regard. It must have been half-past five, and the snow was fall- ing more thickly than ever ; it lay piled up against the doors on one side of the street, whilst in the middle of the road it was more than ankle deep. The silence had grown painfal in the extreme; and, utterly exhausted with his long tramp up and down, Frank was leaning, half-stupefied, against a post, staring at the doer from which Minnie had come, when he was suddenly galvanised as it were into life by the dull sound of wheels and the snorting noise made by a horse. The blood seemed to rush into Frank Lawrence's head as a tingling sensation ran through him, and he started into a listening attitude. She had come baclethen—at last; but he could not speak to her. it was to him—the scoundrel who, under the guise of friendliness, had won upon the weak girl and tore her away from the man who had held her dearer than his life. "If it had been young Ezra I should not have been sur- prised," thought Frank excitedly; "but Ned, the frank sailor ;—Ah, it is too much!" He took a step towards the end of the street, and it was as he thought—there was Minnie—he knew her long water- proof and hit—leaning against the arm of Ned Anson. For a moment their appearance was misty, dreamlike; and then as they came through the veil of glittering flakes of snow, illumined by the rays of the gas, the dreaminess passed away, and with it Frank Lawrence's hesitation. In a half-defined idea he had intended to say a few bitter

words of reproach to both, and then go his 19 ay; but he could not master the passion that seemed to blind him, and transformed him for the time into a creature filled with fury, and ready to destroy. ! " Coward ! scoundrel !;' he cried,oas he sprang at the young sailor's throat. Minnie uttered a faint cry, and made for the door, where she stood trembling in the snow as she saw her lover grasp Ned Anson by the tlroat, the struggle that followed as they swayed to and fro for a few moments ; and then as Frank in his fury of jealous rage pressed back his adversary, the young sailor slipped on the trampled path, and fell heavily, striking the back of his head against a doorstep, and lying without movement on the'snow. " Frank ! what have you done ?" cried Minnie in agony. "Killed him, I hope," cried the young man furiously; "and this is the woran I loved, this is the creature I trusted. Shame upon you! shame!

" Frank !" "I would sooner have stood beside your grave," he con- tinued. "I wish I had, before I had seen you degraded like this." " Frank ! what do you mean" she panted. "Oh, what shall I do ? " • "Bandage your lover's head," cried Frank mockingly. " How dare you!" she cried, from where she had gone down upon her knees in the snow. "Dare I," he cried bitterly. "As you take that tone I am satisfied now." "Frank, let me explain," she cried, as the young man turned to go. "Explain? Bah! What explanation is wanted here?" "But you don't know. I will tell you now." "Tell me now !" he cried with a bitter laugh. This is to be a merry Chtistmas, Minnie Walters, and—ah, heaven help me !—a happy New Year !" He turned and rushed from the little street, lost ha a few moments in the snow, just as Ned Anson came to him- self. "1 say—Minnie—where am I?" he said, putting his hands to his head. ' What does it mean? Was that Frank ?" " Yes," sobbed Minnie. no good would COM of this." "Seems you are right," he said, staggering up to stand with one hand resting against the wall. " There, I'm better now. Go in, little woman, now." "But you, Mr. Edward, are you much hurt ?" " Pretty well," he said," but not very bad. My head's too thick. There, go in, little one, and I'll get home. Didn't—didn't he say—something about merty Christmas ? Oh, my head !" Ned Anson hurried off through the street; and, taking a key from her pocket, Minnie let herself into the dark, chilly house—a house that was not so dark and chilly as her own heart, which found relief in a passionate burst of tears as the poor girl flung herself despairingly into a chair.
"Oh, Mr. Anson, I was afraid
CHAPTER VI. A MERRY CHRISTMAS.

Minnie rose cold and shivering, to go and lie down for a few hours so as to be ready for the duties of the day, for whatever trouble disturbed her spirit, she felt that she could not neglect her home. But it was ha vain that she lay there trying to sleep; rest would not come, and she could think of nothing else but the events of the previous night—how she had laid the ball dress all ready in the box, how Mr. Ned had come laughing and merry to help her into the cab, placing the box afterwards on the roof, and then taken her away, trembling and excited, when, t3.her horrui, she had found that the visit to the ball was to be kept en- tirely secret, Miss Lotty's aunt being in entire ign,orance of the affair, which quite partook of the nature of an elope- ment. She recalled how she had trembled when the cab had now stopped by a pretty villa at Clapham, where Ned Anson made a signal with a few shot, which he threw against an upstairs window. Then there was an answering signal from Lotty's nails upou the pane, and five minutes later she had stolen out, closed the door after her, when Mr. Ned clasped her in his arms, and hurried her into the cab. "I wish I had not promised, Minnie," she had sobbed. "Suppose it is found out ?" "I wish you had not, indeed, Miss," Minnie had replied; and as they went on with an encouraging word now and then from Mr. Ned, instead of discussiug the delights of the coming Christmas Eve ball, pretty Lotty Morris had talked of her fears of being found out, and won by her confidential

mood, Minnie had told of her own troubles and ;he anger of her lover. Then they had reached the great hotel where the &idea was to be. A private room was found, and in due tine Lotty appeared with her beautiful dress fitting her to per- fection. A place was found for Minnie, where she could at- tend to the tea, and look at the dancing as well, and then the , long night slowly glided by, with Lotty coming from time to time to the buffet for refreshment, and looking more troubled each time she came. "I'm afraid it has been a very great mistake, Minnie," she said at last, as the hour arrived for changing her dress and being driven, back. "I dare say it has all been very grand; bet I haven't enjoyed it a bit. Have you?" "No, Miss; I've been miserable," replied Minnie. "So have I. Oh, here's Ned," cried Lotty; and soon afterwards, well-wrapped up, they were being driven back, Lotty creeping back into her aunt's house unperceived, and leaving Ned to drive Minnie back with the result that we have seen. Poor girl, she was glad to rest and bathe her aching head, and then weary and worn to prepare the morning meal, try- ing the while to get rid of her pallor, for her cheeks were like wax.

"Merry Christmas to you, Minnie; happy new year, my precious," said old Tom Walters, as he came down, and he kissed his child fondly." "Merry Christmas to you, father, dear," she cried. "Regular seasonable morning; quite Christmas weather," said the old man, going to the window. " Quite a foot of snow come down in the night. I wish Frank would come; he might help me to scrape it away. What time's he coming?" "Coming, father—Frank coming ?" faltered Minnie; and she turned away warily to lean her arm upon the chimney- piece' and her head went down upon it, as the tears came in spite of all she could do. "Why, why, what now? What's the matter ? " cried the old man. "Has, has Frank been quarrelling? What's he been doing? won't have him behave ill to you." "No, no, father, dear, he couldn't help it," sobbed Minnie "It was all my fault." _ _ _ _

"What was--what was ?" cried the old man quickly; and Minnie told all her troubles. " Well, well," said the old man; "it was enough to make him go off in a passion. He ought to have been told. Young Ned didn't say to me it was to be kept a secret—he didn't say it was to boon the sly ?"

" No, father." "You shouldn't have gone, if I had known." "No, father, I would not have gone," sobbed Minnie; "and now—now—l shall never see Frank again." "Tchah ! Nonsense! He's made, of too good stuff for that. Knocked young Ned down, did he ?"

" Yes, father." " Well, I'm glad of that. It's English, and it's plucky. There's stuff in a man who can stick up for the girl he loves in that way. Tchah ! Tchah! Wipe yoar eyes girl; hell be here by and by." "If he does I will not see him," cried Minnie, with spirit now, as she recalled her lover's words " Elow dared he treat me like that?" " Ah, how dared he?" said the old man, chuckling. "That's better, Minnie. That's a brave little woman. Give him a lesson He ought to have trusted you—little body— ought to have trusted you. But there, there, wipe your eyes; he'll be here presently to beg your pardon." Minnie shook her head, and then finished preparing the breakfast, trying to forget her sorrow, and to make it a cheerful meal for the old man; but, try hard as she could, it was a dreary one, and the bitter weather, the cold, de- pressing reflections of the mind, and the irritable state of her nerves consequent upon being up all night, tended to depress her, so that the preparations that morning for the Christmas dinner formed a weary task. "Never mind, my pet," said the old man, as they sat by the glowing fire that night, "it will all came right—it will all come right. Troubles of this kind generally do. You'll find that Frank has been miserable all the day, and I'll lay a guinea—l mean a sovertkn, for there are no guineas now- a-days—that he's longing to come and beg your pardon for being such a—no, I won't call him a fool, for it was enough to make any men angry, and—hal ha! ha! there he is." For at that moment there was a knock at the door, and Minnie leaped up, looking scarlet, and then turning pale. "Go and let him in, pet; go and let him in," said the old man tenderly. "No, no, I could not," she cried ; and she made a step to run upstairs ; but the old man caught her in his arms. "Stop! stop! No, no; don't run away, he cried. "Here, here; come in, come in." The door opened, and Frank Lawrence entered, hat in hand, looking humbled and piteous, as he held out his hands to Minnie. "I was wrong; forgive me," he said, imploringly. nie, dear Minnie, don't turn away." She remained silent, holding tightly by her father's arm, while the .old mm t looked on curioasly from one to the other. "I was half mad with rage and jealousy last night, Min- nie," groaaed Frank. "Forgive me, my darling! I had been watching and waiting there all night—in tlie snow— and you did not come." Still Minnie did not turn her face in his direction. "I know what you think," he cried, "that I ought to have had faith in you—trust in you; but I am only a weak man, Minnie, anti L do love you so—with all my heart." Minnie had made up her mind not to forgive him—at least not for a long time; but as she heard the yearning agony of his words her heart seemed to leap towards him ; and though she fought hard and set her teeth, a sob rose to her lips and escaped. "I should have been no maa if I had not felt bitterly your want of confidence in me," he cried. "Your want of confidence in me, Frank!" she said, facing him at last. "How dared you speak to me as you did." "Because I loved you so," he said humbly. "Loved me? You insulted me cruelly." "Forgive inn !" he said softly. "I cannot—shall not—l never can forget it—l—oh, Frank, Frank, Frank, how mid you be so cruel ?" she sobbed, and it was with her arms round his neck, and her head upon his breast. It was a very loving and forgiving embrace, bat it was interrupted by the arrival of Ned Anson, and a very charm- ing-looking, rosy-faced girl, whose eyes seemed as anxious as they were bright; but upon entering the room their aspect changed. and a pleasant smile played round as much of her lips as could be" seen for the great far boa that was about her neck. "Oh, Minnie," she cried; "I was in such trouble, I was so dreadfully afraid, I made Ned bring me on at once, but I see it is all right now." Minnie had started away iron. Frank, and stood looking confused, while the letter's brow grew frowning. "If you please, Mr. Lawrence," said the young lady, "I'm very sorry indeed. It was all my fault, and I ought to have known better; bat I don't think I ought to shake hands with you after the cruel way in whica you behaved to Mr. Anson." "Yes ; I say, Frank Lawrence, it was a bit toe bad," said Ned. "Fortunately nature blessed me with a thick skull, and she bad sent some snow for me to fall upon, or my head would have been cracked." Frank drew back a little. "There there; hang it, man don't look at me like that. It was a foolish trick to play, but I wouldn't have done it, only I'm off to sea to-morrow, and I longed for one dance before I went. Comp, shake hands." There was something so manly and honest in the young sailor's way, Find so much faith and trust in the eyes of Lotty Morris that, humbled ae he felt by the events of the last few minutes, Frank Lawrence could hold out no longer, and he put out his hand. "I was wrong, Mr. Ned," he said • "I beg your pardon." "No, no; not a bit of it," cried INel, heartily n Hang it man, ne. I should have done just the same—hang me if I shouldn't; but believe me that you had no maze for what you did." "Yes he had, Nei," said Lotty, quietly. We behaved very belly to Minnie here, and I never before felt what foolish, wayward things we are, and how good it is for us that you are to go away to sea to learn wisdom before— before.--" " We're mtrried—eh ! little woman? Well, perhaps you are right. And now, Frank, is it all right with you ?" Of course Frank said it was, and Minnie's eyes grew bright once more, for the storm had passed, and cold as it was without, there was warmth enough within. Frank gave Minnie a look which she understood, and young Ned and his lady wanted but little pressing to ,make them sit down by the glowing fire, where they stayed for hours, as happy as that young hostess; while old Tom Walters sat and smiled and blinked at the fire unnoticed almost, and happy enough as he was. It fact it was striking ten when Lotty started up exclaiming, What will they think at home ?" Then there was the carefal wrapping up, for the frost was bitter without, and a warm leave-taking; while, as Frank stood with Minnie in the snow just outside the door, almost upon the very spot where early that moraing he had stricken down Ned Anson, the latter turned back at the end of the street, where the gas lamp shone down brightly upon him and his pretty, graeeful companion, to shout in his hearty, ringing voice— " MERRY CHRISTMAS to you both ;" anti, like a sweet, soft echo of his voice, Lottie cried— "And a HAPPY NEW YEAR."

SUPPOSED Loss OP A STEAMER AND ;THIRTEEN LIVES. —A Glasgow telegram reports that the new steamer Dart- molith, of Glasgow, left Dudden with a crew of 13 hands on Saturday fortnight for Newport, with a cargo of ore. The captain's name was Burns. Nothing has since been heard of the steamer, which it is feared is lost. The Glasgow ' agents, Messrs. Raeburn and Verel, state that faint hopes are entertained that the crew have been picked up, as the steamer's lifeboat has been found near Anglesea. There is, after all, something in those trifles that friends bestow on each other which is an unfailing indication of the place the giver holds in the affections. I would believe that one who preserved a lock of hair, a simple flower, or any trifle of my. bestowing, loved me, though no show was made of it; while all the protestations in the world would not win my confidence in one who set no value on such little things. Trifles they may be; but it is by such that cha- racters and disposition are oftenest revealed.— Washington Irving. KAY'S COMPOUND or LINSEED, Aniseed, Senega. THE SOUDAN REBELLION.

Sir Evelyn Baring had not up to Wednesdly received any confirmation of the report that the Mediterraue tn Let would be sent to Alexandria if the Mandi should threaten Lower Egypt. The False Prophet is believed to be ad- vancing in a westerley direction. Baker Pasha will be at Suakim very shortly. The small garrison of Sinkat is hard pressed by the insurgents, and Colonel Sartorius is preparing to march from Suakitu to its relief.

Colonel Harrington has arrived at Suakim with Major Giles and Major Holroyd, and has (the Daily News cor- respondent says) put the placa in an excollent condition of defence by stockades and earthworks. The present garrison is only sufficient to hold the place. Sinkat was provisioned on short rations up to Saturday. It is in urgent need of relief. SI messenger has arrived from Toka, which has been twice attacked unsuccessfully. Toka is also in sore straits. The Egyptian officer commanding at Toka complains that he receives only compliments from Sulieman Pasha here in response to his earnest appeals for assistance. At present any attempt to relieve either with the forces under General Sartorius is useless, but had the endeavour been made six weeks ago, or had. any fortaight or energy been displayed by Eulieman Pasha, both places might have been put in a position of perfect safety. General Sartorius is sending out' to friendly Bedouins inviting them to come in and promising them substantial rewards for any help they may render. These sheiks have often offered their services to the Government, and have been refused. Mohamal Tahir, one of the two chief rebels, is reported killed in the tight with the Soudani troops outside Suakin, in which the 500 blacks were massacred. On the night of Colonel Harrington's arrival at Suakin news reached the town, through the women of a friendly sheikh, that the rebels were mustering for an attack. The colonel at once set to work making stockades, and kept the troops under arms all night. At the setting of the moon, fires were ob- served at a distance from the town, and the gunboat Ranger, at the request of the colonel, continued through the night throwing heavy shells in the direction of the lights. This no doubt prevented the attack. Information has since come in that the Arabs had actually mustered, but as all that hap- pens in the town is known to them, they were fully aware of the arrival of reinforcements, and desisted. Daily recon- naissances by Major Giles show that there is no danger of an attack on Suakin. The Arabs have no artillery. The earthworks, two and a half miles round, have four batteries. Three other detached forts stand outside this ring, which encloses one part of the town, the other part being situated on the island and separated from the mainland by a circular belt of water, with an average of a hundred yards wide. There are twelve guns on the forts and earthworks. The main body af the rebels is still at Haidoob, twelve miles distant.

It is reported from Calcutta that the King of Burmah has despatched a force of 5,000 men against the Shan States. During a gale on Friday night a steamer on Lake Winni- peg,..Manitoba, foundered, and the twenty persons on board were drowned. ASSASSINATION OF THE KING OF ANNAM.—A telegram received at Paris from Saigon with news from Haiphong to the 7th inst., states that the King of Annam was assassinated at the instigation of China by the Annamite mandarins hostile to France. In a letter just published Prince Victor Napoleon dis- avows the action of those persoes who wished to place him in opposition to Prince Napoleon, the head of the Bonaparte family, and concludes by assuring his father of his un- changed filial affection. Her Majesty's Government have decided to resume the control of Basutoland in compliance with the prayer of the large majority of the Basutos. Steps are accordingly being taken for the appointment of a resident Commissioner with a force of native mounted police. FRANCE AND CHlNA.—lntelligence has reached Hong- kong that a French expedition of 6,000 men, with a flotilla of gunboats and launches, had started for Sontay. The troops landed at a point seven miles from the town without firing a shot, and the assault on Sontay was expected to be de- livered early. A new YORE TREATER DEsTuorzu.—The Standard I Theatre, one of the most popular in New York, was destroyed by fire last week before the commencement of the perform- ance. The loss is estimated at $75,000. This house was the first to produce Messrs. Gilbert and Sullivan's operas in the United States. TEE EMIGRANT CRAZE.—A Berlin telegram reports the return from America of 200 German workmen who recently emigrated to the States. They are said to be " utterly dis- appointed in their expectation of things on the other side of the Atlantic," and to have returned much poorer than when they set out. GREAT FIRE IN NOVA Scone. The Queen Building Offices in Halifax, together with Union Mutual, Guardian, and Queen Life and Fire Assurance offices, have been burned dewn. The total damage is estimated at $130,000. Orse person was killed in endeavouring to effect an escape from the building, and several others were injured. HERR MOST IN NEW YORE.—Herr Most, the for.ner editor of the Freheit, delivered an inflammatory speech at a mass meeting of labourers at New York on Sunday. •'he meeting was attended by the newly arrived delegates of French workmen, and Herr Most's violent harangue was in- terpolated with cries from his audience of " Vive la Com- mune "and "Viva le Dynamite." THE SALVATION ARMY IN AMERICA..—A. detachmat of

the Salvation Army, under a chief named Webster, wore re- cently arrested at Newhaven for a breach of the peace, in having noisily conducted their services in the streets. After hearing the evidence, the justice discharged them. He said that he did not think they should be interfered with in singing, praying, and exhorting from the steps of the old State House, but they must not parade the streets, beating drums, FRANCE AND CHINA: CAPTURE BY THE FRENCH. Telegrams receieed on Thursday state that the French troops have captured the principal outposts of Sontay. They met with a stubborn resistance, and on their side 200 men and 19 officers were killed or wounded. The Chinese, whose loss is discribed as heavy, still held the fortress. It is stated by a Paris newspaper that the following fresh bases' of negotiations have been proposed ta M. Ferry by the Mar- quis Tseng: The delta of the Songkoi River, together with the town of Sontay, to belong to France, and the delta of the Songeau, with Bacninh, to China. Srgacri BY KING ./LPHONSO.—King Alfonso, in his speech at the opening of the Spanish Cortes, on Saturday, said the relations with all foreign Powers were excellent. His Majesty added: "You will find a proof of this, and so will the country, which will feel the beneficial effect imme- diately, in the protocol signed with England to improve our commercial relations and in favour of our agriculture, which will be submitted to you without delay, and in the negotia- tions approaching conclusion for rreaties of Commerce with Portugal,' Italy, Denmark, and the Netherlands." Reference was also made to the visit of the Crown Prince of Germany and the forthcoming revision of the Constitu- tion.

MR. McMINNIES, M.P., AT GOLBORNE- STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL. A very interesting lecture on "John Bunyan and his Times" was delivered in Golborne-street Baptist Chapel, on Monday evening, by the Rev. G. W. M. Carey, M.A., of Liverpool, in connection with the re-opening of the chapel. -Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P , presided, being supperted by the Rev. John Yonge, the Rev. E. Moore (pastor), and the lecturer.—Mr. McMitextEs said he was very glad in the first place to congratulate the minister of that chapel and the people who from time to time assembled there for the very remarkable improvement they had made in the aspect of the place of worship. He congratulated them also upon having almost overcome that very great difficulty that always arose in the extension of places of worship, that was the pecuniary difficulty. (Hear, hear.) lie understood they could now see their way to pay for the palpable improve- ment they all observed there. He was glad to notice such a large attendance that night, and considering that there was a very considerable counter attraction in the town, he thought it was very remarkable. Ho had no doubt what- ever that everyone who was present, and who had come to hear the lecture, would be rewarded by what he heard for any little inconvenience or little self-sacrifice to which be or she might have been put in attending. (Hear, hear.) "The Pilgrim's Progress"—the book he meant—was, he supposed, one of the most popular and one of the best known books in the English language. All their young people knew it; all their elder people never forgot it. (Hear hear.) A great essayist who had passed away only a few years ago said that the two men most distinguished in a particular way in literature during the latter half of the 17th century were Milton and Bunyan, and it was a remarkable thing which readers of Milton and Bunyan must have noticed very strong resemblance there was in the style and language of the two. He himself never read the commencement of the Pilgrim's Progress, without being reminded of the com- mencement of Milton's Paradise Lost. There was the same beautiful grandeur in the few opening lines of both, and as far as he was concerned, personally, he never read one with- out being reminded of the other. (Hear, hear.) But he noticed the lecture was not ouly on Bunyan, but also the times in which Bunyan lived. Now, those were remarkable times. He supposed Bunyan was a soldier in the parliamen- tary army when he was a youth, but the greater part of his life would be spent in a period which elapsed between the restoration of Charles 11. and the revolution, and that was a remarkable time—a time in which the last of the male Stuarts filled up the measure of his iniquity, and received just and righteous retribution from the people of England. (Ap- plause.) With such a book such an author and such times he was quite sure they would have a lecture which would instruct, interest, and gratify them all. (Applause.) Mr. l'ilcMinnies concluded by introducing the lecturer, whose address was an able one, and li.stened to with great attention. —Mr. MCMINNIES, in responding to a vote of thanks, said it had been, if any labour at all, a labour of love for him to be there that night. He had been remarkably interested and instructed, and had been reminded of one of the greatest of Englishmen. He was glad to be able to do anything he could for the people who worshipped in that place. (Ap- plause.) It was a very long time since he first knew it, and he had spent many pleasant hours there, and wht,n he had been able to do any service for his friends there it had always been appreciated and he had al ways been rewarded, Applause.)

C ADIS HEAD. CONCERT.—A concert in aid of the organ fund of the Congregational Church was held in the Cadishead Congre- gational School last Thursday evening. The place wee well tille.d. The programme was ably carried out, and gave great satisfaction. First part :—Overture, "Guillaume Tell," Miss Morrison; glee, " Oh ! we'll o'er the downs ;" song, "The anchor's weighed," Mr. Derbyshire; duet. 'Tired," Miss Glasgow and Mr. Longworth; recitation. "Trip to London by electric telegraph," Mr. Bryruer ; song, "In the gloaming," Miss Barlow; banj) solo," The old ma on the common," Master Butterworth; song, "Ring out, wild bells," Miss Longworth. Second part :—Overture, " Semiramide," Miss Morrison; glee, "Belfry tower;" song', "Jessie's dream," Miss Glasgow; song, " Love's request," Mr. Derbyshire; recitation, " Progress of kindness," Mr. Williams; song, " Happy family," Mr. Longworth; song, " Gates of the west," Miss Barlow; recitation, "'Rae Kow• away," Mr. Brymer ; glee, "Sweet to live ; " Natsnai Anthem. Accompanist, Mr. Meeson. This concert was given gratuitously by friends from Manchester, for which they deserved and received the grateful recognition of the Congregational Church. The singers were freque.aitly• encored the eveninz. CULCHETa.

OPENING OF A NEW LODGE OF ORANGENIEN AT CETI.. CHETIL—On Saturday afternoon last about 30 brethren of the Warrington District No. 1 proceeded to Culcheth for the purpose of opening a new warrant. Amongst those present were 'Brother :Bloomfield, D. 51., Brother Lambert, D.D.15.1., Brother Marsh, D.S., Brother Mather, W.M., and Brothers Rosterne, Cross, Henderson, Leftwich, Wright, Armstrong, Johnson, Bowes, Stewart, Irvin, Smith, Coo, er, Lunt, New. all, Hewitt, Breoks, &c. The party drove to the Church Inn, where they were met by several of the gentlemen Who were about to become members of the Institution. A procession was formed and marched in regalia to the " New Church Club-room," where the monthly meet- ings of the Lodge will be held. At the con- clusion of the initiation ceremony (there being nine persons to take the farst degree and three the second degree) the District Master, Brother Bloomiletd read the new warrant, which authorised Brother Jas. Parker and his successors to act as worshipful master of the lodge. He then proceeded to instal the new master, and in the course of his remarks urged upon the newly initiated breth- ren the necessity of doing all in their power to support tte authority which had been invested in their worthy brothet, The regalia which lay before them was, with a few excep- tions, his own private property. He did not now feel justi- fied in giving it away, but for the present would leave it in trust, and if he found their conduct was satisfactory it would afford him great pleasure to make them a present of it.—Brother Parker pointed out that all officers had a duty to perform, and hoped that the undertaking they had entered into would prove succ.f.s.eful. Tile members then adjourned to the Church Inn, where refreshments were provided, and they were entertained by a narty of hand-bell ringers. They shortly afterwards returned to Warrington. FRODSHAM.

FROD6IIAM MUSICAL SOCIETY: MISCELLANEOUS CON- CEUT.—On Wednesday evening the Frodsharn Musical, Society gave a miscellaneous concert in the Town deli, Frodshatn, assisted by Miss Lily Holmes, soprano ; Miss Helena Argent, solo violin; Mr. IL V. Black, bass; and Mr. R. R. Ambler, tenor; each of the principals kindly giving their services gratuitously. A slight indecision was notice- able in the opening chorus, "The Vikings" (FaninF4), bat this was clearly due to the fact that Mr. Argent had to ac- company instead of wielding the baton and inspiring confi- dence by his skilful leadership. The choruses "Blow gentle gales" (Bishop) and " Hope " (Rossini), were well readerki, and the part song "Silent night" (Barnby) and the well- known glee "St. Michael's Tower," were equally successful. The remaining choruses were" Jack and Jill" and " Hurnpty Durnpty " (Caldicott), each of which caused much arnuse- meat. Miss Lily Holmes made a good impression with the song "Some day" (Wellings), and afterwards secured en- cores for the Cavatina `lSing, sweet bird" (Ganz) and 'Going to market" (Diehl). Miss Helena Argent was encored for the skilful execution of violin solo "Scene de Ballett (De Berriot) and " Air a' Gavotte " (Bach), was given with much ability. Mr. 11. V. Black scored a success in "The Bugler" (Pinsuti), while the realistic manner and dramatic treatment of " The Desert" (Emanuel), brought an enthusiastic encore, to. which he responded with "I fear no foe." Massrs. Ambler and Black gave the duett "Love and war" (Cooke) in capital style. The beauty of " The message" (Blumenthal) WAS fairly well interpreted by Mr. Ambler, and "The white squall" (G. A. Barker), by the suns gentleman was very well received, and on a recall the latter per ion of the so:ig was repeated. The last piece on the programme was song and chorus, "Nazareth" (Gounod), in which Mr. Li. V. black was heard to advantage. LITTLE LEGH.

A POACFIISIG CASE. —At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Frank Beech (24), engine driver on a steam tug, and Benjamin • Howard (18), labourer, were charged with having, on the 25th ult„ at Litrle Lee, used a dog for the purpose of taking game.—A keeper on the land belonging to Mr. Ashbroc;k saw the defendants at a rabbit burrow with a lurcher. Beech made off, but Howard was secured and excused his presence there by saying that he was " getting watercress for a woman who had the scurvy." A. ferret was found at the hole, but both of them disowned it.

There was a great quantity and varkqy of game. in the field.—A canal bankman named Taylor said he was walk- ing along the canal bank on Sunday, the inth November, when he saw the two men go away from the rabbit burrow. He picked up the ferret, but he did not see either of them put it in the hole.—Each defendant was lined lOs and casts, or 14 days.

WORKING MEN'S CONCERTS AND ENTERTAINMENTS.— The second of the working men's concerts was given in the Water Works rooms, on Saturday evening, when an interest- ing and varied programme was rendered by the following ladies and gentlemen :—Miss Fox, a reading; Misses Pear- son and Williamson, pianoforte duet; Miss Watson, four songs, three of which ware encored; Mr. Oddie, two songs, both of which were encored; Mr. Blakemore, two songs; Mr. Smith, a reading and song; and Mr. Joinson, a Lan- caihire reading. MT. Richard Dutton presided. There was a good attendance, and there is every reason to hope that these concerts will become more and more popular, as the charges for admission are merely nominal and the entertain- ments very good. The next concert will partake of a sacred character, and will consist of carols and readings suitable to . the season of Christmas tide. LYNN PETTY SESSlONS.—Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Ses- sions, William Arstall, of Partington, was summoned for not sending his child regularly to school, and an (war was made for the child's attendance.—A like order was made against John Henry Clarke, who was similarly summoned. —John Collins, Martha Collins, and Martha Emma Collins, of Lymm, were summoned by Matthew Woodhead, fustian-cutter, for certain damages caused through their leaving work without consent. The case was adjourned. —Charles Harrison, of Hollins Green, was fined ss. ard costs for trespassing on land in the occupation of Mrs. Mary Williamson, at Warburton. in search of game.--Joseph Lloyd, of Sale, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the beerhonse of Mr. Wilton, Altrincham., on the pre- vious day, and also with doing damage to a window to the amount of Bs. at the same time and place. He was ordered to pay 325, 10d. or go to prison for 28 days.—Defendant stated that ho was not in a position to pay the money.

MELANCHOLY Conaciniric—Es-Mr. Caroner Churton, of Chester, held an inquest on Tuesday night at Over, on the body of Joseph •liamblett, bricksetter, who was found dead in bed. While the jurymen were sAting the police reported a second case of sudden death, and that inquest having been taken, the police an hour afterwards were informed of a third sudden death, occurring a few "yards distant fro:a the first case. It is also curious that all those deaths occurred in bed.

WHITLEY INFERIOR. ROBBERY BY A WORKHOUSE 'INMATE. At the Dares- bury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, an old man of 70 years of age, named James Clarke, was charged on remand from the Occassional Court of Warrington, with stealing, oa the Ist instant, at Whitley Inferior, a Brahma cockerel, value 2s. 61, the property of Thomas Bell. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and asked for mercy from the Bench. It seemed. that the prosecutor missed the fowl on the let instant, and information was given to the police. On the same day his daughter saw a man hidiag something behind a hedge. and from tha description she gave him it occurred to him that he had seen such a man whose description corres- ponded with the appearance of prisoner, pass him about three minutes' walk from his house. Prisoner was an in- mate of the Dutton Workhouse, and on the day in question obtained leave of absence. Portions of the fowl were found by P.C. Mellor in the smithy of the workhouse . Haying already bean in custody a couple of weeks, he was now sent to prison at Knutsford for three weeks only.

Christ Church (Weaver Navigatio") WINSFORD. had its choir set*. tnons preached on Sunday last, by tho Rev. R. Marsh, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity, Northwich. There was a full choral service, with an anthem in the evening. The need of this annual set vice may be saen from the fact th tt the choir fund is much in debt, and the only rog,rot any lover of good congregational singing- can feel is that the collections NH far short of clearing it off, being only £3 49. Who WAS RTGLIT?:--TIOMaS WOrrali, a carter, was charged at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on fuesaay, with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Stratton on the 26th November.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.— According to the evidence of P.C. Mellor, the latter found defendant drunk, lying on a load of coal which was being drawn by the horse. The officer tagged at \Vonall's leg and asked him to open his eyes, upon which defendant got off and adjourned to the Cat and Lion •beerhouse.—Defen- dant maintained that he was sober, and went into the Cat and Lion for the purpose of obtaining a friend to testify to his condition.—The police officer's evidence, however, being confirmed by a servant girl at the beerhouse, the magis- tratea imposed a fine of 5s and costs or seven days.

div.head: ,---_ THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1883. ---------
div.p: ,---_ THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1883. ---------

SIR CHARLES DILKE and Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, the two most advanced members of the Cabinet, spoke at Birmingham this week. The speeches of both are invigorating pro- ductions, and the utterances, more especially of the former, and which are full of hope- fulness for the future, must have been read with the keenest interest. Sir CHARLES was careful to inform his hearers that he had no commission from his colleagues, that he was not able to speak in their name, or to announce what may be their decisions with regard to the business of the coming session; at the same time the President of the Local Go- vernment Board clearly indicated, we think, what will be the chief measures announced in the Queen's Speech in February next. It has been suggested by a leading Conserva- tive organ that to pass one measure of first- class importance in a single session is enough. Like most people, however, we fail to see why when in previous sessions we have, received so much more than one measure of great magnitude we should be so easily satisfied now. We are sure the Liberal party are not less anxious at the present day than in previous years to carry out the reforms they were sent to St. Stephen's to enact; and it must not be forgotten that their facilities for the trans- action of business are now much more com- plete than they have hitherto been. It is true that in recent years obstruction has attained to a degree of perfection which it was never anticipated it could achieve ; but then we have the rules of procedure, which sere passed at the expenditure of so much time and trouble to suppress obstruction, and these will have to be rigidly enforced if anything like satisfactory progress is to be made. The devolution of work to the Grand Committees, too, has, it is admitted on both sides of the House, worked well, and if the legislative arrears are to be wiped out, greater advantage will have to be taken of these Committees than has yet been the case. Sir CHARLES DILKE had very little difficulty in showing his Birmingham audience that during Mr. GLADSTONE'S first administration it was customary to pass several measures of first-class im- portance in a single session. Forinstance, in 1869, the first year after the present PRE- MIER acceded to power, the Irish Church was disestablished and partially disendowed, and we all know with what inestimable bene- fits to Ireland. The same year witnessed the passing of the Endowed Schools Bills, a Bankruptcy Act, the Assessed Rating Act, and other necessary measures. In 1870 the first Irish Land Bill, which was the founda- tion of other reforms on the Irish land ques- tion, became law; and so did the Bill which placed a sound elementary education within the reach of every child in the land. Other measures of• considerable magnitude were passed in the same year. The Session of 1871 was made memorable by the abolition of purchase in the army; a " Trade Union Act, which aimed at putting an end to the costly disputes between capital and labour, and re- moving vexatious disabilities under which trade unions suffered; the Local Government Act, extending to small towns and village dis- tricts the advantages of Municipal Govern- ment; and the University Tests Bill, abolish- ing religious tests m the National Universities —a Bill which found its principal opponent in Lord Salisbury." In the Session of 1872 Mr. Gladstone passed the Ballot Bill, which has since enabled the voter—and particularly the working class voter—to exercise his pri- vilege without any fear of future consequences; and in the same Session important alterations were made in the licensing laws, not the least beneficent being" the one which les- sened the hours for the sale of drink. The Session of 1873 was scarcely less remarkable for the passing of measures which have been of great value to the country. It may be that we have been accustomed to so much legisla- tive work in a single session that we are now hard to please, but having regard to past ex- perience we see no reason why we should be satisfied with one measure a year only. Sir CHARLES DILKE has, we think, indicated that we may expect next Session a County Franchise Bill ; a London Government Bill ; a County Government Bill ; and a Bill for the reform of the London City Guilds. Now, with the exception of the last- named, these measures unlike some passed by Mr. GLADSTONE'S first ad- ministration—have been before the coun- try for a considerable time. The electors have made up their minds that these Bills shall be carried, their representatives, or the majority of them, have been instructed by their constituencies to urge the Government to rush them on, and there ought not, in our ?pinion, to be any difficulty in obtaining the judgment of Parliament upon each of them. It is certain that if each member of the Cabinet and of the Government manifests the desire and determination of Sir C

Dn.KE to get through the work, and if the Liberal majority remains loyal to their chiefs, the task—not by any means an arduous one —will be mastered, and that very satisfactorily and expeditiously. Of course the House of Lords will have to be reckoned with, but we may take it that the difficulty with the Peers will not be insurmountable. The House of Commons will not tolerate spending days, weeks, and months in maturing measures of reform to have them contemptuously thrown aside at the bidding of one man in the Upper Chamber. Sir C. DILKE and Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN have spoken out unmistakeably on this point; and Mr. FORSTER, the late Chief Secretary for Ireland, was no less emphatic some years ago when the Peers threw out the Compensation for Disturbance Bill. The opinions of these gentlemen accurately reflect, we believe, the voice of the country; and any forced appeal to the constituencies on the lines laid down by Lord SALISBURY must as- suiedly recoil upon the noble Marquis him- self. The numerous speeches which Sir C. DILKE and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN have already delivered during the recess have done much to impress upon the electorate an appreciable conception of the questions which have to be decided between the two great parties, and we doubt not that the electorate will in the future, as in the past, prove faithful to the party of progress.

CHURCH 01 ENGLAND TEMPANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES. —The weekly meeting was held in the National Schools on Thursday, when the Vicar delivered a lecture. The report of the Tontine Society, which was read, showed a dividend of £1 4s 2d to each member. RUNCORN ANNUAL DIVIDEND SICK AIM BURIAL SOCIETY.
