Bd. available for dividend between 33 full members, who each receive 12s. 10d. HALTON Murreet. latraoverateerr SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, in the Wesleyan school-room, when a paper entitled " The Hand of tied in history" was read by Mr. John Haddock. The following gentlemen took part in the debate :—Messrs. Chrimes, Hughes, Barrow, Basnett, Hancock, and Wilson. Mr W. H. Bradbury presided. PRESENTATION TO AN ASSISTANT MISTRESS AT RUNCORN. —On Thursday afternoon an interesting presentation took place at the National Infant School, Runcorn, to Miss Spencer, assistant mistress. During the time Miss Spencer has been connected with the school she has won the esteem of the mistress (Miss Mack), of the managers, and of the whole of the children under her charge. The present con- sisted of a locket of chaste design set with pearls, which was the gift of the children, an] an illuminated portrait album, the gift of the teachers. The Vicar made the presentation In an appropriate speech, and Miss Spencer suitably replied. Ilneorc RESCUE FROM DRowpritto AT Wtmeis. The facts of an heroic rescue from drowning have just tran- spired. About dusk on Saturday last, as John Smith, time- keeper at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., and captain of thetWidnes Football Team, was walking by the side of the canal he noticed an object in the water. Dis- covering that it was a human being be jumped into the water, seized the drowning person, and swam to the canal side. Being unable to get from the water unaided he shouted far help, and several men arriving on the spot pulled rescued and rescuer on to the bank. It transpired that he whom Smith bad saved was a boy also named Smith, who bad slipped into the canal. He was quite unconsciaus when taken from the water, and had it not been for the plucky conduct of Smith he must inevitably have been drowned. WIDNES CHORAL SourrY.—li preference to holding con- certs, which in the past have scarcely paid expenses, the Widnes Choral Society intend to hold during the winter a series of "open rehearsals." The first took place in Lacey- street school-room on Thursday evening, when Randigger's " Fridolin" was given to a fair audience. The leading characters were ably represented as fulloos :—EAlantlne, Countess of Saverne, Miss Madeline Roe; Waldemar, Count of Saverne, Mr. Eustace Carey; Fridolin, page to the Coun- tess, Mr. Henry Latham ; Hubert, squire to the Count, Mr. 11. V. Black. The members of the society formed the chorus, and the piece was performed in such a manner as to earn the hearty applause of the audience. The second part of the programme was of a miscellaneous character, songs being given by the Misses Bond, Miss Haddock, Mr. Joseph Morrison, Mr. Latham, and Mr. Black. Mr. W. I. Argent conducted. IytemisT AT Thrriate.—An inquest was held before Mr. Rowbottom, the deputy-coroner, at the Ball Inn, Ditton, touching the death of the illegitimate child of Hannah Har- rison, 20 years of age, a domestic servant in the employ of Mrs. Bowertnan, wife of a labourer, living in Duke-street, Ditton. The following facts were attested by Mrs. Bower- man, Mrs. Jessie Beesley, of William-street, and Mrs. Esther Fazackerley. On Tuesday the girl Harrison was confined of a fully-developed- child. There had been no attempt made to conceal the birth of the child, and the mother had never denied that she was pregnant. Dr. Booth deposed that he had made a post-mortem examination of the body, which was that of a fully-developed baby girl. From its appearance he found that the mother had not had the as- sistance of a nurse, and he was of opinion that the child was stillborn.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child was stillborn. CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCOD.N AND WIDNES. The streets at Runcorn, on Thursday evening, were thronged hy people who had turned out to witness the tradesmen's Christmas show, and the sight was truly a cheering one. Almost every shop was well stocked and decorated for the festive season, the butchers having made extensive prepara- tions, and their establishments were viewed with the greatest interest. The drapers' shops were one blaze of light and brilliant colour, Messrs. Unsworth Brothers having an espe- cially tasteful display of gentlemen's goods of all desci ip- tions. With reference to the drawing at this establishment, we may state that the police have forbidden the event on the ground of its illegality, and the firm have therefore decided to offer the pictures to the Free Public Library Committee, to be plaeed in the reading room. Mr. J. Beesley exhibits a number of paintings which he has executed at different times, amongst them being a life-like portrait of Mr. John Harrison, who was for so many years the Runcorn ferryman. The grocers and poulterers each showed their respective goods to the best advantage, and many were the longing glances cast upon them. At Widnes preparations of a similar description had been made, and in the gas light the town had a much more cheerful appearance than usual. SERVICE or SONG AT WIDNES.—With the object of in- creasing circuit fund of the Widnes United Methodist Free Church a service of song was given in Zion Chapel, Oak- land-street, on Monday evening. There was a good sandience. The piece chosen for representation was "The desire of all nations," with selections appropriate to the season from the Cantata, "The lion of Judah," and the members ef the choir acquitted themselves in a manner which reflected great credit both upon themselves and upon their conductor, Mr. John Betney, whose services in con- nection with the church are highly valued. The singing of those ladies and gentlemen who rendered the various duets and solos was of a very enjoyable nature, and they were loudly applauded. The quartet " Tie night on the silent mountains " was sung by Mr. Joseph Betney, Mi. A. Price, Mrs. Lock and Miss Cawsey; trio " Nunc dimitis," Miss Cawsey, Mrs. John Betney, and Mr. Jeaeph Betney; duet "Beautiful star," Mrs. John Betney, and Miss Cawsey ; quartet "Weep ye mothers of Bethlehem," Messrs. Robert Bushell and A. Price, and Miss A. Betney and Miss H. Robinson; duet "While Shepherds watch," Mrs. Lock and Mr. John Betney, and Miss Cawsey and Mrs. Lock; dnet "Christians awake," Mr. Joseph Betney and Mr. John Betney. An efficient band accompanied and played a march from the "Lion of Judah" in excellent style. Mr. Alfred Ogden presided at the harmonium. AN I RISHM AN AND His FELLOW-LOD CHIRt the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Edward and James Murray, farm labourers, in the employ of Mr. Pimblett, farmer, of Appleton, were charged with stealing a purse and 5s 'lid, the property of Michael Cennolly.—Prosecutor said he slept in the same room with the prisoners at the "Irish House," and on the 13th he put the purse and money into his waistcoat, which he hung on a nail in the bedroom. I There were two two shilling pieces, two sixpences, and 701 in copper. On the following morning the money was mis- sing. The prisoners were in the room at the time, and he charged them with the theft. They showed him a purse which was not his. They went to a public-house, and he eventually went there himself on the same day. The vri- soner Edward said, "Here's sixpence; don't mind it." Prosecutor took the sixpence, and defendant Edward paid for him a pint of beer. He did not recognise the sixpence. —Mr. Jenkins, who appeared for defendants' said they had spent each other's money ad libitum.-4'.C. Mellor said he apprehended the prisoners and searched the "Irish house," and found 35 among some coal, is among some straw, and on the prisoner Edward 3s in silver and 90 in copper. On prisoner James be found two 2s pieces, 6d, and 7p. He did not find any purse.—ln answer to the charge, Edward said he did not know anything about it.—Mr. Jenkins sub- mitted that he had no case to answer; and after Mr. Pimb- lett had spoken to the excellent character of the prisoners, the case was dismissed.

Teen Jr:mum SINGERS AT RUNCORN.—TIin Canadian Jubilee Singers gave a concert of sacred music in Bethesda Chapel on Sunday evening. Bishop Disney had previously preached to a large congregation. The total amount col- lected in aid of their mission was £l4. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—At Hie court, which was held on Tuesday, before Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, the cause list comprised 60 original plaints four adjourned plaints, and 25 judgment summonses. None of the cases were of public interest. The offices of the court will be closed from the 24th to the 26th inst. inclusive. Ruieconer VESSELS IN THE GALE.—Tho Maria, from Runcorn to Findhorn with salt, and the schooner Wallachia, with coal, were driven ashore between Findhorn and Nairn on Thursday, and on account of the rough weather were expected to become total wrecks. The Daring, from Run- corn tee Newcastle with salt, was on Thursday assisted into Great Yarmouth In entering the harbour she struck the pier and sustained some damage. She had lost both anchors and chains. Tins WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD xr WORK. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. 11. PALL OF • CHIMNEY AT WlDNES.—During the high wind on Friday evening. a chimney about 60 feet high at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. was blown down. I The heavy pile of bricks fell across a joiner's shed, which 1 was completely destroyed, and between two flats in the , canal. The craft were uninjured. The damage to the joiner's shop alone is estimated at £lOO. No person was injured, but the workmen had only left the shed a few ' minutes before the accident. THEFT FROM TIM ROYAL OAK, WESTON —At Runcorn , Police Court, ors Wednesday, before Mr. John Brundrit and , Mr. James Handley, Michael McGrath was charged with etealing a gill of whiskey, value is, the property of Phoebe ' Barrow, of the Royal Oak Inn, Weston. The evidence I pointed' to the fact that an Irishman, named John Whitney, who was in the inn with the prisoner, was the delinquent, and the Bench discharged the prisoner. A warrant is out for the apprehenmon of Whitney. who has absconded. ALLEGED TIIEFT OF A DUCK AT WIDNES. Charles I Pratt, a painter, was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. charged with stealing a duck. It appeared that about midnight, on Sunday, P.C. 407 met the prisoner in Warrington-road, and noticing that he had something bulky under his coat he stopped him. Under his coat he found the duck (produced) which was quite warm.—The defendant stated that he had purchased it from two noted poachers.—On the application of Superintendent Barker, the prisoner was remanded until Saturday. WESLIIYAN MISSIONS AT RONCORN.—SUMORS in aid et the Wesleyan Home and Foreign Missionary Society were preached in Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, in , the morning by the Rev. S. Mees, and in the I evening by the Rev. H. T. Allen. On Tuesday evening the annual meeting was held in the same place, under the presidency .of Mr. John Simpson. The Rev. George Hack , read the report, and aeriresses were delivered by the Rev. ' J. H. Goodman, of Birkenhead, and the Rev. Albert Clay- , ton, of Liverpool. The collections, with the subscriptions, were considerably in advance of last year. A WIDNES HERB Bass Sewn% Ix Mounts. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Emma Green, a herb beer seller, Waterloo-road, was charged with keeping an un- licensed refreshment house.—Mr. Heal, the supervisor of I inland revenue, Runcorn, prosecuted, and he explained that a house where liquors were sold after 10 o'clock p.m. re- ; quired a refreshment license, and in Oceober an officer of I inland revenue called upon her. He asked her to take out a license, but she refused, saying she had been advised that she was not liable.—Mr. Tighe inland revenue, said on the 7th November, at 10-55 pin., he went to the house of de- fendant and asked for a glass of "stout." The defendant supplied him with a bottle. The house was fitted up like the bar of a public-house.—The defendant was fined 108 and costs. PROPOSED SHOPKEEPERS' HMS-DAY HOLIDAY AT WIDNICS.—A meeting of the shopkeepers of Widnes with I reference to starting a movement for a half-day holiday in 'each week was announced to tike place in Lacey-street School, at eight o'clock on Wednesday evening, but at that hour the room did not possess a single occupant. A few ! minutes later Mr. Peat, the convenor of the meeting, put in an appearance, and by about a quarter to nine some 10 per- sons. On the motion of Mr. McCollon a committee, con- sisting of Mr. Worrell (chairman), Mr. Peat (secretary), and , Messrs. Tebbutt, Wharton, and Brooks was appointed to ' draw up a circular calling 'Another meeting on the subject. The shopkeepers present were unanimously in favour of the project, and every confidence was expressed in its success. There is no doubt the sparse attendance must be attributed to InsuMelent advertiaiug. CHANGE RINGING AT Sr. NICHOLAS CHURCIL—Seven Gersten ringers, with the assistance of J. Large,‘Vidnes, all of whom are members of the Lancashire Association, met ii Saturday, by the kind permission of the Rector (Rev. T. Chambers), and rang a true and complete peal of grandsire triples, 5,040 changes, Hott's ten part, in good style in two hours forty minutes. The ringers were as follows :-Ist, S. Gough; 2nd, William Turner ; 3rd, Peter Barton; 4th, C. Newton ; sth, J. Large; 611, William Hughes; 7th, G. W. Hughes; Bth, W. H. Weaver; tenor (11 cwts.), first peal for C. Newton, W. Turner, William Hughes, the last two named being only 17 years old, and their ringing reflects great credit on them. This being the first peal since the bells were consecrated, the ringers and a few friends sat down to a first-class tea provided by Mr. Land (Derby Arms); after tea a vote of thanks was passed to the Rector and churchwardens for their kindness for the use of the bells, and also to the Halewood ringers for their kind re- ception. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN. -- Mr. W. Shaw,the missionary in charge of the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions, has recently increased the accom- modation for the children at the school, and on Monday evening, with the object of defraying the expense involved, Miss Gentles' pupils gave an ex- cellent entertainment to a large audience. Mr. Shaw pre- sided and delivered a short address. A variety of songs, glees, kc., were sung by the scholars in an excellent manner, testifying to the careful training they had undergone at the hands of Miss Gentles. During the evening the mission's band performed several selections of music with their usual efficiency. Miss Edwards performed the duties of accom- panist. Mr. George Howard moved, and Mr. George Mort seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to Miss Gentles and her coadjutors for their kindness in giving the entertainment, which was highly creditable to the school. The motion was carried with acclamation. On the proposition of Mr. , Gleaves, Mr. Shaw was accorded a vote of thanks for pre- siding. A fitting acknowledgment was else made to Mr. , Holmes for the use of the piano.

RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. Even under the new name of tlie Runcorn Musical Society the Madrigal Club fails to succeed in attracting an audience of encouraging dimenaions. At the first concert of the season, held on Tuesday evening, there was only a sparse-muster of the townspeople, although a most attrac- tive programme had been announced. The vocalists in- cluded two local amateurs of well-known musical ability— Miss Lillie James, of Runcorn, and Mr. Joseph Morrison, of Widnes ; while the professional element was supplied by Miss Richardson and Mr. Eaton Batty. Mr. Ernest Batty had been announced, but being enable to fulfil his engage- ment his brother, who is a fuvourite with Runcorn audi- ences, attended in his plaeo. The programme opened with the overture "Anacreon," Mr. Argent being at the organ, and Miss Harrison and Miss Speakman at the piano; and the fine execution and conspicuous taste of the instrumen- talists were loudly applauded. The chorne,who sang without the customary aid of a string band, then gave the chorea "The vikings," in a manner creditable alike to themselves and the conductor, Mr. J. Argent. Their other performances, "Little Jack homer" and "lime Li ouse that Jack built," although very enjoyable, lacked finish. Mr. Eaton Batty was in splendid voice, and his robust, but cultured, tones were heard to great advan- tage in the songs "The Raft" and "The Desert." For his pleasing interpretation of the latter song he was enthu- siastically encored, and favoured the audience with "The Bristol Coach." In Smart's charming ballad, "The Lady of the Lea," Miss James confirmed her reputation al a voca- list, and she was recalled with much warmth. She possesses a voice of great purity of tone, which she uses with much intelligence, and with a taste and expression that leayes little to be desired. Her second effort was "Daddy," which she rendered with great patties, and, being encored, bowed her acknowledgments. Mr. Morrison is a cultured singer, with a tenor voice of good range and power, and he gave a moat pleasing rendering of Balfe's song, " Didat thou but know.', He greatly surpassed this effort, however' in the pretty song, " Norah, the pride of Kildare," and he nar- rowly escaped an encore. The second part of the pro- gramme consisted of the performance of Sullivan's comic opera, "Trial by Jury." The following was the caste : Plaintiff Defendant Counsel Mr Morris. Judge Usher Foreman Chorus of Jurymen. Brtdesataids. and General Public, by Members of the Society.' The comical ities of the piece were excellently-pourtrayed by various charaeter, each performer taking his part in a manner which left little to be desired, and the audience were frequently convulsed with laughter.

EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A MEMBER Or A SCHOOL BOARD.—At Northampton Police Court on Wednes- day, Mr. Owen Miller, described as a gentleman occupying a good social position and a member of the Earls Batton School Board, was charged with being concerned in exten- sive thefts of leather from the warehouse of Mr. Randall, shoe manufacturer. A detective officer sail that there was sufficient evidence to connect the prisoner with the charge. A remand was granted.

THE SPEAKER-DYNAMITE SCARES-JUDGES ON CIRCUIT-THE WEATHER AND THE SHOPS- THE FUNERAL OF RICHARD DOYLE -MISS MARY ANDERSON-M. VLADIMIR PACHMAUN, ST. JAMES'S HALL-THE ROYAL INSTITUTE OF PAINTERS IN OILS-SIR FREDERICK LEIGHTON AND HI § CRITICS-BEGGARS AND " GHOSTS "- CHRISTMAS BOXES AND LETTER BOXES.;
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Mr. Arthur Peel is safe to be the new Speaker, and the opposition to be offered to his election is only a matter of protest. The Tories do not themselves expect to bring in their candidate. They desire indeed not to be ignomi- niously beaten, and therefore they select Sir Matthew Rid- ley, who was chairman of the Grand Committee on law when the Criminal Code Bill passed under consideration last session. The other candidate they could have put for- ward would have been Mr. Raikes—he would have been the natural candidate, but he was not popular. His flirting with the Fourth Party would have cost him many votes. The operation of the new rules is thus making a great change in Parliamentary procedure. Hitherto the election of a Speaker was scarcely a party matter. Impartiality, experience, and patience were the desired characteristics, and a Speaker like Sir Henry Brand, who was proved to peeeeee these, though be might be elected as the Speaker of ens party, would be retained after a change of Government. That state of things will ne longer exist, and after a general election the first contest in a new House will be the appoint- ment of a new Speaker. The Conservatives do not conceal the fact that their opposition to Mr. Peel is only to create a precedent for a more important occasion.

It is curious that London did not participate in the scare got up after O'Donnell's execution of a great dynamite ex- , plosion to be expected at every moment. Except for the posters of the daily papers, O'Donnell passed out of the world very quietly. I think people were more interested about the kelt case. I don't think even the police seriously thought that London Bridge or Nowgate were in the least danger. As to the threats to the Prime Minister, I believe that it is not against the owner of Hawarden Castle, but against his guest that they were directed. The Home Secretary is naturally very unpopular with the dynamite party, and no member of the Government is so carefully watched by the police as Sir William liarcoua. In the case of the other ministers the supervision is relaxed, but Sir William is steadily and continuously protected. His is the most unpopular office, and he has discharged the duties of it so fearlessly that he has the honour of being greatly disliked. Once a year only will a Chancery Judge go circuit, and that once will be in January. The compromise is good. ThegEquity Judges are wanted at home, and their one an- nual excusion bringing with it the incident of taking com- mon law cases and trying prisoners at the assize towns will give them experience in testing the truth of witnesses, and freshen their general knowledge of the law of evidence. But I wonder how a little matter of finance will be arranged. In the case of the Chancery Judges it was expressly stipulated that, if they went circuit., they should receive another £5OO a year for their increases expenses. Will they get all this money now for a single circuit? If so, they will be much „better off than their common law brethren. The shops are wonderfully gay this week, and I hear that business has been unusually brisk. Of course, ;people buy most in bright weather, but just before Christmas time this tells very specially. When this week is tine Lladon empties, but it does not empty till the Saturday before Christmas Day. All the accustomed presents hava to be bought, and, in addition, the presents for country cousins and the friends who are going to be visited. It is admitted amongst London tradesmen that a disagreeable Christmas , means a brisk sale of beef and turkeys, and a bright Christ- mas satisfactory dealings in fancy wares. The group of distinguished artists and men of letters that gathered round the grave of poor Richard Doyle this week included some of the oldest of his fellow-workers and acquaintances. Foremost am3ngst them was Frederick Locker, whose little volume of "London Lyrics " Doyle fancifully and delightfully illustrated. One of these lyrics is a most touching poem on the death of Thackeray, who, , nine years before, had written in Rome his (;hristmas story, of "The Rose and the Ring," and had brought it sheet by sheet to the invalid daughter of Story, the sculptor. The illustration to this poem by Doyle is one of the best portraits we have of Thackeray. Society papers did not exist when "It. D." left off book illustrating, or he would have been one of the happiest, and certainly one of the kindest, of these pencil satirists. His "thumb- nail sketches "in the Cornhill were full of portraits. Near Locker, at the funeral, stood Holman Hunt and his wife, and Charles Hall 6, and Herbert, the academician, all old and trusty friends, and a whole troupe of lesser celcbrities. Ile lies in the Catholic part of the cemetery at Kensal Green, net far from his co-religionist and compatriot and friend, Foley, the sculptor.

Next to Mrs. Langtry no actress has been so much talked about in town as Miss AMICTSOII, and I think part of her success in attaining this n quit has been her disinclination to prominence. The pretty American has:oeen most eclectic in her choice of the people she will know and the circles within which she will permit herself to be included. It followed as a necessity that some rumour should be started about her marriage. Given youth, beauty, talent, wealth, and a desire for seclusion, the necessary lover could not be far distant. In her case at last he has been announced, and the announcement is a little surprising. We are returning to the days when art and aristocracy seem to make a natural alliance. Miss Anderson might have looked for a peer. I am told she is engaged to Mr. 11. E. Abbey, the great American itnpressario, and not only that she is engaged, but that her marriage will not long be postponed. When she leaves London it will not be to return to Americt, but to make a tour of European cities, where reports of her beauty have already preceded her. St. James's Hall has rarely been fuller for a recitll than it was on Wednesday afternoon for M. Pachmaun. His suc- cess this season has been quite unprecedented, and since his bethrothal to a pretty English girl I think he is playing better than ever. Of course she is younger, much younger than he is, and he being very squat and lumpy, of course she is tall, slight, refined, and elegant. On Wednesday he played the "Moonlight" sonata not very satisfactory. Beethoven still remains the test for all executants. M. PaCbillatlll is too fond of the soft ped 11, and too much delights in violent transitions of tone, and when he sought to produce effects with Beethoven the rendering verged,on vulgarity. In other parts of the programme his success was great. Probably there never has been such a renderer of Chopin. All the morbid beauty and all the dreamy grace of this composer M. PAChtnalln knows how to appreciate and how to render. It was with Chopin he made his success last year, and it is here his commana over his audience remains undisturbed. By the way, no- thing can be handsomer or in better taste than the entranco hall and approaches just opened to the great concert room. The hall itself will remain for another season in its pn•sent condition of dirty gaudiness—but only for another season.

In art, the great event of the week has been the opening of the Royal Institute with an exhibition.of MI paintings. We have suddenly become possessed of a sort of second Royal Academy, and not only have we the galleries, but we have evidently the men to fill them. There are more than 700 pictures hung, while over the way last 801SOTI there were only 1,000. Outsiders will think that the academicians should not send in their work here, but it is to be remem- berel that the Royal Academicians have no longer the right to their eight canvases at Burlington House. An institute certaicity Is able to command a high average. I wish the best pictures in it were not by R.A's or A.R.A.'e., but they undoubtedly are. Mr. Tadema carries off the first prize by a remarkable unanimity amongst the critics. Of course the picture is one of the Roman series--drapery, marble, tiger skin, the latin costume. Tadema has painted this kind of thing a hundred times. No one elss can do it, and he cares to do nothing else. A little variety would be charming. Briton Riviera comes next. I think he understands the comical side of dog life better even than Landseer. There

is a cur of low degree slinking off with a hunch of cake up a flight of steps leading into a dreary Court, while a group of aristocratic hounds in the foreground eye him with envy and disdain. Nothing is forced in the pic- ture, but the crawl of the cur up the stops shows wonderful knowledge of dog anatomy and character, with no less won- derful skill to reproduce it. Another A.R.A., Macbeth, takes his inspiration from dog life, but the difference is very apparent. In his" Dog Days" you can see that he admires the beautiful lines of the animale, and the fluffy feel of their coats, but he never gets into the dog nature as Riviere does. His animals are pretty or noble, or strong, but the character is missed, and of course there is no humour. One thing is very remarkable about the present exhibition, and that is the number of light pictures. In that respect it more resembles the Salon. This effect is rather heightened by the comfortable crimson carpet that covers all the gal- leries, and is of great value to the pictures. If the Academy is as rich as it is said tc be, Sir Frederick might take a hint.

Poor Sir Frederick is suffering from his eminence and from his friends. I rather agree with Lord Coleridge that the scathing criticisms ef Mr. Justice Manisty will not be fatal to the President. It is curious what partisanship this trial of Belt v. Lawes has awakened. Even educated people seem incapable to see the distinction between art and the capacity to reproduce resemblance. Tiore are in London a class of beggars who recline silently on a pavement clone by some sketches in chalk presumed to be their handiwork. There is a hit of salmon on a ptate. There is a ship going down in a storm. There is a snow scene and a sunset. Here, indeed, you have resemblance, but I don't think you have art. I mention these cases because even with regard to them I have heard reports of "a ghost." One craftsman who has a little skill in this kind of thing is said to do the work for all. Certainly there is a remarkable resemblance both in subject and in "handling."

The Postmaster has published a very wile caution to the public not to give drink to the postmen, and thus make them associate Christmas with reprimand or dismissal. I suppose this bint is chiefly for country districts. I never saw a London householder paying a letter-carrier with sherry. The proceeding would be unpopular with neigh- bouring residents. No one but a miser stints the customary half-crown. Still, in London there is one Christmas-box that would be even better for the postman than that annual two-and-sixpence. I mean a letter-box. Quite an appre- ciable percentage of houses are without them. The people who give the most trouble are generally the people who give the least money.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC OFFICES
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC OFFICES

- ---- - A epecial meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, for the purpose of deciding upon a plan for public offices. Mr. E. Carey was voted to the chair, and there were present, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. F. 11. Pankhnrst, W. 11. Kershaw, T. Handley, E. Manley, J. Houghton, B. Dutton, D. Wright, S. Sadler, R. Webster, J. Midwood, and J. T. Allen, (clerk.) On the proposition of Mr. SADLER, seconded by Dr. O'KEEms, the Board was resolved into committee. On resuming in open Board, after a discussion of two hours duration, Dr. O'Kurra moved the following resolution: "That this Committee recommends that public offices be erected forthwith; that none of the plans now submitted be adopted ; that advertisements be iesned offering premiums of £5O, £3O, and £2O for let., 2nd., and 3rd. prizes respectively for designs for a Town Hall, so arranged , that offices for present requirements may be at once erected. Designs to be sent inty the February Board meeting." Mr. F. H. PANRHURST seconded the motion. It was pointed out that the Board had borrowing powers to the extent of £25,000, and the following words were added to the resolution :—" The total cost of the whole building not to exceed £15,000." Mr. DUTTON in moving an amendment, said he looked upon the proposal as exceedingly extravagant, inopportune, and unseasonable. They had come now to a polet which touched very closely upon the principles which he. together with a considerable number of the memiJers of that Board, were sent there to advocate, viz., the principle of strict economy and a close Inspection of the outlay. Therefore be could not sustain or help forward the proposal. He considered the public re- presentation and the public officials were in a very comfort- , able position at the present time, and there had certainly been a great deal of money spent on the offices, which he had no doubt the ratepayers felt. In the first place they had built large and convenient offices in connection with the gas works, and in every way adaptable for the time when they were built, But these did not suit the pride el the representation of the town, who desired offices in a public thoroughfare. They had been gratified, and there they were at an expense of £7OO for furnishing. The old offices were not considered to be inconvenient or uncomfot table for the officials of a large works in the town, who had rented the offica trout the Board. In Alteree Latanahore the Duara hail all the facilities and comforts necessary for carrying okthe business of the Board, and now arose again," We must have something new." He objected to spehtting the ratepayers' money in the lavish manner proposed, and he begged to move an amendment that no money be spent on public offices for the present. Considering the state of trade in Widnes, he thought it was a very in opportune time to spend £lO,OOO or £15,000. The imaginative threat—lie did not wish to charge any person with making a false state- mmt—hut he meant to say that the landlord if ever he threatened to raise the rent had retracted it, and there would be no increase, lie did not know whether the Board was justified in joining with the School Board in this matter. The Board had no right to provide accommodation for them; they had to consider their own duty as representatives of the public. Let the School Board Officers provide their own offices. He considered the Local Board were sufficiently and comfortably housed without inflicting upon the rate- payers a further burden of £lBOl year —Mr. Maserhuv seconded the motion on the ground that the present was an inopportune time to build oflius.—Mr. KERSHAW supported the proposition, and remarked that it WAS not intend:al to spend the £15,000 now. The offices could be erected for between £2,000 and £3,000. lie spoke in favour of offering premiums for designs.— Mr. HANDLEY said a charge of extravagance had been made against the Finance Committee, and it was time the public should know the work of that committee during the past three years. Three years ago, when he became a member of the Board, and the Finance Committee there WAS owing to the Board and by the Board thousands of pounda. The i accounts, too, were in a very complicated state. All the I money that was owing had since been got in, the accounts, which were in a muddled state, had been adjusted and paid to a certain extent. At that time the rate was 2s Gil in the £; now it WAS only 2a. (Mr. Durrote: Enough, too.) Over £50,000 of loans, on which the Board was paying 41 per cent., had fallen due, and the loans had been renewed at 3i to 4 per cent. interest. On thee." loans alone there had been a saving of at least £2OO a year. lie hail no hesitation in saying that the accounts of the Board were in a very good state, and would compare favourably with any Local Board in the country. Ile did not take the credit of this to the Finance Committee. The credit was due to the clerk. (Hear, hear.) A more efficient clerk the Board could not have. (Hear, bear.) The efforts of the committee to keep down expenses had had their due effect, but he thought the Finance Committee ought to have a little credit for the way in which the flhancee had been managed during the last three years The charge of ex- travagance did not lie at the Finance Committee. They had been anxious to do the best they could for the Board, and they had succeeded to some degree. It was not the Board's officials who complained about the present offices. It was a member of the Board who assembled there month after month. They complained of noises, which In- terfered with the deliberations of the Board, and the pro- posed new offices would not burden the ratepayers with any additional rates. The amendment was lost by six votes to two. Tho original proposition was then carried.—Mr. Derrros : I will have a public meeting. and make it a hot shop for somebody.—The CHAIRMAN : Do you wish to move another amendment P—Mr. Durron : I move that the offices be on Pex 11111.—Mr. Witham': And make you caretaker.--The CHAIRMAN: Is that a serious amendment P—Mr. Darrow: Yes; I really am in earnest.— Mr. SADLER, so that the public might know, seconded the 'motion.—The CHAIRMAN suggested that it was only a joke, and Mr. Durrow acquiesced.—The meeting then termi- nated. _

div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held at the Bo.sr.i-iliootn, Vic. toria-road, on Thursday, Mr. T. S. Timmis in the chair. Present—Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, Imioon, Shaw, Glover, Davies, and G. H. Denby (clerk).

div.head: I' ISTRICT XDUCATION COMMITTEE,
div.p: I' ISTRICT XDUCATION COMMITTEE,

The minutes of the District Education Committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. DEAcox, stated that during November there had been 75 applications for payment of fees, which were recommended to be paid in 70 cases. For contravention of the Educition Act 276 persons appeared before the committee, 64 were prosecuted, and 00 con- victed.

(TnE PAYMENT OF TEACHER. The School Management Committee subimtted a scheme for the payment of the Board s teachers according to a fixed scale.—Mr. I)Avins, in moving the adoption of the scheme, drew a comparison between the Widnes schools and the Liverpool schools. The cost of teaching at Liverpool was 7e. fild. per head, whilst at the Widnes Hoard schools it was only 2s. At Widnes the Government grant was 17e. 41. per head, and in Liverpool 17s. sfd. Therefore, in asking the Board that day to consent to an increase in some of the salaries there need de no fear because (tie work the Board got was very good work, and did not cost too. much.—The subject was discussed in committee, and subsequently a& journed.

div.head: MONITORS.
div.p: MONITORS.

The School Management Committee recommended Sheen. gagement of the following monitors Sarah Stringer (Shout's Cross School), William Jones (West Bank School), at salaries according to the scale of the Board, via, at the rate of £5 per annum in the oase of females, and £8 in the case of males, the engagements to date from January Ist, 1884. The committee recommended that a bonus of £5 be paid to Mr. It. Conant', assistant master of the West Bank School, for his exceptional services during WI past twelve months, having passed the whote of his class at the recent Government examination without a single failure in any subject, it being distinctly understood that this is not to be taken as a precedent; that the children attending the Board schools be allowed to compete for the prizes offered by the Widnes Council of Education, under the conditions set forth in the scheme, a copy of which is enclosed; and that the rules for the government of Board cchools be amended ac- cordingly. The recommend Wong were adopted.

The school fees for November were :-81mm's Cross school, £67 5s 10,1 ; War- rington-road, £3O 9s ; and West Bank, £57 Os 6d. The Government greet for West Bank school amounted to £844 12s 4d. div.head: FOOTBALL MATCH AND ASSA.ULVAT-
div.p: FOOTBALL MATCH AND ASSA.ULVAT-
ARMS AT RUNCORN.

It will be remembered that last Christmas the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association incurred a debt in pro- viding a treat to the aged people in the town; and a free breakfast to the poor children. With the object of lignida. ting this debt a football match between Runcorn aid lUiver- pool Gymnasium took place on Thursday afternoon in•tbe presence of 1 500 spectators. The game, which was an ex% cited one, ended in favour of Runcorn by a try to nil. The teams were composed as follow : RUNCORN.—W. Hughes, back; Broadie, Speakman, and Johnson, three-quarter backs; Hughes and Andrews, half backs; Wright, Lewis, Cox, Liatley, Joule, Lightburn, Hei- der, Mason, and Clark, forwards. GYMN&SIIIM.—WiIIiams, back, Lycett, Rigg. and Kerr, three-quarter backs; Alsop and Coulthurst, ha!f backs; Re-ails, Davis, Davies, Trevitt, Leicester, Roberts, Paton, Macros, and Dutton, forwards. In the evening the members of the Liverpool Gymnasium gave a performance in the Public list!. Mr. J. R. Frith, the president of Runcorn Football Club, was In the chair, ' and he was supported by Mr. Meadowcroft (chairman of the Improvement Commissioners), MesSrs. W. Whittaker, S. C. Beckett, J. Taylor, J. Humphreys, K. Evans (secretary Y.M.C.A.), and C. Pow-nail. There was a large audience, which Mr. Frith briefly addressed, dwelling upon the in- terest he took is athletic exorcises, and expressing the con- viction that the more youths and men improved their muscular power the litter they would be for mental work. lie highly eulogised the members of the Gymnasium, and advocated the establishment of a similar institution in the town. The athletes were under the command of Mr. Alex- ander, and their feats of strength and skill were of a most astounding description, the audience signifying their ap- proval by frequent outbursts of applause. Mr. Meadow- croft, in moving a vote Of thanks to the members of the 7MtIAC, UM an,l ltimenrn Vnntbill Chlh, rh:treiCterised their entertainment as the most surprising and splendid ever given in Runcorn. (Applause.) lie only regretted that they did not possess a Gymnasium in Runoorn. (Applause.) Mr. Beckett seconded the motion, which was carried with loud cheers. Mr. Alexander, who was received with great enthusiasm, replied, paying a high compliment to the Runcorn Football team. There were loud calls for the captain of the Runcorn team, but he declined to come , forward, aud Mr. W. Wright responded.

WESLEYAN MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN. In connection with Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School a musical festival Was given in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. There WAS a large and appreciative au- dience. Mr. John Simpson, who presided, delivered a short introductory address, in which he observed that this was the fret entertainrnent.ot its kind that they had held in connec- tion with Brunswick Sunday School. Behind him there was a specimen of their schelars and teachers, and he hoped they felt pleased atith the sight. Ile said only a specimen of them, for he should like to state that very frequently on a Sunday afternoon (hero were present at Brunswick Sunday School 400 or 470 scholars—sometimes more than that, and they had at the present time between 50 and 00 teacheraand officers. Ile could itesura them that the singing they had in that school on Sunday afernoon would please anyone who C4lllO to listen, to it. It Was one of the greatest pleasures be had to listen to the singing in Brunswick Sunday School They hal the help that evening of a number of kind friends. who had put themselves to considerable trouble in practicing with them both in singing and playing. They were kind enough to help them in connection with this work, which he be- lieved to be a very good work, and he Was sure that the :aadience would feel at the close that it had been a very great pleasure to come and listen to the singing. The festival was of an entirely sacred character, the pro- gramme including well-known hymns and excerpts from those great oratorios tho " Messiah " and " Elijah." The chorus, which consisted of 2(10 persons, principally scholars and teachers of Brunswick Sunday school, was aided by an eftlzient band of stringed instruments, under the guidance of Mr. T. Simkin, the conductor. Of the performance of the chorua we can only speak in terms of praise, the various difficulties in the musical selections being overcome in a highly creditable manner, and they succeeded in winning from the audience unstinted applause. Mr. Appleton sang the recitative "For behold darkness" and the air " flas people that walked in darkness. He is a cultured singer, with a well - toned voice and a pleasing style, and his interpretation of the pieces WAS warmly applauded. Later in the evening he favoured the audience with a rendering of the air "Why do the nations," in which he surpassed his previous effort!. The duet " Hymn of the Moravian nuns" was sung by Miss Jones and stias Clarke with good expression and Piste. Miss L. JIIIIICA bore off the 1 palm of the evening, for her exquisite and artistic rendering of the pieces put down to her name. "He Was despised " was given a pathos that secured for her a hearty encore, to which she responded by singing " He shall feed his fleck." A similar compliment was paid her at a later stage, when she favoured the audience with a tasteful interpretation of "Oh Best in the Lord." She bowed her acknowledgments. A pleasing piece of vocalisation was the chorus Adeste Fideles," the soli Miss Jones, Miss Clarke, Mr. Chens, and Mr. Appleton, taking their parts with groat efficiency. Miss Morton and Miss Leadbetter sang the duet "He wipes a tear" with requisite pathos and feeling, their voices blending most harmoniously. They were heartily encored, and repeated the feat versa, The sweet song. " The Better Land" was given in a pleas- ing style by Miss Jones, who was deservedly 'applauded. An enthusiastic encore was accorded to Mr. J. 11. Harrison for his fine and artistic rendering of "The Pilgrim Fathers," RIO Mr. It. Morris sang in his usual accomplished style, "Light and Darkness," for which he received hearty plaudits. The programme coneludet.l with the Hallelu- jah Chorue," which Ivo given in a trnished manner. On the proposition of the Bev. George :Mock, eeconded by the Rey, 8, Mee a hearty vote of thanks was accerdeil Mr. Simpson for presiding.

romeg PitINIAIITIONS IN Lowrion. —Th., police authorl- ties are still exercising the greatest vigilance for the pro- tection of life and property in London. Instructions which were issued and regulations made when the dynamite fac- tion commenced their operAtions in the metropolis continue to bc carried out to the letter, and wherever extra precau- tions are required they are as a matter of course ifmtediately taken. On certain occasions certain of the New York papers have announced that various public buildings in London would be attacked, and these, with others, I,articu- lady Government offices, are being clusely watched by the Scotland Yard authorities. The same precautionary measures have been taken in reference to the chief public institutions in London, and the police authoritiea :lave every reason to believe that the watch they hre keepiAg is amply nutilcient to prevent the possibility of surpris, and outrage from any quarter. Suspected persons are kent under close surveillance, and their movements duly reported; whilst the well-known Irish quarters in London. aid other ensplcions localities, are subject to the greatest police vigil tree

Ttiitro to Mr editor. MR. MULL'S REJOINDER TO MR. ATKINS. fear that you can afford me but little space to reply to Mr. Atkinaletbsr -which appeared in your paper last week, but I will condenra my reply as retseh as possible. I begin with furnishing testimony of greatest weight regarding the Character of the people of India. An eminent citizen of Bombay was Sir Charles Forbes, whose mercantile firm still ranks as one etf the foremost amongst Indian business houses in the city of London, and his statue adorns the former city. lle thus wrote to a cattet of Infantry who was leaving for India:—" Fitzroy-square, 18th Dec., 1839.—8 e Mad to the Natives ; treat them as your equals and fellow-subjects --give them your confidence, and you will be amply repaid: 'Gratitude 'is their natural motto. They may forget an injury, but a kindness never ! This I say after living among them 22 years, and 28 years after leaving them.—CHAS. F4)1111F.5." I might leave that to stand alone, but "to doubly re- double the stroke," I quote from a Charge of Bishop eber's, that is lying before me, these sentences :—" They ore a nation, with whom whatever are their faults, I, for one, should think it impossible to live long without loving them." This outburst of human affection for the people was occasioned by a missionary—of the Atkins' stamp, I suppose—declaring "that the principal , persons ameng them are sold to all manner of wickedness and cruelty, without mercy to the poor," tic. The Bishop continues, "I leave found them a race of gentle and temperate habits, with a natural talent and acuteness beyond the ordinary level of mankind, and witlka thirst for general knowledge which even the re- nowaml and inquisitive Athenians can hardly have surpassed or Walled." This further passage may tend to expose the want of insight and penetration into the constitution of Indian society so deplorably displayed by that gentleman, Mr. Atkins—l refer especially to his ridicule of the custom of early marriage (which is, of course, abused in practice): —"They are exempt, perhaps, by the fortunate circum- stances of their climate and habits, from some of those more outrageous and appalling vices of which so dreadful a pic- ture is drawn in those nations to whom the Apostles preached." I have a mass of such testimony as the above, but this is all I can at present here give. Mr. Atkins makes much of the fact that dancing girls are Attached to some of the temples. Why will he give such painful opportunities for retort? He compels me to do it. A clergyman, the Rev. W. B. Galloway, late of Brompton, -wrote, "There is sin most damnable in buying and selling the souls of the people for mere pecuniary considerations. What blush is felt for the open exposure of them in their own advertisements ? This is spiritual fornication These, and such as these among , ourselves, are they who taught Balak to eat things sacri-i Iced to idols, and to commit spiritual fornication." Now, Mr. Atkins, tell us what you have to say about this foul demoralisation, which has eaten like a canker into the very vitals of the Church? And if I could add the testimony of the Bishop of Peterborough, of like awful import, his pious lies ought for ever to be closed about the degraded Brah- mmical temples of India. Now let us hear the Times as to the elevation at which we all stand in the matter of truthfulness and good faith : "It is easy enough to quote instances in which the letter of Oaths has been violated by honourable men, generation after generation [those in holy orders more particularly], for the sake of emoluments to which they believed themselves en- titled according to the spirit. It is to be feared that there is just now a tendency to explain away all verbal obligations in diplomacy, politics, or co.nmerce. Veracity and good , Data are not the characteristic virtues vt snits age.-- rray draw the curtain; enough! Let no depraved Hindu see this picture! But this is only a taste of my nauseous budget, which Mr. Atkins has compelled me to unfold. Professor Seeley, in one of his Cambridge lectures, says "It becomes most clearly visible to me how little teaching of morality there really is in England, and in how unen- lightened a condition is the moral sense of a great proportion of the nation. When great public scandals arise, the cen- sorship of the Press is vigorous and useful; but where is the censorship of the Pulpit ?" I might refer to the ap- palling revelations of the polling booth, upon which turns not only all that concerns us as a nation, but that of India too. I hope to say more on another occasion. As to the danger of corruption on the native Bencb, Mr. Atkins should let that alone; he seems ignorant of a per contra account, and I will not enlighten him, unless he wishes it privately—it would, perhaps, close his month. One more shot I wish here to plant in my adversary. Good reader, will you believe it, that these very gentlemen who are so horrified at the superstitions and idolatries of India, dip very deep indeed into the public money chest of 1 a heathen people to sustain their Christian churches! There's defilement for you! Listen to a protest against this sin delivered by a Church of England Government chaplain, now deceased, and who was a dear friend of my own :—" We are compelled to ask how far the Government of a heathen country is justified in appropriating any por- tion of its revenues to the support of a Christian Church? It must be admitted that by no ingenuity of reasoning can it be shown that such a portion is applied to the benefit of the people of India; it is for the exclusive benefit of an alien section—and thes it must be regarded." Need I say more—but I have much more to say—than to plead that the beam may be cast out of the eye of those who see so many motes in those of the too-awfully wicked Hindu? With reference to the silly charge that Mr. Atkins tried to fasten upon Lord Kimberley, it may be pointed out that on the arrival of Mr. Atkins in London, some months ago, from India, be announced that his mission was absolutely non- political, yet he has become the active tool of one political side. His good faith, then, is at least sullied if not shattered. —Yours faithkly, M. MULL. might pass by the two aionymouS writez,s whose letters you published last week. Stroh letters, if they please the writers, don't hurt me—they contribute to strengthen my side. One writer calls it a pauper request to ask the Conservative Club to engage the Public Hall for me, wil- fully overlooking the grounds of that suggestion, that it was they who had incurred the grave responsibility of so disloyal and exasperating an address being delivered as that of their protege, Mr. Atkins. Besides, I thus showed my confidence in the great " Constitutional " party, but, as it has turned out, only to be reviled for it. Among the letters I have received from some public men upon this episode at Warrington, one writes, "I would not advise you to put yourself in the hands of the Conservatives, as you seem dis- posed to de." Really, your two correspondents would seem fully to justify this caution. But I am still un- shaken in trusting to their fairness and willing- ness as a body to give a calm and respectful hearing, if the opportunity wore afforded. I have not the least doubt thaj the gentleman who talks so glibly of pauper pro- positions, has receired a pauper education—using the phrase in the same perverted sense—that is, he has enjoyed the ad- vantages of a public and endowed school, or his sons or rela- tions have. I can trace one of the writers, I believe, and certainly large numbers of his class have enjoyed the pauper education alluded to. But lam happy in the knowledge that there are net wanting many self-respecting Conserva- tives in this town who have thrown in their lot with my advocacy of what I think is but justice to an abused and calumniated, silent and long-sufferieg, people. As to the charge of self-righteousness against the British race, your correspondent cannot be abreast of the great utterances of the day if he does not knowthe original source from whence that spruga; and the above letter, besides, is justification enough to prove this charge. A little honest indignation on my Part seems to have taken their breath away. But I wonder how they felt on reading the extracts a gave from the letters of Mr. Tom Hughes and Sir George Lirdwood ? I have done no harm But I remember now I am in this earthly world, where, to do harm, Is often laudable; to do good, sometime, Accounted dangerous folly! M. M.

of her son's despotic and tyr natives, not given w;• conduct towards the h. Ara the view of drawing course, and not attention to it, ,4t rather as a matter of asve rhe;ad to be interfered with. Those (yard Macanlay:s essay on the trial of tiens of ..ags will not soon forget the vivid descrip- who Warren h a his civr j.eand lust on the part of the Anglo-Saxon in , Ailing efforts in India. To hold the face of the ...an Prince to the grindstone seemed to be the happy and ettnliar privilege of those who wished to return .home, here to .grire as Indian Nabobs. The doings of the East India P*Compary alone would ha enough to blast the right of Eng- land to be called India's friend; her crimes there connot BOOM be expiated. The Jingo part in an Englishman's nature seems to entirely preclude him from seeing that his conquests should -be from a high and unselfish motive. We gain outlets for our manufactures. We send missionaries teaching that "All are eqaal in the sight of God ;" surely this is not done for merely selfish purposes, and we really believe what we teach! The civilising power of England is strong only when her example is of a kind leading steadily, yet surely, to independence. To be called a dependency is to acknowledge slavery's chains. With the view of striking off these shackles England's statesnaen, independent of par- ty, have for years encouraged native talent, and as a safe- guard *aye so surrounded the natives with obstacles that it has become necessary for him to lose caste before he could reach t'aose high positions of trust so desirable if India is to become in time a free nation. Mr. Atkins, in his letter and in his speech (by the way, how vas it no newspaper dared to print this speech?) gives only such evidences of human depravity as are to be found all the world over. Not a magistrate in this land but what could tell him that perjury and chicanery are the most baf- fling elements that appear in police court. As for usury, no money lender in India can surpass his English prototype; and a very few years ago the perjured villain was to be found at every street corner willing to sell himself fer the merest trifle. Mr. Atkins speaks of . dancing girls. Why, bless the man, he need not go twenty yards from his own lodgings in London to see sensualism carried to a perfection Indian girls know nothing of, and but for the law, not a theatre or singing room but would seek to swell its incomkt by pandering to the taste that now ezists for Arcadian costumes. But what does Mr. Atkins tell as of the Med Bill? I know not how long we Euro- peans have been in India, but I must confess to a severe shock when I am told that all our inte:course with the na- b I . yes, of a religious and social character, has not even yet produced a sufficient number of them to undettake magis- terial duties. lam disinclined to believe this. Mr. Ebert certainly does not believe it, and he has the sanction of all responsible parties for his measure enforcing the Queen's proclamation given during a Conservative administration. India wants to be saved from the blight of a rampant alien race. From one end of India to the other England governs in a most reckless and lavish manner. To hide this the Indian Budget and accounts are "rushed through" Parliament at the fag end of each session; and it is the universal belief amongst natives, that England is intention- ally sucking India dry. We tax some of India's products, yet, 'in the words of Mr. Keswick, given at an indignation meet- ing, held in Calcutta against the Ilbert Bill, and in direct opposition to the doctrine enunciated at the Public Hall by Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett when referring to Lancashire's trade with India, "We abolish the import duties on cotton goods to please the supporters of the political party in power." A more complete knowledge of native necessities on the part of Englishmen would prevent them from believing what Mr. Atkins says respecting "an orthodox Hindu shed- ding human blood to save the life of a cow." The cow is to the native the means whereby human life can at all exist, and were Mr. Atkins to speak the truth in re- gard to this matter he could tell a very dif- ferent tale, as in fact I could did space permit. Now, as to the Bill, about which Europeans make so much unseemly disturbance, I notice in a book—" India, the land and the people," written by Sir James Caird, that "The time has come when the prosperity of India under our rule can only be maintained by honestly carrying out the Queen's proclamation of 1858, whereby it was promised that her subjects, of whatever race or creed, should be freely and impartially admitted to all offices in the service of India, the duties of which they might be , qualified by their education, ability, and integrity to dis- charge." This is not the opinion of a novice in Indian matters, but of one who has had immense experience, and, not like Mr. Atkins, biassed by egotistical notions of himself and his class. The bill, if passed, would confer jurisdic- tion over Europeans on only two persons in India. The number who would rise to that position during the next few years could not exceed four or five, these men being, moreover, the very cream of the native civil service. The policy of admitting natives to that service is not a new policy. It was carried into effect by Lord Lytton'a rules of 1879. Such is a short outline of this most important measure, and the sooner Englithmen reconcile themselves to the inevitable the better. We have looked upon India as we have looked upon Ireland, as a sponge existing only to be sucked. The Indian Mutiny was brought about in con- sequence of a reckless want of respecting the native reli- gions and their prejudices. Our difficulty in Ireland is to- day due to the same cause. As we sow the wind so shall we reap the whirlwind.—Yours, CLIFFORD DIX. Warrington, Dec., 1883.

True, the subject is familiar almost as household words but there is to be set against this fact the other, almost a coral- lary' that a proportionately keener sense of discrimination is always b. ought to bear upon its rendering by a listening pal lic. Well-worn as is the "Messiah "it needs no special Sagacity to foretell its continued popularity. There is so much solid substance, if we may use the term, about the work that latitude seems always to remain for the exercise of genius in the manner in which this is laid before us. The Musical Society proper, both band and chorus, showed convincingly their competency to deal effectively with that part of the music which falls to their share. The singing of the members of the society in the choruses, those calling for delicateas well as for robust treatment, indicated, at least to our minds, that they needed only the direction of a faithful baton to yield all necessary subtleties. Dr. Riles, the accomplished conductor of the society's concerts and private practices, was of course at his accustomed post, and although the choruses were in many respects ably and efficiently rendered the light and shadows of the musical picture were often but vaguely per- ceptible. Referring only to the soft and loud passages in the oratorio it has been the custom,—perhaps a mere con- ventionalism,—to look for a rather subdued vocalization on the part of the chorus up to the point of declamation of Wonderful! Counsellor! The mighty God! in "For unto us a child is born." A. most appropriate and telling effect is then secured by the emphasised fortissimo thus rendered possible. This was a point missed. And opportunities of marking more refined effects in this regard in each chorus separately and apart from others were often lost. "Surely He hath borne our griefs" is probably the best instance which can be cited of a chorus depending largely upon the observance of marks of expression for much of its impres- siveness. But waiving this question of details there was, as we have said, much that was excellent in the part played by the society in the performance. All the fugal and more involved choruses showed the attainment of a degree of pre- cision in taking up the disjointed parts, which reflects the highest creflit • upon Dr. Mime' Wition. A pity it is that sotne confluc,tor does not lead the way in modifying the ' tempo of All we like aheep." The literal interpretation here put on Handel's " Allegro " would suggest the idea that the qualifying term " moderato " has somehow been overlooked. The consequence its that the interested listener is often struck by the jauntiness of movement, if not actu- ally led to the conclusion that "to go astray" must be a line of conduct to be proud of. The orchestra, which, we are glad to noiice, continues to be made up in the main of localj instrumentalists, played with com- mendable taste and skill. The aid of professional musicians was of course called in to lead in each part, but undoubtedly much progress has been made of late in bringing up an amateur orchestra to the standard which it is necessary to ' reach before it can be admitted as an integral part of the musical society. Except for a little uncertainty in answer- ing to the beat in the overture, the accompaniments were well played, and almost all Mozart's instrumentation under- taken. Mention should perhaps be made of the trumpet obligato as being a very creditable and finished piece of work. But we must not forget that this accompaniment was shorn of much of its difficulty by being played upon the cornet instead of the slide trumpet, for which it is scored. 'I he principal vocalists were Madame Clara Suter, Miss Helen D'Alton, Mr. Edward Lloyd, and Mr. Frederick King. The weakest of these was the bass, and the strongest the tenor. Mr. King seems hardly to possess weight enough to cope with the roulades in many of the heavier bass solos. Still his efforts were marked with some degree of conscientious- ness, if not always by .a high degree of refinement. Mr. Edward Lloyd was in splendid voice, and sang the tenor airs and recitatives with true artistic finish. Indeed, it was only in regard to Mr. Lloyd's 'Thy rebuke" and "Thou did'st not leave" that any degree of enthusiasm was shown by the audience. Both ladies sang in the manner which was to be expected from artistes of eminence, though it was noticeable that both were suffering from some little indispo- sition. The Public Hall being thronged in every part, it is only reasonable to suppose that the concert was the success financially that it undoubtedly was from a musical stand- point. •

div.head: ILBERT BILL.
div.p: THE ILBERT BILL.

Sir,--I hope I may be pardoned for daring to say a few words upon this important measure. I was present at the Confervative meeting, and saw Mr. Mull seemingly snubbed for attempting to vindicate the natives of India from the foul ridicule heaped upon their religion and morality by Mr. Atkins. Since then I have read Mr. Mull's high-toned and chivalrous letter,:also the answer (?) given in your last hum by Mr. Atkins, but I am sadly afraid that notwith- standing all that has been said and written, the public of Warrington are vs much in the dark respecting the objects Of the bill as they were before the advent of Mr. Atkins. To understand the measure and to conceive a just intention towards it, it is necessary that a little thought should be given to India's past history. Her history, like that of Ireland's, is so interwoven with 4,England's past insatiable spirit for conquest, that little attention has been given to the misery we were Causing, so long as we were enabled to add another "bright jewel to the British Crown." Scarcely a book about India has been published since she became a dependency of England, but what has teemed with examples

CHAPTER LV (CONTINIJED).—UNEXPECI;ED Vomits. "Feeling as Ido the disgrace you have brought on us by this mad freak," began Lord Harle.xton, the moment the Major had passed out of hearing, b I yet desire to relieve you from a false position, and to secure you all reasonable help in shaping your future." "You are very kind, but I have shaped that out for my- self," responded Stephen. "Well, as you please. Miss Vandeleur waits with her attendant to deliver a message from your mother." " Message !" echoed Stephen, and looking disturbsd. "Of what nature ?" "The Countess is fond of secrets; I have not yet been ' admitted to this one. I believe Miss Vandeleur is only a little less in the dark. I will now bring her, reminding you beforehand how desirable it is that your meeting be as brief as possible." As he moved away Stepheetried to prepare himself by more than his usual attitude of careless indifference; but whether to assume the old half jesting tone with which she was so familiar before their unhappy parting, or in respect of her suffering at the time, and the remembrance of Which might still hang about her, observe a quiet seriousness more befitting also to his own feeling, he felt too confused to de- cide. He wondered if they were engaged. Lord Harlaxton, he thought, if they had been would have said so to prevent all possible recurrence on his (Stephen's) part to his former re- lations with Miss Vandeleur. And then there came over him the recollection of the affair with the Sergeant, and the instantaneous resolve to make the meeting shorter even than Lord Harlaxton expec- ted it to be. With such a frightful danger overhanging, his first care must be to hurry her and the Earl away, before anything fresh could happen! His thoughts stopped suddenly in mid-career. Lord Har- laxton came with Miss Vandaleur, who was accompanied by Mrs. Davis, Gentleman Jack's former wife, both dressed in black and deeply veiled. The latter, in obedience to a silent intimation from her mistress' retired to wait out of sight; and Lord Harlaxton, then addressing Miss Vande-

said— " You wish to speak to my brother alone ?" Miss Vandeleur lifted her veil before answering— "l mast de so. Not believe me of ray own choice, but as obeying the express instructions of the Countess." " You won't forget the shortness of the time ?" he added, taking out his watch. "We are late now." "I will remember," briefly said Miss Vandeleur. Short as this dialogue was, simple and seemingly unim- portant as it may appear, Stephen was deeply affected by it. Not only because her presence, the very sound of her voice, brought back in the most vivid manner .every inci- dent of their last meeting at Gualtmore, and the eventful preceding separation in London, but brought also he hardly knew how, a consciousness of some change in her, the nature of which he could not guess, but which perplexed him greatly, and which he felt a strong desire to under- stand. Under this impulse he was when she began to speak ; and it presentlf became so powerful as to make him forget nearly everything else. When Lord Harlaxton had gone she turned towards Stephen, and he advanced respectfully to meet her. Holding out her hand, wbile a gentle smile which Stephen felt to be inexpressibly sweet, passed over her features, which were altogether more sedate in their expression than he had known them before, she said:— "We meet as friends, I hope ?" "Let this answer you!" responded Stephen, grasping her fingers in deep but glad emotion. • "I fear you must have thought it strange when you saw me, and perhaps also saw your mother, that we should have undertaken this long journey and voyage, wretched sailors that we both are, even though under the kindly care of Lord Harlaxton 2" "When unexpected comforts do come I am not inclined to ask heaven reproachfully the why and the wherefore," said Stephen, recovering rapidly his spirits the moment the long burden of self-reproach seemed taken away by her sweet behaviour. "I am glad to find you have not quite lost your old gaiety of heart," said Miss Vandeleur; who was equally in- fluenced by his tones, lsoks, and attitude, to put aside the first embarrasment of the meeting. "Say my old assumed gaiety! Which had as little of heart as of truth!" he replied. And then he paused for a moment as if fearing to be on dangerous ground, but soon swept aside the scruples that hindered him in a plain duty, to say—" Miss Vandeleur, I thank God you have come, if it be only that I may apologise for the brutal lines I allowed myself to write, no matter under what real or fancied provo- cation." "It is perhaps hardly a topic to be again referred to," said Miss Vandeleur, in tones of tremulous music, "nor could I do so, but for two reasons: the one that I have so earnestly wished you might know how all that was most painful in the incident has passed entirely from my—" tompuct....-'.il l-Pla.tn omy " This is indeed an unexpected, an inexpressible relief! " "The other," continued Miss Vandeleur, "is that I have since found a soul of good in what seemed se much the re- verse !" "I do not.—cannot—deserve such sweet, such generous magnanimity," cried Stephen, in deepening emotion. "It was as if I had been wandering in some primrose path, heedless as a child of the near precipice, seeking only food for mirth and joyous excitement, and then was sud- denly waked as from a dream to find myself a woman; stripped of all childhood's excuses—a woman who had yet to learn all that it most needed her to know." She stopped, turned a little aside, as if to recover herself before she could again speak. e," Such a revelation can only be received in silence, and with the most profound respect," said Stephen. But his voice revealed how infinitely beyond anything his words expressed was the effect of the revelation upon him. Mastering herself at last, and again able to smile, she continued, in a lighter vein, "But I hardly know whether it is I who have to forgive you, or you to forgive me, for being so tardy in acknowledg- ing my debt !" The smile smile and the words were alike enchanting to the listener, who said, "Let me then hasten to seal -so profitable, if one-sided, a bargain of mutual forgiveness before you can retreat," said Stephen, as he lifted her hand, and pressed it to his lips. "I know now-we are indeed friends." "And now, Stephen, as we must quickly separate—" began Miss Vandeleur, trying to veil her agitation under a show of quiet friendliness,— Bat Stephen interrupted her: "Pardon me. Give me a few moments to speak of my present position and motives in coming here. If not for your own satisfaction, then for my mother's, and if you please for my brother's." "Yes," was the faint response. "Where you and he End me, I came as a private soldier. He calls it a freak, and does not think it a creditable one. Permit me then to explain. After I left home, on that sad day df March, I found myself confronted with a hard problem. I had no money, no friends that I could or would think of appealing to. What then was rto do? knew not. Not a very cheerful prospect, you'll own, for my future." He smiled in saying this, and Miss Vandeleur smiled in response as she said— "No, indeed !" but beneath the smiles both were painfully conscious how different was the true feeling. "Bet briliant in comparison with the worthlessness of my past life. In sheer weariness and disgust I had often wished that it would somehow be broken up, but lacked the courage to initiate the w.ork. "Now I had to question myself in a sterner fashion. Was I, as men said, a mere butterfly, content so long as I found plenty of life's sunshine to bask in. Or was I, as others de- scribed me, a cynic who tried to forget his own follies in laughing at the follies of the people around me? "The answer was appalling. It told me that while the very possibility of indulgence and enjoyment from such sources had gone to wreck, nothing seemed left behind in compensation. " Nothing !" queried Miss Vandeleur with touching earnestness and incredulity that went home to Stephen's heart. "So I felt, or believed," he rejdined. "Conscience, as I have lately found, can be a stern judge," said Miss Vandeleur. " But does it not sometimes blind our eyes, as the sculptor's fillet blinds the eyes of justice in our courts of law, so that nothing may be seen of those redeeming elements which friends knew well to exist?" "Ah !" said Stephen in answer, "but is not justice pro- perly.so blinded that she may not see what is put into her scales, nor by whom, and so decide without bias?" A strange little laugh broke from Miss Vandeleur at this moment, whether at the oddity of the episodical topic they had fallen upon, or merely as an impulse of relief from the overcharged heart and brain, the reader must judge. "Oh, 'Stephen, did you think of all this, when you set your conscience so unkindly to work ? " There Miss Van- deleur stopped, a change passed over her face, and when she spoke again it was to say, "But Lord Harlaxton will be impatient!" "I know, and will listen. Born in the lap of luxury, trained in its habits, denied, by My mother's fond indulgence, the vigorous corrective of a public school, to be followed by the activity and interest of a public career, I had now to earn my daily bread, accept all kinds of hardships and humilia- tions, and while doing this know that I could at any moment end all by returning home. "I knew well that I could play no such heroic part. Neither could I descend to the shame of such a return. Again aeked myself, what could I do? The army had been from boyhood a fancy of mine; but then it was a part of the fancy I should enter with all the advantages of the officer's rank and duties—ani then move upwards, step by step, till even the glories of Wellington and Marlborough should grow dim by the side of my great victories over half the world. . "You laugh, and no wonder, as I have, many a time since then laughed at my own folly, but such was the boy's vision; and it came back unpleasantly and inconveniently when I a man, found myself contemplating an entrance
