"So I see I" exclaimed Miss Vanieleur, and she laughed excitedly; then abruptly stopped as she caught sight of Stephen's grave and wondering, but also sympathetically anxious face. 'You are shocked that I can laugh at such a story. Forgive me, it is the first time I have laughed for many a day !" And then she burst into a passionate fit of tears, which she vainly strove to conceal by covering her -face with her hands, and struggling to repress the agitation which shook . .

her so violently:- " Dear Miss Vandeleur," said Stephen, hardly knowing or caring what he was about to say, in his deep feeling and sympathy with her state, but she hurriedly interfered. "I am ashamed so to have forgotten myself !" "It is I, who have forgotten or been shamefully blind to your nobler self, as I begin to understand it through every look, word, and act. Is it permissible to say now, with my *bole heart and sant what I was once before about to say

in lip•worship merely, Frances, I He had neither the opportunity nor need to finish the sentence; his attitude, look, the tenderness of his voice, and kindling glow on his cheek, all warned Miss Vandeleur of what he was about to say, and which in great trouble and distress she instantly stopped : " No, no. I thought you knew! laston must have told you." " What ? That you are engaged to him ?" "Yes," she said, bending low her head, to avoid h piercing, stern glance. He dropped the hand that he had been holding, and moved away, so that she no longer was able to see his
I thought Lord Hat-

face. "Forgive me! I have been very foolish and weak. But your story so deeply interested and moved me "Why did you come here ?" asked Stephen passionately. "The blow under any circumstances might be hard to bear, but if you chose so to act, that it had to be borne in any case-." Then stopping abruptly fGr a few seconds, added, "Bur 'tie no matter. lam silenced !" "But your attitude does dot allow me to be silent

too !" "We can have nothing more to say to each other. I have already been tempted to say a great deal too mach !" "Tempted asked Miss Vandeleur, with flashing eyes. "If the word displeases 'you, I will take it back.' "No !" also cried. "I love better a true speech, even if indiscreet, than a false speech, designed to cover a cowardly desire for safety. I cairn to defend myself in nay engage- ment with your brother." "I was wrong to seem to impeach it; doubly wrong to allow you to see how the knowledge of it affected me. At all events I have only committed myself,' urged Stephen. "And so imposed a duty on me." Here all the anger and sense of injustice died away, and in gentle, sweet tones she continued, "Stephen, we are relations—we must be friends —must therefore respect each other. The future ware too dreadful for me to look at in any other aspect. "For some time after your departure I sank so low in my own esteem that I needed some external aid to raise me. Lord Harlaxton's delicacy in ignoring the cause of the trouble that he could not but see; his constant care and kindness in ministering to my possible wants or desires; the unfailing respect that was as a balm to a still rankling sore; these were things to feel and be grateful for, hut they were not all. "He had been often bitter about you before, never since. On the contrary, he more than once expressed an earnest wish to aid you to an honourable, that might prove if you chose (these were his wvrds) a distinguished career. "At last he spoke in a manner that admitted of no mis- take. But in doing so he conjured me before answering to consult with my best friend, that is to say, the Countess. To that I consented—l fear somewhat disingenuously—for I thought—indeed I felt sure—that I knew beforehand what she would say. I was mistaken. In great depression of spirit she advised the to accept. What she hoped, she said, she would hope no longer—(here Miss Vandeleur paused, then spoke slowly as if troubled to find suitable words to express the substance of the rest of the Countess's sentence), —"after your departure, your prolonged absence, and your silence to us all. She ended with a remark that was in- explicable to me, but that sank deep. She said I might by so acting be the means of a permanent reconciliation be- tween the brothers. That, and that alone, decided me." It was with difficulty and in a broken voice only, that Stephen found power to answer,— "You have nobly justiflal yourself. Would that I could say it leaves me happier ! ' "And now Stephen," said Miss Vandeleur with a forced smile, and a slight recurrence to her former gaiety of man- ner, as seeing how he was affected, and herself no less deeply the while, "I should be all that I feared you still thought me, when I came here, if I did not say this must be our last word on such a subject for evermore." "It shall be so P' rejoined Stephen, " unless—" But she interrupted him. "There can be no such unless !" Pausing a moment or two, she then said,— "You will of course leave the army the earliest moment

you can: - "No," was the reply. "I have passed through the worst —at least I hope so," he added hurriedly, as he remembered his new danger; and with that remembered what he had so entirely forgotten in the interests and excitement of the meeting with Miss Vandeleur—the necessity of hurrying her and his brother away before anything could happen. So he purposely endeavoured to close all he would have liked te say, in a very few words. '1 shall work for a commission, and then return to my family and friends no longer ashamed to meet them." 'oh, Stephen, if what your Major said to Lord Hades- ton, as we came here, be true, you have already achieved in the humblest capacity, a distinguished and houourable re- cord! And is not that a truer glory than if you had done as much in a higher rank and capacity 2" "Perhaps only a mere flash in the pan?' remarked Stephen. "But we shall sea. I have again to ask forgive- ness for so much talk about myself, while I have only just called to mind that my brother waits, and that you have some messuage to deliver from my mother." Gentleman Jack with his usual inquisitiveness, which. meant his usual desire to make eavesdropping profitable, no matter in what way, had passed by twice before while this interview was proceeding, which deeply interested and greatly puzzled him.. He now again came by, and in so doing caught the la words, anti at once found a hiding place in the previously empty hut: which, being open, had been gleaced into by Stephen, as he was about to meet Miss Van Wear, and who turned away satisfied it was empty." " Yes." "She did not know of my being at Gaultmore?" "No one knew—or knows from me." "How then did you learn ?" "From a soldier in your own regiment who read the advertisement—knew you, and then learning we were at Gaultmore, wrote to the Countess claiming the re- ward." "Oh, yes. I understand !" ejaculated Stephen. my interruption." "The Countess being herself too ill to seek you in person, and in such a scene, so earnestly requested me to take her place, that I could not refuse; for she had already won a reluctant assent from Lord Harlaxton. She would not write even for me to bring the letter, ia fear of accidents. ' "I may not remember her precise words, but lam sure of the substance, for she repeated them a second time. Tell Stephen,' she said that his vocation and whereabouts having at last become known through a letter from the person that calls himself Gentleman Jack, and who will presently re- ceive from the solicitors the promised reward, I ask him to apply to the Horse Guards for his discharge, so that at the earliest possible moment he may come here to receive a communication of the highest interest and importance to him persmtlly." Miss Vandeleur tried to Say this in a tone of comparative indifference, so as to attract no attention to the thoughts and feelings which were comsciously excited within her by the words she had to deliver. She was not very successful, for Stephen was the listener. And she still more decidedly failed in her determined pur- pose of seeming equanimity in what remained to be said. . "And that I charge him to keep absolutely unknown to any but himself and you the nature of this message, which Lord Harlaxton will consider to. be springing simply from me. natural desire for Stephen's society." -" Can you throw any light on the subject of what she has to say?" inquired Stephen. "None whatever !" responded Miss Vandeleur, hurriedly, and with an excitement that neither his question nor her answer appeared to suggest or justify. "And nothing would have induced me to bring such a message but my conviction that if I refused the Countess would herself, no matter at what risk, have endeavoured te come to you." "She has known, at least, how to send a messenger whom I cannot gainsay. Tell her, then, I will return the moment I can get leave. There may be some delay. And I cannot possibly apply for my discharge at present. Where shall I find her ? " At Lord Harlaxton's marine villa on the Devonshire coast." "And where, I presume, you will all be?" "No doubt," replied Miss Vandeleur. And then, becoming more and more conscious of her own agitation, and struggling bravely to keep it down, she said to him, as again she tried, to smile, "Well, we have had a long talk, and Lord Harlaxton has been se indulgent that I must now wish eon good-bye," and she held out her hand. Taking and holding it, Stephen said te her, in accents and words of measured strength, and tender, earnest, and profound respect, "Whatever the future may have in store for either of us, I shall feel henceforth, and profit by the knowledge, that I have not lived so entirely in vain as I thought, for I have known you." He stooped, kissed her hand, and turned away. Lord Harlaxton, who had been getting impatient, had moved by degrees nearer, but still waited for the natural cicese of the interview. Then, again stepping a few yards further he saw the separation of the two, and hurried on. As he came to them, Miss Vandeleur said, "I was just comieg to you! lam ready!" And so they separate, Stephen and Lord Herlaxten not

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

The Orange demonstration in Derry on Tuesday passed off without disturbance. There was no assemblage of " Nationalists," and the authorities managed without.diffi- culty to curb the enthusiasm of the Apprentice Boys. A farmer, named John Moylan, was shot dead at ten on Wednesday night, at Annaydown, four miles from Galway. The murder occurred within 300 yards of a police-hut, in which were stationed five men.

MEETING or Lusa MEMBERS.—Arrangements are being made to summon the members of the Irish Parliamentary party to assemble and meet Mr. Parnell in the City Hall, Dublin, before the opening Of next session, to decide on their programme. MURDER OF AN ULSTER FARMER.—A verdict of wilful murder has been returned by a coroner's jury concerning the death of Philip Maguire, a farmer, who was killed at Killycreeny Bridge, near Cootehill, last Sunday night, when returning from a Salvation Army meeting.

THE RATHFARNHAM MURDER: SENTENCE OF DEATH. Peter Wade, labourer, was found guilty at Dublin, on Satur- day, of the murder of Patrick Quinn, at Rathfarnham, on October 27th. The prisoner had some illwill toward the'de- ceased, and on the night of the crime he induced him to go out to meet some one. He then attacked him in a lane, where he left him in a dying state. Sentence of death was passed. A. WEALTHY PAUPER.—At the North Dublin Guardians' meeting, on Wednesday, it was stated that a female- inmate of the workhouse, named Collins, had died, and it was since ascertained that she was worth .E6OO in deposits. A fir m of solicitors now sent a cheque for £3O for her maintenance ard funeral expenses. A guardian remarked that the in- mates were kept so comfortable that they had an inducement to live there. SMOCKING MURDER IN COUNTY ANTRIM. A terrible murder was committed in Lisburn, county Antrim, on Men- day. A man named Doherty, residing near that town, while In an insane condition shot his sister-in-law dead and wounded his wife. Doherty went out with a loaded eun, which he aimed at two girls who were passing on the road to a factory. His wife, however, succeeded in diverting his aim, but she was herself hurt in the struggle. Re-loading the gun, he fired at his sillter-in-law, causing instantaneous death. EXECUTION OF "JOE" POOLE: MORE BUNGLING.—The

notorious Fenian, " Joe " Poole, sentenced to death for the murder of an informer, named John Kenny, was hanged in Richmond Gaol. Dublin, on Tuesday morning. A man who gave the name of Jones, hailing from the neighbourhood of Belfast, acted as executioner. A thrill of horror was sent through the spectators by the discovery, almost immediately after the drop fell, that the condemned man's feet touched the bottom of the pit below the gallows. Death, however, had already taken place. The prison doctor, who was in the pit, said that life was extinct in three and a half seconds, and it was not until soml minutes had elapsed that the feet, through the stretching of the rope, touched the

ground. THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE AND THE LABOURERS' Act.—At a meeting of the Irish National League in Dub- lin, on Wednesday, attention was drawn by one of the speakers to the unfriendly attitude of the farmers in some districts in reference to the Labourers' Act. Mr. Harrington, M.P., however, thought that, considering the time the Act had been in operation, there was no need for complaint, and he expressed the opinion that in this matter mach depended on the character of the representative bodies of a district. He said that in the Limerick Union, where the Board of Guardians had for its chairman an ex-suspect and for its vice-chairman a tenant farmer, no less than £65,000 had been applied for under the Act, and he mentioned a large number of unions in the same province any ene of which, he declared, was applying for a larger sum than the whole province of Ulster, where the labourers were as badly housed as in any part of the country.

THE REV. JOHN Yi-iNGE ON BETrING. In the course of an excellent sermon to young men in the Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge thus made reference to the practice of betting among young men :—Young men are often fond of excitement, consequently, they like to spice oven their re- creations. At one time of day it was enongh excitement for young men to engage in a hearty and healthy game, such as football or cricket. It was enough excitement for such as did not care to play, to be spectators of such sport. But now, and I suppose for some time, another accompani- ment to these trials of strength or of skill has been added in the form of betting and gambling as to the issues of the game. From what I hear, betting is getting as common about games as it has long been about horse races. And what is worse is that many youths who would shrink from betting on a horse race, see no impropriety, or very little, an betting about a match. A spirit of betting seems to be abroad. You bear it in the slang talk of the day. You find I it in quarters where once it would have been shunned as a plague. And, unless lam considerably in error, it is grow- ing very fast. Now, Ido not hesitate to say that in this exciting pleasure, for- I suppose it is c ansidered to be a pleasure, "There is death in the pot." Gambling, however carried on, and whether for little or for much, is the or winning of money upon mere hazard. Now, there can be no question at all that that is a wrong use of money. It is an idle use of property. It is a use of money or property which aims at contravening a providential arrangement; and, that is, that, in the majority of cases, men shall work for their support, for their progress, for their prosperity in the world. The betting man aims to grow rich aiithout effort—without honest toil either of brow or brain. And, he is willing to enrich himself by the accidents of chance, at the expense of his fellow, who must lose in order that he may win. If no other evil were in gambling, there is thus the evil of unmitigate; seiti4liness. Of course, it may be said that where both par. l!s v,nture a risk, the loser has no ground of complaint. P }s,ioly not. But neither party would run the risk, save in the exciting hope, even in both cases the pretty confident expectation that he is safe to win ; and so the sin of egregious selfishness, which minds not another's suffering, if only our end is gained, is mani- fest. It seems to me impossible to indulge in gambling and retain a sensitive conscience and a generous soul. At any rate, it is certain that gambling has been the snare of many a youth. The bat of pence which were his own, has led him on to the bat of pounds which often have not been his own. Many an office lad, or clerk, bas pilfered from the cashbox, or the stamp drawer, or purloined money re- ceived for accounts, in order to carry on this practice. Prob- ably his idea has been with his first gains to replace the " borrowed " money. But, he lost ; and he is lost now, to sight at any rate, behind some prison wall. For that youth, there was social death in that pot. It will be hard work for him when he comes out of his time. A brand will be on his forehead which will take year,s to hide. Ala! and a scar will be on his soul that he at leakt will never forget. I wish that theee-woris could stop any youtla, here who %to begun this pr actice. Depend hpon it, it is bad. Bad to play for halfpence among your friends; bad to play a game on the understanding that the loser pays for the game; bad to bet on any principle or in any way. It may bo an ex- citing pleasure; it may add spiae to your recreation. But it will lower your moral tone ; and it may set you on a line of life that may have a wretched ending. " There is death in the pot." Beware !

A SHORT ROAD TO HEALTH AND WEALTll.—lnstead of bottle of champagne every day at dinner, drink a liottle of CAMMACK'S sparkling PommErrE.—.Advt. THE LANCASHIRE Curros TRADE.—Short time in the cotton trade commenced pretty generally throughout North- East Lancashire on Thursday. The strike is extending, and there are few towns in which there are not some mills stopped. The masters will, it is believed, resume full time after the New Year holidays. RIVER PLATE BANK FRAUDS.—In the London Bank- ruptcy Court, on Thursday, an application was made to re- gister the resolutions passed by the creditors of John Davis WattPrs, stockbroker, convicted of participating in the bank frauds. These were to the effect that the estate should be liquidated by arrangement. A dividend of is. in the Xis expected. A HORRIBLE SITUATION.—A workman in the employ of Messrs. Paddon and Company, of Wrexham, was sent to Buckley on Thursday to do some work at their branch line, and having completed the job he was walking home via the Wrexham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway when he was overtaken by a goods train. He was endeavouring to get off the line to allow the train to pass, when the heel of his boot got jammed in between the points. The train was corn- ing down upon him, and be tugged with desperation to loose himself from this horrible situation. The waggons being close to him, he drew himself sideways off the lino, and had the presence of mind to draw his foot out of his boot (an elastic•side one), and the next moment the train passed over his discarded boot, cutting it into ribbons.

, TERRIBLE DISASTER AT SEA: A MAIL STEAMER BURNT. —A fearful disaster at sea was made known at Dartmouth on Thursday morning. The Norweigan steamer Meta, from St. 'Ubes, and bound for Christiansund, arrived in the morn- ing, and landed data chief officer and 13 of the crew of the Spanish mail steamer St. Augustine, Captain Juan, which was bound from Manilla for Liverpool with a cargo of to- bacco and sugar. A fire broke out on board the Yess?l on, Sunday last while in the Bay of Biscay, and the crew and the passengers eighty-two in number took to the boats to save their lives. The first boat was successful in reaching an English brig. The second boat, however, for some unexplained reason, returned to the burning ship; and the third boat which left has not since been heard of. The fourth boat, which contained the fourteen men, landed at Dartmouth on Thursday, managed finally to reach the Meta, but only after much difficulty and great danger. When they left the burning ship there were still thirty persons on -board, but, as a large steamer was bearing up to them, they are hopeful that they may have been saved. The St. Ang:ustir e was originally the Balmoral Castle, of Donald Currie's I.ne of steamers, but was sold to a Spanish company two years ago. WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.

PAPER ON "THE ATMOSPHERE." The third meeting of the above society was held in the Lecture Room at the Museum, on Thursday evening, when a paper on "The Atmosphere" was read by Mr. Frederick G. Ruddoek (chemist to the White Cross Wire and Iron Company). Mr. Runnoex, in dealing with his subject, observed the atmosphere that surrounded our globe was far too vast a subject to be exhausted in a single }Japer, and the utmost he could do that nieelliwa to draw their attention to a few of tne most interesting chemical and physical changes which were constantly occurring around them. The first problem that presented itself to them was—to what distance from the earth did the atmosphere extend, and: how were they to determine its limit ? Several means had been adopted for the solution of that problem, and the results bad varied from 30 to 200 miles. Air being an elastic fluid, and capable of great expansion and contraction, it was evident that the height must vary considerably with the temperature of the earth's surface immediately beneath it. At the poles, in consequence of the superior attractive force and great degree of cold, the atmosphere was denser than at the equator, and, like the earth, must be shaped as an oblate spheroid. Air then being elastic, those portions nearest the earth, which had to bear the weight of the whole superincumbent mass, must be denser than the portions more distant, or in other words, the atmosphere increased in bulk as the pressure on it was diminished. The celebrated philosopher Mariotte thus first determined the law of the compression of gases, viz., "The volume of gas is inverseleyeas theY pressure to which it is exposed,"and it had also been established that if the air be examined at heights increasing in arithmetical progression, the density de- creased in geometrical progression, as for instance if they took the density of the sea level to be 1, at 3i miles it would be 1, at 7 miles it would be I, at 101, t, and so on; here then they had a means of obtaining the height, and Idiot by entering into a full discussion of the subject, and comparing the observations of Gay-Lussac, Humboldt, and Boassingault, came to the conclusion that the atmosphere could not be less than 30 miles high, at which height it would be about the same tension as they could get it by means of an air pump. There were, however, other methods which were more accurate, viz., the measurement of the penumbra in a lunar eclipse, which gave the height at about 60neiles, and calculating it from the observed length ef twilight. Philosophers from very early times conjec- tural that the air had weight. Aristotle, to prove it, weighed a leather bottle first empty, and then when inflated with air, but finding no difference, concluded that the air was imponderable, and it was not till the year 1650 that Otto de Guinicke, the inventor of the air pump, determined its exact weight. The fact, however, that the air was ponder- able was previously shown by Gallileo in 1640, from ob- serving that a pump was unable to raise water more than 3e feet; he explained this by saying a column of water of that height must be in equillibrium with the weight of the atmosphere. This was confirmed by his pupil Torricelli, who went still further, and reasoned that if this was true the atmosphere %mild support a column of mercury which was about 13i times as heavy as water of 29 inches; this he found to be corree, and to this tube of mercury Pascal gave the name of barometer, and the space between the top of the mercury and the top of the tube was named in memory of its inventor the " Torricel- lien vacuum." At the surface of the earth the atmosphere had a pressure of 151bs. to the square inch, or about 14 or 15 tons weight upon the body of a man of average stature; that pressure was equal en all -sides, the upward pressure being easily proved by filli g a glees full of water, laying a sheet of paper over it and inverting it, when none of the liquor would be spilt. That great weight, instead of crush- ing them to the earth, was absolutely necessary, for the brothers Weber in Germany had proved that the thigh bone in certain positions was kept in its place entirely by atmo- spheric pressure, and the well-known fact of aeronauts bleeding at the nose and ears if they ascended to any great distance was explained by the small blood vessels being un- able to withstand the force of the blood when not counter- balanced by a corresponding pressure from without. The atmosphere was their most important vehicle for the conveyance of sound, which was caused by the vibrations of the particles of some substance acting upon an elastic me- dium connected with their organ of hearing. Though the mast convenient it was by no means the bast conductor. As light in coming in contact with a smooth surface was re- flected, so the waves of sound corning in their course in con- tact with obstacles were also reflected, giving rise to the echo. For an echo to be distinctly produced there must be a minimum distance of 56 feet—a tenth of a second—between the person speaking and the reflector, at a less distance the voice and the echo were confused, making a ruin's voice in some buildings impossible to be heard. In Woodstock Park the echo would repeat 17 syllables in the daytime' and 60 at night, and a portico was built at Olympia which would repeat sound 20 times. Without some conducting medium there could be no such thing as sound; this could be proved by striking a bell in a vacuum when it would net be heard, but as the air was let in it it became more and more audible. Air, when confined in a smooth tube, would conduct sound to a great distance. Blot found that in this way he could carry on a conversation in a low tone at a distanc3 of 3,300 feet. Sound could be heard at great heights, and Flammarion stated that during the silence of the night frogs and crickets could be heard at a height of 3,000 feet ; and asesia, ea. 05 him at:loot:do, hoard m ailyr ay train when at the height of 22,000 feet. The atmosphere received most of its heat directly from the earth's surface, that was to say that the sun's rays passed through the air to warm the earth, from which theywere again radiated; that accounted for the lowering of the temperature as they ascended, the temperature being again lessened by the increase of latent heat which all gases underwent on rarefaction. The tem- perature of mountains was also determined to a great ex- tent by the geographical surroundings. That was very for- cibly shown by the different heights at which the reeeion of perpetual snow commenced on the Himalayas —on the northern slope it was 15,600 feet, and on the southern only 12,200 feet above the level of the sea. As he had just said, the atmosphere was chiefly warmed by the surface of the globe. that was the immediate cause of winds either on a small scale, such as land and sea breezes, which took place on the coasts of tropical countries, or on a large scale as the trade winds. The air at the tropics being heated to a high temperature rose in immense volumes, that which was nearer to the Poles rushing in to take . its place. When the air had risen to a considerable height it proceeded in a horizontal direction towards t'ne poles, gradually descending as it got into cooler latitudes, until, when it had got to about 30 degrees it divided, part returning to the equator as the trade wind and the remainder 'dewing over our own lati- tu les thus causing the south-west wind to be so prevalent with them. The return current from the poles to the equator battling with this was the chief cause of the variable winds in this climate. The trade winds for many centuries were an enigma to meteorologists, and Halley was credited with being the first to suggest the explanation which had since been developed. It was possible, however, that the laws govern- ing winds were known in very early times, for in Eccles- iastes they read :—" The wind goeth towards the south, and turneth about into the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to His circuits." Me now came to a consideration of the composition of the atmosphere, and of some of the numberless chemical changes dependent thereon. These changes were for ever working quietly and invisibly, the results showing them that some great agerty was at work nourishing and vivifying plants and animals, and building up mighty geological formations which at the present rate must have taken ages to produce by the means of animalculte among the lowest of nature's organisms. To carry on life as it was now supported, there were four necessary constituents of the earth's atmosphere—oxygen, nitrogen, aqueous vapour, and carbonic anhydride. These gases existed in a state of mechanical mixture, as shown by the fact that the air dis- saved by rain contained a larger percentage of oxygen than the atmosphere did, a circumstance to which fishes owed their life. Oxygen was necessary for the support of all animal life, by means of the lungs it was brought into contact with the blood, when a • chemical action analogous to combustion took place. Carbonic anhydride was elimi- nated with the production of ht. oxygen was the great supporter of combustion, and they all knew how brilliantly such elements as phosphorus, sulphur, carbon, Sec., burned in the pure gas. To produce carbonic anhydride there were several processes at work. It was formed by the respiration of all animals by the cambustion of carbonised matter, and was evolved in immense quantities from volcanoes and mineral springs. Nature, however, did not allow it to ac- cumulate, but had provided ample means for its use. Plants under the influence of the sun's rays absorbed it, the chlorophyll containing organs being acted upon by the rays, appropriated the carbon lor their own nourishment, and liberated the pure oxygen; thus the carbon was conveyed from them to the plant, by which means it was made fit for the subseqaent nourishment of the man. Everything they ate and drank had already been eaten and drunk millions of times, nothing was destroyed, there was a never ceasing process of putrification going on a the laboratory of nature. Carbonic anhydride in its con- eentrated condition was irrespirable, though not poisonous, for by producing spasms of the glottis it was prevented from entering into the lungs; when mixed with air to the extent of 3 or 4 per cent. it weakened the action of the heart and acted as a narcotic poison, and even when it was present to the extent of only 0.3 per cent. as in crowded rooms which were badly ventilated, its action was very dele- terious, though in this case the effects were very much ag- gravated by the presence of voltile organic germs or par- ticles. It was generally believed that the vitiated !or in a room rose, but that was not the case—the heated air did— but the analysis proved that the composition was the same in all parts of a room. Carbonic anhydride was the choke-damp of the miners, the suffocating gas which was left after an explosion, often causing still further loss of life. In various .parts of the world this gas issued in large quantities from the earth. At Naples there was a small grotto called the " Grotto del Cannes," the air of which contained as much as 70 per cent. of the gas. The keeper had a dog which, having tied its legs to prevent it running away, he placed on the floor of the cavern for the edification of the spectators. The animal at. once began to struggle, and when it appeared to be dying it was taken out and allowed to recover itself in the open air. The blue of the sky was caused by the absorp- tion of the blue rays of the sun by aqueous vapour, and the thicker the atmosphere the more they disappeared as shown by the red or gold colour of the sun as it approached the horizon. Having spoken of the formation of clouds and the remainirrg constituents of the atmosphere he said the causes, &c, he said the causes influencing climate were many, chief among them being the latitude, geological

formation, proximity of the ocean, height above the sea level, mountain ranges, oceanic currents, and prevailing wines. He should like to say a few words on the south- west monsoon of India, a most wonderful phenomenon, and of the utmost importance to India and to the world. Those rains, commencing about the middle of June and lasting for about four months, were ushered in and departed with the more violent thunderstorms, and upon the continuance of that yearly visitation depended the whole of the sum- mer crops. At the vernal esquinox the sun crossed the equator into the northern hemisphere, on May 15th it was verticls over Bombay, and on June 21st reached its summer solstice. Returning, it wae again over Bombay about July 27th, re-entered the tropic of Capricorn Septem- ber 23rd, and reached its winter solstice December 22nd'. It shined tw;ce as long over its solstices or turning points - as over any other part of its course, hence the lands about . latitude 23 degrees were barren. The sun's rays pouring down upon the plains of Cenral Asia and the deserts of North-West India caused an immense volume of air to rise, and a general inrush from around to fill its place. The cur. rent of air from over the Indian Ocean thus occasioned was- strong enough to reverse the north-east trade winds, and even to deflect the south-east from their coarse. This wind, laden with the moisture of the Indian Ocean, struck the West Indian coast, at right angles, the vapour being cooled by the mountains and forests became condensed, and from June to October poured its waters down on the thirsty land, at the same time tempering the heat which would be otherwise unbearable. The pro3perity and fertility of India depended largely upon the deserts of Rajpootana and Scinde, and any large decrease in their area by extended cultivation would probably bring about the most disastrous resnits. Having referred to the oical effects of the atmos- phere, he concluded by observing that meteorology had not yet attained to the dignity of an exact science; of late years, however, it had made great strides, and .though at present meteorologists did not attempt to forecast the weather for a longer period then 24 hours, it seemed probeble, as observations became more numerous, and scientific men were able to study the various moods of nature more closely it (and they must never fcrget that every change was brought about by undeviating laws) ,that she would succumb to the unwearying search after trath, and that man humbling himself before her would subdue her to his uses, to the incalculable benefits of the human race.
THE COST OF A STOLEN KISS AT WARRINGTON.
:MPUDENT IMPERSONATION OF A HUSBAND..

John Brown, a powerful•looking man, about 25 years of age, was charged in custody at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with committing an aggravated assault on Eliza- beth Leigh, on the 3rd of August, 1880; and he was further charged with assaulting Sarah Ann Poole and Joseph Poole in Castle-street, on Saturday last.—Mr. Percy Davies ap- peared for the prisoner.—The Chief Constable said Elizabeth Leigh was the wife of Thomas Leigh, and in August, 1880, resided at Lloyd-street, off Mill-lane, near Sankey Green. The prisoner was a single man and at the time referred to lodged next door but one to the Leighs, and was employed at Monks, Hall, and Co.'s It appeared that about eleven o'clock on the night of the 3rd of August, 1880, Mrs. Leigh locked her door, and placed the key in the scullery window in order that her husband might get it when he returned from work. Her husband worked on the rail- way, and it was Mrs Leigh's custem to leave the Rey in the scullery window when her husband was working in the night. Mrs. Leigh, after locking the door on the night named went to bed, and some little time after the prisoner got possession of the key by breaking a equate of glass in the scullery window. He unlocked the 11. ck door, went to Mrs. Leigh's bedroom, and committed the assault com- plained of. When the prisoner entered her bedroom Mrs. Leigh thought it was her husband returaing from work, but on discovering that it was the prisoner she screamed, the children also screamed, and the prisoner went to the bedroom window and dropped into the yard below. The prisoner afterwards left the town, and was not apprehended until Saturday night last. With respect to the second case, it seemed that on Saturday night Mr. and Mrs. Poole were passing through Castle-street on their way home. Mr. Poole had occasion te leave his wife for a few minutes, and while she was proceeding slowly along the causeway the prisoner came up, put his arms round her neck, and kissed her. She told her husband what had occurred, and he went to the prisoner and asked him what he had done it for, whereupon the prisoner felled him and ran off. Mr. Poole followed, but the prisoner even- tually escaped..—Mrs. Leigh said that on the night of the 3rd of August, 1830, she was at home, and had the company of Mrs. Heath, a neighbour, with whom the prisoner lodged. During the evening the prisoner came to the door and asked for Mrs. Heath, and the latter invited him in. She expected j her husband to returzt home during the evening, but he had not returned at about 11 o'clock, when Mrs. Heath and the prisoner left for home. Before she bade them "good night," she remarked that her husband had not yet returned, and that she should leave the key for him in the scullery win- dow. She went to bed, and fell asleep, but was rudely- ' awakened by a noise in her bedroom. At first she thought her husband had returned home, and was coming to bed. She, however, soon discovered that her surmises were wrong. The witness then corroborated the Chief Constable's 5 statement regarding the assault. When she and the children screamed the prisoner escaped through the

bedroom window, dropping into the yard.—Mrs. Heath, who was called for the defence, said that Mrs. Leigh was "as bad as the prisoner ;" that during the afternoon of the day referred to she paid for him some beer at the Corpora- tion Inn, Market-place ; and that while_ at the latter place . . .

she " smacked him in the face."—The Mayor thought they could not have been very friendly if she smacked him in the face.-Mr. Davies explained that that was only making love to him, and that it was customary for women in a public- house to express their love for a man by smacking him in the face.—The witness, continuin!,o, said that Mrs. beigh in- vited the prisoner to supper, and that while they were get- supper she "made a lot of him." After supper the prisoner paid for several quarts of the best ale, a share of *hich Mrs. Leigh drank. It was about 12 o'clock when she left the house, and they were then "all drunk together." She left Mrs. Leigh and the prisoner together.—Mr. Davies' defence was that Mrs. Leigh was a condoning party.—The Bench decided to hear the second case before giving their decision in the first, and Mrs. Poole was called. Sc said that about 11 o'clock on Saturday night she went into the town, and in returning through Castle-street with her husband the latter had occasion to leave her for a few •aainutes. While she was walking slowly along the street the prisoner came up to her, placed his arms round her neck and kissed her. She said to him "What did you do that for, you great big fool? Wait till my hus- band comes." He, however, did not wait till her husband came, but walked off. Her husband was immediately on the spot, having heard the noise. He went to the prisoner, who had walked some distance away, and asked "What he had done that for." The prisoner struck at him, knocked him into the mud, and eventually made good his escape.: The witness (addressing the prisoner indignantly) : Before you pat your arms round any woman's neck to kiss her you should know who she is, you big fool.—Joseph Poole, husband to the last witness corroborated with respect to the assault upon him, and ;hewed the Bench the coat and trousers he was wearing at the time, and which were be- spattered with dirt.—The prisoner was fined .£5 and cop in the first case, and £2 and costs'in the second, in all £8 is., and in default of payment, he would be imprisoned for three months.

TRE M1:7111:!ER OF A 13111 DE.-A youn woman, named Emma Clarke, died at Birmingham, on Wednesday, from terrible wounds inflicted on her head by her husband. After only being married a week Clarke was apparently seized with madness, and fatally injured his wife with a hatchet.

THE SOCIALIST PLOY—At the Bow-street Police Court, on Thursday, William Woolf and Edward Bondurand were committed for trial, charged with having had in their pos- session at Westminster, explosive substances for an unlaW., ful purpose. It is supposed that the explosives in question were intended for use in a Socialist plot against the German Embassy. -- -

At Leamington, on Wednesday night, a large and hand. somely-ornamentpd Roman Catholic church was almost totally distroyed by a fire which originated in the organ loft. The tower and adjacent presbytery were the only por. tions of the building saved. No estimate is given of the amount of damage caused, but it will certainly he many thousands of pounds. Some men had been tuning the organ just before the fire broke out. AT TEMPTED MURDER IN LIVERPOOL.—WiIIiam Griffiths fruit salesman, was on Thursday committed for trial for attempting to murder his wife, and also with attempting to commit suicide. The prisoner chased his wife into the street, knocked her down, and stabbed her in three places so seriously that her life is in danger. He then cut his own throat in a shocking manner. The wife's solicitor wished to withdraw the charge, but the stipendiary would not allow it, the case being too serious. SHOCKING MURDER AT MARSEILLES.—A collector of the Credit Lyonnais° at Marseilles was recently stabbed and suffocated between two mattresses by some persons occupy- ing a flat on whom he had called to meet an acceptance. They immediately decamped with the 60,000 f. in the victim's portfolio, having merely hired the flat and con. cocted the acceptance for the purpose of inveigling a 001. lector. Three men have just been arrested for this crimes two in Paris and the third at Marseilles. The latter has been identified by the owner of the house, and in his pOS, session was found a sum of 30,000 f., for which he could not satisfactorily account. One of the other men is an old offender; and his companion is an Italian, who was an emigration agent at Marseilles, and disappeared immidiately after the murder.

GERMANY AND NEWSPAPER CRITICISM.—Germany mai be a very pleasant country to live in for some people, but not, it would seem, for editors of newspapers who cannot live happily without gazing upon Royalty. The editor of a Spires newspaper visited Kissingen recently, and in a go& eiping contribution to his newspaper, expressed regret that the King of Bavaria did not more frequently make his 04 pearance. Insteal of being commended for his desire to look upon Royalty, the unfortunate editor has been ssat tO prison for two months, the judge remarking that no one is at liberty to criticise the action of the King. The London journalists who some years ago used to not infrequently commenLon the fewness and farness between one of the Queen's visits to the metropolis may congratulate thertv selves' that they did not exercise their liberties within the jurisdiction of a German law court. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. I', Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Dec. 20th) : The moms of money seeking investments over the supply of channels of outlay, with the necessary undoubted stability, has a great effect on prices, and tends to counteract the adverse effect of gloomy forebodings, tcuching of foreign troubles, and the unsatisfactory relations between capital mid labour in this country. The rbsult is, that though markets are not frisk, values remain very steady, with not a few instances of better prices being established. speaking generally, the money seek- ing employment does not to any extent find its way into the shares of trading concerns, and conseciueutly these classes do not participate much in the effect of the above-named influ- ence; but on the whole these shares maintain their position very well, notwithstanding a very meagre account of business done for the week. Foreign Funds are goad, several advances being masked, while the adverse changes are confined to only one or two stocks. WARRINGTON CIRCUS OF VARIETIES. A DRAMATIC LICENSE GRANTED. On Monday, at Warrington Police Court, Mr. Percy Davis, on behalf of Mr. Brinsley Sheridan, applied for a dramatic license for the Circus of Varieties, Sankey•street. —Mr. Davies said he thought Mr. Sheridan was well known to the Bench, and especially to the Chief Constable, because that was, he believed, the 17th time he had made a similar application to the present one. He was told that during the 16 or 17 years Mr. Sheridan had been lessee and manager of the theatre in Scotland-road, which was now being rebuilt, no complaint whatever bad been made against him. The present application was being made to enable Mr. Sheridan to carry on his business at the Circus until the theatre in Scotland-road was rebuilt. Mr. Sheridan in catering for the public amusement, had made arrangements with certain actors and companies, and the only place in which he could carry out these engagements was the Circus, as the Public Hall was engaged. The only objection against the Circus was that being constructed of wood it was in danger of fire. Mr. Sheridan, however, promised to obviate the possibility of fire by covering all the inflammable material with " cyanite." *Mr. Davies said that wood covered with this substance would not burn, and he quoted a number of authorities in support of the statement. Not only would Mr. Sheridan use the cyanite, but be would have fire ex- tinguishers on the premises, and he would be willing to make any alteration the Corporation might want. Mr. Sheridan also promised to give to the Infirmary the proceeds of the first performance at the new theatre.—The Mayor said the question of Mr. Sheridan giving the proceeds of the first performance to the Infirmary would not have the slightest weight in inducing the Bench either to grant or refuse the application. They would dismiss that from their minds altogether.—Alderman Burgess asked what was the capacity of the Circus, and Mr. Davies replied that it would accom- modate about 1,000 or 1,200 persons.—Mr. John Fair- dough: How many months will you want it 7—Mr. Davies: Five or six.—Mr. Sheridan said that the new theatre was being pushed on as rapidly as possible, but the date of its completion would depend greatly on the weather.—The Bench retired, and on returning the ' Mayor said they had given the questiln their very serious

MYSTERIOUS DISCOVERY IN LIVERPOOL.—A mysterious discovery, in some respects not unlike the famous Waterloo Bridge mystery, was made on Thursday morning in Liver Mill Place, Love-lane, Liverpool. A working man who was passing that way found in the doorway of a warehouse a bundle containing some blood-stained articles of wearing apparel and also a piece of human skull and scalp. The neighbourhood was afterwards examined by detectives, but according to the latest report nothieg in the nature of a clue has been discovered. div.p: DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Harry Hoff Wager, aged 23, who is an able seaman on board the schooner "Corsair," was drowned in the Alford Dock, Runcorn, on'Wednesday. It seems that it was necessary to mo,-. the vessel from one part of the dock to another, and the to4,e instructed Wagner to take a rope to the opposite site of the dock in order to accomplish this. The deceased en- tered a punt, and whilst rowing he dropped an oar, and overbalAncing himself he fell into the water. He was not rescued until five minutes had elapsed and Dr. Muritz, was at once sent for. Every effort was made to restore anima- tion and he seemed in a likely way to recover. He suc- cumbed, however, about two hours afterwards. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body on Thursday afternooa. After hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of accidental death.
VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A YOUNG WOMAN AT RUNCORN.

At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Hugh Goldrick was brought up, under a warrant, charged with committing an aggravated assault upon Eliza Webster.—The prosecu- trix resides at Widnes, but on Saturday evening, the Bth indent, she attended a dance at Runcorn Drill Hall, which she left about 10 o'clock. As she was proceeding to the Bridge, along Bridgewater-street, the prisoner, who was ac- companied by two other men, blocked up the footpath, telling her that there was plenty of room for her in the street. She asked him to allow her to pass, whereupon be took her umbrella from her and broke it upon her face, making both of her eyes black. He also struck her with his fist and kicked her, and then ran away. P.S. McMichael endeavoured to execute the warrant opon,the prisoner, who had, however, absconded. On Wednesday morning, how- ever, the prisoner gave himself up at the Runcorn Police Station.—He was remanded until Monday in order tkat wit- nesses might be called.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. TRIENNIAL ELECTION: NOMINATION OF CANDIDATES.

Mr. H. Linaker, solicitor, is the returning officer in this election, and he yesterday (Friday) gave notice that the undermentioned persons bad been duly nominated as can- didates for election as members of the Board :—John Bar- clay, The Vicarage. Runcorn, clerk in holy orders; Peter Briscoe, Bridge-street, Runcorn, grocer; John Buckley, 37, Wellington-street, Runcorn, surveyor; William Fennelly, Albert Terrace, Runcorn, Roman Catholic priest; William Fisher, Highfield. House, Runcorn, agent; John Robert Fritb, Belle Vue House, Halton-road;Runcorn, gas engineer; William Handley, 83, Bridge-street, Runcorn, bootmaher ; George Stewart Hazlehurst, Sonthlands, Rhyl, gentleman; Frederick Arthur Lake, Stanley Villas, Runcorn, gentleman; Richard Lea, High-street, Runcorn, postmaster; Finlay McDougall, High-street, Runcorn, surgeon; Thomas Nor- man, 17, Greenway-road, Runcorn, pipe manufacturer; Samuel Pope, Halton-road, Runcorn, manager of alkali works; William Preston, Higher Runcorn, clerk in holy orders; James Pritchard, Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, ship owaer ; Robert Shaw, The Highlands, Higher Runcorn, alkali manufacturer; Matthew Steele, Heath House, Run- corn, alkali manufacturer; William Whittaker, Mough- lands-lane, Runcorn, gentleman; Walter John Wigg, Halton Lodge, Runcorn, alkali manufacturer. The number of per- sons to be elected is seven, and nineteen gentlemen have been nominated. In the event of more persons remaining as candidates after four o'clock on Monday, the 24th De- cember than there are members to be elected a poll will be taken on Monday, the 31st December. Mr. Simpson, the vice-chairman of the Board, having announced his inten- tion of withdrawing, was not nominated. With this excep- tion all the retiring members are nominated.

div.head: COWLEY'S BRITISH SCHOOLS, ST.
div.p: COWLEY'S BRITISH SCHOOLS, ST.
HELENS.

The annual re-union in connection with these schools took place in the Town Hall. on Wednesday evening. Major W. W. Pilkington presided, and there was a good number of people present. Previous to the commence- ment of the proceedings a number of drawings, specimens of writing, kc., by the scholars, were en view in a side chamber and were deservedly admired. Some draw- ings, both of landscape and of animals, and a pen and ink sketch executed by a scholar named J. Mcßryde, and only nine years of age, were in particular much com- mented upon and praised. The Chairman, in a few intro- ductory remarks, said he had been very kindly asked by Mr. Dutton to preside there that evening, and he came very gladly for several reasons, He looked upon the Cowley Schools as one of the best institutions in St. Helens. (Ap- plause.) They all knew that the operation of the laws with regard to education rendered it advisable that there should be a change in the distribution of the endowment, and that had undoubtedly been a very wise change, and one which had produced a echool which was a credit and would no doubt be a great benefit to the town of St. Helens. At the same time they must remember that the present Cowley School was very near what the old Cowley School had , been. He believed that at the present day, if not the lead- ing school, it was one not behind any other elementary school in the town. He hoped the scholars belonging to the Cow- ley Schools—the old scholars as well as those that were there new—would takea real pride in the old school. There was no reason why they should not be as proud of Cowley School as come Eton, Ruby, and Harrow boys were of their schools. It should be the aim of the boys at the Cowley elementary schools to step up to the higher school, and he thought the old elementary school should be a great feeler to the higher Cowley School. (Applause.)— After he bad distributed the prizes won by scholars for good attendance, good conduct, and drawing, .the Chairman said that the inspector's report stated, with regard to the boys' school, that discipline was very efficiently maintained throughout this large school; the tone and organisation being equally satisfactory. The work, taken as a whole, both as rsgarded mechanical finish and intellectual value, wac much better than it had been for some years. With regard to the girls' school, discipline was excellent, and the instruction as a whole good. The girls displayed a credit- able amount of accuracy, neatness, and intelligence in their work. The infants in elementary subjects were on the whole well advanced. The number of boys, girls, and infants was 777, viz.: 344 boys, 232 girls, and 201 infants. The average attendance was 648 (Applause.)—ln the course of the evening a programme of music and songs was per- formed by the boys in a way which showed excellent train- ing. A number of them also performed a portion of Shake- peareis "Julius Caner" j a most creditable style.

div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY—Before Mr. W. Blinkhorn and Mr. W. L. Evans. UNION PEOSECUTIONS.—WaIter Bushell was charged with running away from Widnes, on the sth November leaving his children chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. Mr. B. H. Hartley prosecuted, and said the prisoner had agreed to pay the costs, a Is. 6d.. and take his two children from the Workhouse; apd it the magistrates approved of that course he would ask for a remand until the 26th instant, to give the defendant the desired opportunity. The prisoner was remanded.—Nicholas Gillon was charged with neglecting to obey an order of the Bench. Mr. B. H. Hartley said the mother of the defendant was admitted into the Workhouse in January of this year, and on the 7th February the court ordered the defendant to contribute Is. 6d. per week towards his infirm mother. He paid nothing whatever, and in November he was summoned for disobedience of the order, and an order for im- mediate payment was made. Hs had also disregarded this order, and a distress warrant was issued. It had been returned marked "no goods." He now asked their worships to commit him to gaol. Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, stated that the amount due to the Guardians was £5 10s. The defendant was working at Messrs. Muspratt's, in Liverpool, and was in receipt of £1 14s. per week. He was fully able to pay. The defendant, who did not appear, was ordered to pay the money forthwith, or go to gaol for six weeks. _ .

A HARD OA—SE.—John McCann was summoned to show cause why he should riot contribute to the support of his two children, who are inmates of a Liverpool Industrial School.— It was stated that the defendant was in receipt of 15s. 4d. per week, with which he had to support three childiren. He had promised to pay is. 6d. per week; and the Bench made an order for the payment of that sum. BLEEPING OUT.—John Skelly was convicted of sleeping in a chemical works, this morning, and sentenced to seven days' hard labour.

OBSTRUCTING THE RIVER WEAVER AT SUTTON.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Heys, boatman, was brought up on a summons charged with having, oa the 11th bast., obstructed the river Weaver at Sutton.—Mr. Trafford, of Northwich, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Weaver Navigation Company, and stated that the defendant, who pleaded guilty, was in charge of a manure boat, named Christopher. On Tuesday night he moored 'his boat to the wharf at Sutton, and about ten o'clock a steamer came past. One, of the ropes which held the defendant's boat broke, the boat collided with the bridge, which could not be turned. James Fletcher, the bridge tenter, asked the defendant to assist in removing his boat out of the way, but he refused to do so. A great number of people wished to pass across the bridge, but in consequence of the defendant's conduct they were.compelled to go round by the viaduct, which considering the wildness of the night was not very pleasant. About one o'clock the other rope which secured the boat broke, obstructing the river entirely. A steamer and several boats came up at the time,,bint the defendant would not allow his boat to be removed, and they had to stay there until six o'clock.—The Bench tined the defendant £l, and costs Os ad.

div.head: SHOCKING SCENE ON GREENBANK.
div.p: A SHOCKING SCENE ON GREENBANK.

Mary Kate Ford, a young-looking woman, was on Tues- day charged at the Gt. Helens Police Court with having been drunk and disorderly on Monday night.—P.C. Hander- son said he apprehended the defendant for having been drunk and disorderly, and took her to her house in Short-street, Greenbank. He there found three children, two of them being completely naked, and there was nothing in the house to cover them. There war no furniture in the house with the exception of an old dirty bed in a corner. It was the filthiest and most destitute house he had ever been in.— P.C. Cottam said that he had seen one of the children sit- ting crying, and be had been told by some neighbours that on the previous night they had watched the children sitting at the fire-grate chewing cinders to appease their hunger, the mother being out at the time. He went to seek a relieving officer, but not finding one, he went back to the house and saw one of the children, completely naked, crawling down the passage. The night was a very cold one. He bad seen the prisoner twenty minutes before in the Grapes Hotel buying a pint of beer.—The prisoner said her husbmd was working at Tyldesley.—Superintendent Johnston slid she had been thrice convicted this year of drunkeimg3.—She was seat to gaol for 14 days

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 22, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 22, 1883.
WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.

ANNUAL CONCERT. The annual concert in connection with the People's College, Warrington, took place at the Public Hall on Thursday evening, and all concerned may be congratulated upon the very successful manner in which the programme was carried out. The event .is always looked forward to with considerable inserest by the scholars, and consequently there was a large gathering. The body of the hall and gal- leries were filled with with parents and friends, the raised platform being reserved for the young people—who were tastefully attired—forming the chorus, and which consisted of about 400 voices. The chair was taken by J. G. McMin- nies, Esq., M.P., there being also present Aid. J. R. and Mrs. Pickmere, Alderman C. J. Holmes' Councillor Monks, Mr. E. Brewtnall, Mr. S. Barlow, Mr. Milner (secretary), Mr. Twiss (head master), clzc. Mr. McMitexiss, at the outset, said he was very glad to see so large an assembly that night, and he had no doubt they would all be rewarded by spending a very pleasant evening. He should not take up their time by announcing each piece in its turn, because he supposed the programmes were pretty well distributed. They would therefore proceed at once with the concert. (Applause.) Part 1 then commenced by the chorus singing "The hills resound," which was inspiriting, and rendered with ptecision. The applause which greeted this their first effort of the evening was not merely that which is frequently termed " friendly" in such an assembly, but it was thoroughly well merited. This was followed by the song. ",Oh! the oak and the ash," which was no less successfully given. Throughout the concert we were particularly struck with the precision and harmonious blending of the voices— evidently the result of careful practice and training. Mr. J. Spence Hodgson, of Altrincham, next gave a recitation, en- titled, "King John and the Abbot of Canterbury." In this as in his other recitations, Mr. Hodgson displayed a fair amount of elocutionary ability, but his happy style of delivery and his keen sense of humour were the chief characteristics of his contributions. Generally speak- ing, recitations at school entertainments are stale and lengthy, and the reciter is often looked upon by many as a bore, but Mr. Hodgson's selections were judicious, and indeed to the listener most entertaining. Following Mr. Hodgson's recitation came the favourite song "Three merry men," the rendering of which was 'satisfactory. Hntchi- son's popular song, "Dream faces," was charmingly sung by the juveniles, and. in the succeeding refrain, Bath's "The old brigade," the full strength of the voices was heard to advantage. Miss Wilson sang with much expression and sweetness "Fair Zurich's waters," which secured her an encore, to which she responded by singing the last verse. The well known "Soldier's chorus," from Gounod's Faust, was well given, and Mr. J. Spence Modgson having recited "The pied piper of Hamelin," by Browning, the first por- tion of the programme was brought to a close by the ever. welcome song "Sailing." During the interval Mr. Councillor MILNER addressed the audience. He said he thought it was very desirable that they should know year by year what Her Majesty's Inspec- tor said of the school. (Hear, hear.) Since he last read a report in that hall many were aware that there had been a very considerable change in what was called the Govern- ment Code. They had had many new Codes, and hitherto every new Code had been looked upon as something terribly hard to be met and which would ruin all the schools in the country. But he might say that the elementary schools of England had stood those advances very well and had steadily improved in quality from year to year. (Hear, hear.) The last Code was supposed to be worse than any of its pre- decessors, but that was not proved so in their case, and would not be so proved in any school which was thoroughly well managed, and had such an efficient staff of teachers as they had. (Hear, hear.) He mentioned that so that his hearers might understand the reference made to the Code by the Inspector. Another thing in the New Code was that an entirely new grant had been made which was at the discretion of the Inspectors—a kind of good conduct grant. Schools were divided in their reports now into "fair," "good," and "excellent." The first, "fair," ob- tained a grant of is per head, " good " 2s, and " excellent " 3s. He was very pleased to state that on this first inspec- tion they had received the highest grant. (Applause.) As another evidence of the successful teaching in the school, many, he dare say, would know that in the examination for free scholarships at the Warrington Grammar School, which took place last week, two of their boys were again successful. (Hear, hear.) Last year one of their pupils also took a scholarship there, and this year that same boy had walked off with a considerable number of the prizes given in the Grammar School. (Applause.) It was a great satisfaction to learn of scholars from that school, when in competition with the Grammar and other schools, being so often successful in carrying away the prizes, but that was not done without very considerable work on the part of the teaching staff. (Hear, bear.) He had just been thinking over the number of their teaching staff some years ago, when they had a total roll of 159, and he had added up the present staff, which was 32, one-fifth of the total number of scholars say 12 years ago. (Applause.) Councillor Monks had reminded him of another success of pupils of that school, which he was very glad to mention. Miss nettle Twiss, daughter of the headmaster, had obtained a first class Queen's scholarship, and was 109th out of a total numer of 4,200 pupil teachers examined. She would go to the Stockwell Training College for the next two years. Mr. Herbert Cook had also been successful in ob- taining a situation in the Civil Service, and at the examina- tion was 33rd out of 1,500 candidates. (Applause.) The following report of Her Majesty's Inspector, W. Scott fs'largisvFeo=49olPnlerroenrisdißgritA3PchllB34 Was thc'n rliag oar are presen e this year in excess of the number last year, the average atten- dance showing an increase. The effort to prepare so large a number for examixation (804) under the new code must have been considerable, but the school has very successfully and creditably fulfilled every additional requirement; and its in- struction in all subjects and classes taken as a whole is main- tained fully at its former high level of thoroughness and in- telligence, the discipline, organization, and gene al tone being equally satisfactory. The singing from note for a first attempt Is successful and promising. A good deal of taste characterises the songs. The drill and needlework are also good. The pupil teachers have passed very creditably indeed, and knowledge both of the theory and practice is much above the average of the pupil teachers of my district. The greatest credit is due to the diligent and able master and staff for these results. The only points that need attention are the reading of the boys In the fifth standard as regards ease and fluency ; and arith- metic in the third, where old work is Lot very well known. The Branch Infants' Schools.—Bank Quay: "The order maintained amongst these little -.;:hildren continues to be very good indeed, and they have been carefully and intelligently grounded in the elementary subjects. They also showed a good knowledge of the matter of their object lesssons."— Cairo-street: "These infants are in excellent order, and are generally well and successfully taught in most respects, th.dr Instruction showing much impcement. A good and sensible attempt has been made to sa isfy the requirements of the new code, and with promising results. I should like to have readier, brighter, and more general answering." The second portion of the programme was equally pleasing, and consisted of the following :—Song, "March of the men of Harlech ;" song, " Spring, gentle spring recitation." A Yorkshire ghost story." Mr. J. Spence Hod- son; song, "Cuckoos ong :" song, "Love, I will love you for

ever ;" song, Powder—monkey ;" song, "Two sp-oons ;" recitation, "The bashful man," Chapman, excellently given; song, "The blue bells of Scotland ;" song, "The last rose of sutnmer ;" song, " The British grenadiers ;" ." God save the Queen." One of the best items was the song " The powder monkey," in which a novel feature was introduced in a whistling accompaniment by the boys, and which was exceedingly effective. The audience showed their appre- ciation of this by demanding a repetition, which was com- plied with. Credit is due to Mr. Spence Hodgson for his assistance to the chorus, whilst Mr. Pattison presided at the organ with his usual ability. Altogether a most enjoyable evening was spent. A vote of thanks was at the close accorded Mr. MeMinnies for presiding, this being proposed by Mr. Brewtnall, and seconded by Councillor Monks. Mr. McMinnies, in respond- ing, alluded to the very liberal manner in which Mr. J. Gros- field had always supported the College.

div.head: CHRISTMAS DECORATIONS.
div.p: THE CHRISTMAS DECORATIONS.

It. might almost be said that Christmas is stealing in upon us unawares, the usual accom- paniments of frost and snow—distinguishing charac- teristics which to the strong and healthy are so necessary to a due appreciation of Yuletide—having failed thus far to put in an appearance, and to act as gentle reminders of the approach of this the great festive season of the year. Dar- lag the week, however, the tradesmen of the town have been busy making preparations for dieplaying their respective goods to the best advantage, and a great many of the shops and shop windows have therefore assumed a very gay and attractive appearance. As in previous years the shop of Mr. William Lawless, Corporation•street, is replete with the usual appurtenances to a poulterer, and has been the centre of ,nauch attraction. It contains some fine French geese, Norfolk ducks, and game, the latter having been killed at Knowsley. Mr. A. Riley, of Sankey-street, also makes an exceedingly good show of goods of the description :just mentioned. The various butchers' shops present a most unfaminelike appearance, and those of Mr. James Bowcock, Iforsemarket-street, Mr. W. Gill, Mr. J. Shaw, Mr. A. Bowcock, Mr. Grounds, Mr. J. Hatton and Mr. Mellor, all of Bridge-street, and Mr. J. Cross, Market- place, hive been an attraction to hundreds cf peeple. The carcases in several eases have been arranged In semi-circle and bear the names of the feeders. As having special attractions in provisions, we might mention the Liverpool House, Winwick-street, Mr. G. E. Price, Mr. J. B. Isaac, Sankey-street. and Mr. William Isaac, Buttermarket- street. Mr. N. B. ,Percival's establishment, Buttermarket- street, has an attractive display of groceries., such as pre- served fruit, bnecuits, and cheese; as also have those of the Lendon and Counties Tea Company, and Mr. Henry Horsemarket-street, and Messrs. Lawlees Brothers, Market-place. Mr. John Buck, Sankey-street, Mr. Frederick Wright, Horsemarket-street, and Mr. Virilliam Hoklgkinson, Bridge-street, are making cplendid shows of millinery, art needlework, fans, gloves, ; while in clothing Messrs. linswortla Brothers, Market Place, the Manchester Tailoring and Clothing Depot, Horsemarket-street, and the Grand Clothing Hall, Bridge-street, are deserving of notice. Mr. T. H. Po:qr.., Horsemarket.street, aud Mr. W. J. Dun, Sankey-street, have their windows bedecked and made at- tractive with fire arrays of hosiery. Messrs. J. and W. Dutton. Sankey-stseet, have a splendid show of carpets, cur- tine, and also a quantity of fancy , goods. . WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.—Mr. W. S. Woods has been appointed Professor of Music at the above college in succession to Dr. Hiles, resigned.
