PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIA- TION.—On Wednesday evening, the members of the above association met in the Wesleyan Day School, when a very excellent essay on "Robert Burns" was given by Mr. H. Fitton, Runcorn. ODDFELLOWS' BALL.—The Co-operative Hall was the scene of a gay assembly of Warrington Oddfellows on Tuesday evening, when about 60 persons were present, and dancing kept up vigorously from, nine o'clock until the early hours of the morning. An enjoyable time was spent. BANK QUAY WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.—A public Band of Hope meeting was held in connection with the above place on Thursday week. There was a very good attendance, and at the close two aged men took the pledge. The chair was occupied by Mr. H. Pickersgill. An excellent pro- gramme of songs, recitations, &c.' was admirably executed The usual compliments concluded the proceedings. ELECTION TO FREE SCHOLARSHIPS AT THE WA.ZEING- TON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—On the results of an examination held on Saturday last at the Grammar School, the following boys have been elected scholars on the foundation :-1, J. W. Isherwood, People's College; and 2, H. Kay, People's College. Proaime accesserient:—J. F. Dabsou. People's CAlege ; G. J. Wilde, National School, Church-stmt. Tuere were eleven candidates.

PENKETH ELEMENTARY DAY SCNOOIS. The scholars, to the number of 200, attending the above schools, broke up for their Christmas holidays on Thursday afternoon, when an invitation had been sent by the master, Mr. James Watson, for all parents to be present. We noticed amongst others who attended Mr. and Mrs. D. Garnett, Mrs. R. Gar- nett, Mrs. Griffiths, Mrs. Lee, Mr. John Mainter, tkc. The master had proviaed a good programme, which was ex- cellently rendered. THE MAINTENANCE OF PARENTS.—James Boyle, baker, 21, Baldwin-street, St. Helens, was summoned to the War- rington Borough Court, yesterday, to show cause why an order should not be made upon him for the maintenance of his mother, who is chargeable to the common fund of the Workhouse. Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, applied for an order for 2s 6d, which WAS wade accordingly.—Thomas O'Brien, labourer, 46, John-street, was summoned under similar circumstances, the case being also proved by Mr Shearer. There were arrears in this instance amounting to £2, under an order of ds per week previously made. De- fendant pleading poverty, the magistrates reduced the order to 3s per week, and directed him to pay the arrears by in- stalments of is per week in addition. Sr. THOMAS'S CHURCH, STOCKTON HEATH..A choral ser- vice was held in the above church on Tuesday evening, when the choir performed the oratorio, "Th. Prodigal Son." The service was commenced by the Vicar (Rey. T. 8. Tofts) reading the Confession, Absolution, and the Lord's Prayer, after which the hymn, "All people that on earth dc dwell," was sung. The oratorio was then gone through, the solos, recitatives, and arias being taken by Messrs. Green- house, Pearson, Howard, Leghorn, and Risley, and a duet by. Messrs. Greenhouse and Howard. Several hymns were in- terspersed. The Rev. T. S. Tofts conducted, and Mr. J. R. Timsen ably presided at the organ. An offertory was made on behalf of the choir fund. There was a large congrega- tion pres nt. THE ROPE STEALING CASE.—On Wednesday, at War- rington County Petty Sessions, William Flannagan and Ed- ward Foy, rag gatherers, of Bank-street, were charged, on remand, with stealing 60Ibs of rope, value 55., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co.—Mr. Pres- ton, jun., of Chester, appeared for the Company.—lt seemed that on Saturday, the Bth inst., the rope was used for moor- ing some flats on the canal at Watermeetings, near Burton- wood. The prisoners were seen going in the direction of Watermeetings in the afternoon, and on the following Mon- day morning the rope was missing. Enquiries were made, and it was found that the rope had been sold for 3s. to Pat- rick Mannion, marine store dealer, of Bank-street. The prisoners, when apprehended and charged with the theft, said that they bought the rope off a man at Winwick.—The prisoners were sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. LOYAL ORANGE INSTITUTION OF ENGLAND.—At the monthly meeting of the Earl of Beaconsfield Lodge, held at the Blue Lion, Warrington, on Monday evening, Bro. Jolley presiding, the following resolution was unanimously carried :—" That we, the members of the Earl of Beacons- field Lodge of Loyal Orangemen, do hereby express our in- dignation at the conduct of the Government in the suspen- sion from the commission of the peace of the Right Hon. Lord Rossmore, and beg to tender to that nobleman the best thanks of this meeting for his manly, outspoken, and patriotic action against the attempted encroachments of sedition and reballion in the loyal province of Ulster; and further, we desire to express our opinion that the action of the Government will tend to encourage the seditious and disloyal, and produce a feeling of dissatisfaction among the loyal inhabitants of our sister country." How THE WARRINGTON PUBLSCANE ARE IMPOSED UPON.—Yesterday, at the Warrington Borough Court, John Cook, farm labourer, last from Knutsford, was brought up on the charge of being on the premises of Alfred Woodhead, Higher Angel, Buttermarket-street, on the previous after- noon, for an unlawful purpose.—P.C. Hennessey haying deposed to receiving the prisoner into his custody, Mrs. Wilndhparl. the landlady. at.t.d th.f prig"... Laic. house and asked for a glass of whiskey. He took the glass in one hand, and with the other he felt in his trousers' pocket with the evident intention of paying for the liquor, but he then said he had lost his money.—Mr. H. B. White: He did not lose the whiskey ?—Witness: No, he tonk eire of that. (Laughter.)—Captain Reynolds: They don't often serve you like that, do they P—Witness : A great many come in with that intention.—He was sentenced to a week's hard labour.
PRESENTATION TO TEACHERS AT WARRINGTON.—Coun- __ .

cillors Monks, at the request of the headmaster of the People's Collige, prismted Miss Hettie Twiss, Miss Alice Dignum, and Mr. Herbert Cook, each, on Tuesday, with a handsome writing desk, as marks of esteem and good wishes on the completion of their apprenticeship as pupil teachers in the school. Miss Dignurn has been ap- pointed assistant-mistress in the Sankey National School. Miss Twiss obtained a first-class Queen's scholarship at the July examination for admis.ion to the training colleges for schoolmistresses, her name standing 100th mit of a list of over 3,200 candidates, and will complete her studies at the British and Foreign School Society's Training College, Stockwell, near London. Mr. Cook has been appointed clerk in the commercial department of the Board of Trade Whitehall, he haying successfully passed the Civil Service examination in August last. His name stood 33rd out of close upon 100 candidates in the final examination.

SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENT Ar ST. PETER'S, WARRING- TON.—On Monday evening another of the series of enter- tainments for the winter season took place, the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar of Halton, presided. As the majority pre- sent were parents of children in attendance at this school, the Chairman, in his opening remarks, pointed out to them the necessity of punctuality, as well as regularity, and the many advantages accruing thereby. The rev. chairman re- marked how pleased he was to hear from their own clergy- man what an excellent head-mistress Miss Jones was, and how gratifying it was to him to hear, and satisfactory to the managers of St. Peter's to have received, from Her Majesty's inspector recently, so good a report, as well as an increased grant from the Education Department. This was all the more pleasing to him (the chairman) because it was in his schools at Halton that Miss Jones had received her early training, prior to entering St. Elphin's Training College. A capital programme was subsequently carried out to the evident satisfaction of the audience. Miss Riley and Mr. Hill, of He!shy, presided at the piano. EFFECTS OF INTEMPERANCE AT WAuntretnote.—Margaret Ball, 51 years of age, a widow residing at Ileaton-square, off Orford-street, died suddenly on Monday morning. Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, held an inquest at the Waggon and Horses Inn, Buttermarket-street, on Wednesday afternoon. Evidence was given showing that the deceased had been a widow for about three years, but that daring the last few months she had cohabited with a man named John Griffiths. Of late she had drunk very heavily, and she and Griffiths were intoxicated on Saturday night. On Sunday she had a black eye, and complained that Griffiths had ill-used her on the previous night. Dr. Starkey Smith made a past-mortem exaraination of the body on Tuesday, but found no marks of violence which could account for death. The liver and kidneys were vary much congested, and indicated drinking habits. He was of opinion that the deceased died from epilepsy. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from natural causes., probably epilepsy. The. Coroner remarked that the surroundings of the case were very deplorable. TRINITY COLLEGE LOCAL EXAMINATIONS: DISTRIBU- TION OF PRIZES AT WARRINOTOIL—OE Tuesday evening the prizes and certificates awarded iu the Warrington centre at the ex tminations, held in June last, were presented in Cairo-street schoolroom by Mr. John White. Mr. Newcombs, in the absence of Mrs. Newcomb, who acts as local secre- tary, referred at some length to the examinations, and then gave the following list in the order of merit of the success- ful candidates, whom he heartily congratulated :—William Thistlewaite, first prize, value £1 108' special musical hon- ours, 2nd class; William Brown, 2nd prize, value 15s, special musical honours, 3rd class; Annie Sewards, special musical honours, 3rd class; M. E. Haworth, honours, 3rd class; A. Mary Swift, honours, 3rd class; Flor. Toft, 3rd prize, value 15e; Ada Cie rimes, 4th prize; F. Maybury, Clara Podmore' C. L. Runeorn, and Hettie Twiss, equal; Mary Fletcher and John Healey, equal ; J. E. Cunningham, H. Allen, M. E. Robinson, E. A. Place, M. Chandley, Any Place. h Mr. White having distributed the prizes, said Mr. Newcombe had placed in his hands a statement of the result of the last examination, from which he saw that there were 23 candi- dates who offered themselves at the examination in June last. Two did not put in an appearance, and only two of the remainder failed to satisfy the examiners, which he thought was a very satisfactory result for the first examina- tion in the town. He urged them to make every use of the advantages offered by the Warrington Musical Society's elementary class, so well conducted by Mr. Woods, and of the local centre connected with Trinity College. Though Warrington was not a musical town, it was wonderful in many respects for the diffusion of learning. Few towns could boast of such a Museum and Library, or such a Liteeary and Philosophical Society and Art Gallery. They had also science classes and lectures on many subjects and now they Aeemeci to be taking up this much neglected act of , ' music.

HIS 80TH APPEARANCE AT THE POLICE COURT.—John Rohan, of Cropper's-brow, made his 80tia appearance at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, when he was ordered to pay 10s. and costs, or go to prison 14 days' for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, ea Saturday night.

RHELOW, THE ILLUSIONIST.—It Will be noticed from our advertising columns that this talented gentleman is to give a series of his entertainments in the Workmen's Club, next week, commencing on Monday evening. '.The entertain- ment is entitled " Pidianuktathceka," introducing experi- ments in prestidigitation spirit manifestations, and sensa- tional wonders. Mr. prestidigitation, illusions are, we believe, new to the Warrington people; and what is called his "light seance" is brimful of laughter and incbmprehen-, sible. We bespeak for the professor that fair share of public support which his entertainment merits. WARRINGTON INFTRMARY AND DlSPENSARY,—House- surgeon's report for the week ending Thursday, Dec. 20. Patients admitted and discharged: Home patients, 7; out patients, 35; accidents, 16; total, 58. Cured, 0; dead, 0; discharged, 0; total, 0. Present number of home patients, 23. In-patients: Admitted, 1; discharged, 2; remaining in hospital, 14. Hon. treasurer, J. R. Buckton, Esq. ; hoc. secretary, Joseph Davies, Esq.; house-surgeon, Mr. C. E. Richmond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for con- tributions of old linen, •Izc. Medical officer for ensuing week, Mr. Joseph. THE COST OF A DRUNKEN FREAL—Thomas Maguiness, of Angel-yard, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with steaing three pairs of socks from Mr. Poole's, Horsemarket-street.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, but said that he stole the socks in a drunken freak.—lt seemed that the prisoner was seen to take the socks from Mr. Poole's shop and then to walk away with them. Mr. Poole was in- formed reoe u ght him back. of the v occurrence,irheh charged thhe tfhoel theft at initheauPdolbi Sta- tion the prisoner said "I could not help it."—He was or- dered to pay 20s. including costs, or go to prison for a month.

A MAN WHO REFUSES TO MAINTAIN HIS WIFE.— Richard Lee, plumber and ga.sfitter, last from West Brom- wich, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, with disobeying an order of the court. On the 15th January the prisoner was sent to gaol for assaulting his wife, and a judicial separation and an order for lOs per week were granted. Since his incarceration the prisoner had not paid anything, and the amount now owing to his wife was £ll. —The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprison- ment with hard labour, and the Bench told him that if ho did not try to pay the amount due when he was released from gaol he would again be imprisoned. THE NEW THEATRE AT WARRINGTON.—Within the last week or two rapid progress has been made in the erection of the new theatre on Scotland-road, and the public an now have a pretty adequate idea of what the building will be when completed. The front wall is almost finished, and workmen will soon be employed in roofing the structure. Mr. Sheridan, the respected proprietor, is anxious to have a theatre worthy of the town, and where the comfort of both actors and audience will be studied.. A few months will, we. think, show that in this he has succeeded. During the interim Mr. Sheridan has engaged dramatic companies to appear at the Theatre of Varieties, in Sankey-street, which was this week specially licensed for the purpose. THE PANTOMIME AT THE ROYAL ALEXANDRA THEATRE, LIVERPOOL. —lt Will be noticed from our advertising columns that the enterprising lease of the Royal Alexandra Theatre, Liverpool, has made ample provision for the wants of her numeroas patrons daring the Christmas season. To- day (Saturday) the pantomime of Jack the Giant Killer is to be produced for the first time. Neither time, trouble, nor expense have been spared in order to make the pantomime a success, and some of the best talent in the country is en- gaged upon it. The scenery, the music, the costumes, mad an the properties are alike highly spoken of by the Liver- pool Press, and we bespeak for the pantomime stitch a run as will amply reward_ the caterer for her efforts.

POST OFFICE, WARRINGTON.—The following are the postll arrangements for Bank Holiday for Warrington and district :-1. No delivery will be made after the morning or first delivery. 2. The public counter at the head office will be closed at 12 noon for all business except telegraph work, the accepting of parcels, the sale of stamps, and the regis- tration of letters. Money order business will also be sus- pended at all sub-offices at 12 noon. The only collection of letters, &c., for that day will be made from the pillar mad wall boxes for the night mail despatch. 4. Rural posts will work as one other days, except as regards the devatch of day mails to the sub-offices. 5. Parcels will be received during the same hours as on other days it those offices kept open. There will only be one delivery and one collection of parcels. 6. Special notices will be exhibited as to what day mail bags and baskets will be suspended.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, December 15th, 1883.—The mean temperature was 401 Fahrenheit, and therefore 6.2 warmer than preceding week. The maximum temperature 55 Fah- renheit, was recorded on the 13th instant, and the minimum temperature 24 Fahrenheit on the 9th instant. The rain- fall measured 148 inches. The general direction of the wind was westerly. During the week, which was the 50th of the current year, 30 births and 16 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 18.9 per 1,000, against 18.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 7•3 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 3 from bronchitis, 3 from heart disease, 3 from debility, and 1 from opium poisoning suicidal.—Tbree cases of scarlet fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JOHN H. GORNALL, medical officer of health. tiOW THE 1-taTEs Go.—Edward Nor man, apparently an able-bodied man, and an inmate at Warrington Workhouse, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with being drunk at the Workhouse, on Saturday, and also with leaving the Institution without having claimed to be die- charged.—Mr. Currie, porter at the Workhouse, said that about four o'clock on Saturday afternoon, the prisoner asked him for permission to go to Market Gate, and he told him that he must obtain permission from someone else. The prisoner had been out of the House several times previous to that during the same day. He next saw prisoner come into the House shortly after eight o'clock, and he was then drunk. —Mr. Mackay, master of the Workhouse, said that the pri- soner and his wife and five children were inmates of the Workhouse, but previous to their entering the prisoner was offered double wages if he would work overtime for Mr. Longshaw, and he refused.—The prisoner said that the work just referred to was not suitable for him, as it made him ill. —A sentence of one month's hard labour was inflicted.

NEW Musw.—Fifteen voluntaries for the organ, and anthem for Christmas "There were shepherds"; London: Novelle., Ewer and Co.—We have pleasure in calling attention to these, the latest compositions of our •townsmen, Mr. T. Mee Pattison. Viewed in connection with other and not less important contributions to music from the same pen, they serve to show that Warrington is by no means behind in yielding its quota of men of cul- ture whose careful and honest work enables Englishmen to hold their own as a musical people. The organ voluntaries are written in a flowing and graceful vein which cannot but be to them a great recommendation. The present seriee, at least, consist chiefly of subjects of a deliberate tempo, in which scope is found and taken advantage of for the scoring of distinct though simultaneous parts indicating on the part of the writer some fertility of contrapuntal resource. There is in some, indeed, treatment of so near an approach to the stricter sort as to suggest the promise and potency of future work of much more severe a character than has yet been undertaken. The anthem is peculiarly singable, and, there- fore, well adapted for the wide and general use of amateur choirs. The music has both variety and unity. •Alternated with a measured movement for the male voices in unison, a pleasing ensemble twice occurs, in which there is some effective part writing. The publication of the anthem at a seasonable time like the present is well calculated to give it an impetus to the popularity which we have no hesitation in saying it deserves. THE CANADIAN JUBILEE SINGERS AT THE PUBLIC HALL. —Two concerts of jubilee music were given by the Cana- dian Jubilee Singers in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings. The attendance each evening was small, and the proceeds would barely cover the expenses. Mr. Robert Garnett presided on Tuesday even- ing. The Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), who presided on Wednesday evening, said there was a disposition on the part of many people to pooh-pooh the sending out of missionaries to foreign lands, because, said they, there are plenty of people amongst us who want civilising. No doubt there were ignorant, vulgar, uncivilized people amongst us, but that was entirely their own fault. We poured out our money in almost copious streams for education; we paid instructors both temporal and spiritual; and if people would not avail themselves of the advantages thns afforded the fault rested with themselves and not with us. If we had people amongst us who wanted civilizing surely that was no reason why we should not try to do a little toward enlighten- ing our fellow-beings plunged in mental and moral darkness in foreign lands. We frequently heard of the savage sacri- fioing human lives to their gods, and if we could do nothing more than teach them that this was wrong we should be doing a great good. He thought that the object of the singers was a commendable one, and he regretted there was not a larger attendance.—The programme each evening• was creditably gone through and the audience showed their appreciation by frequent applause.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WIGAN: ELECTION OF MR. N. ECKERSLEY.—Yesterdav morning, Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley (C), banker, of Standish Hall, near Wigan, was nominated for the vacancy in the represenation of Wigan, caused by the death of Mr. J. Knowles. He was proposed by Mr. A. Hewlett, J.P., of Standish, and seconded by Mr. William Bryham, J.P., Ince, and there being no opposition was de- clared duly elected.

FIFTY YARMOUTH FISHERMEN ROWNED.—It is estimated that about fifty fishermen from Yarmouth were lost during the gale of last week. Five smacks, the Selina Dora, Vixen, Scorpion, and Huntsmen are still missing and little hope is entertained of their safety. They would each carry six hands, and, with the crew of the steam cutter Marie, twelve in all, and other losses reported from different smacks, the total amounts to about fifty SOWS. EXTENSIVE BOBBERIES OF CHEMlCALS.—Yesterday after- noon the Birmingham police arrested five persons on a charge of being concerned in a great and systematic course of rob- beries from the premises of Messrs. Philip Harris and Co., the well-known chemical firm. Three of the prisoners were employed by the firm, and the others are alleged to have felonioualy received the goods. The property stolen is said to be of the value of several hundred of pounds. THE DYNAMITE SCARE.—The precautions for the safety of public buildings in London were continued on Thursday night at the House of Commons. Three policemen in uni- form were on duty, and the undergrocnd passage leading to the Westminster Bridge Railway Station and the gate oppo- site the embankment were closed to traffic. Loudon Bridge was wacched by no fewer than six policemen in uniform, and extra policemen were also on duty at the Home Office, the Law Courts, and the Mansion House. _

INTER-TRIBL DISTURBANCES IN THE SOUDAN. - The Khedive has rec3ived a telegram dated the 10th inst. from the Governor of Taka, near Kassala, stating that serious dissentions have broken out among the different tribes along the Suakim-Berber route to Khartoum, and that some sec- tions of the Hadendua tribes are taking up arms against another section. Two of the principal rebel chiefs on the Suakim-Berber route intend proceeding to Khartoum to have an interview with the acting Governor-General of the Sou- dan. The telegram adds that tranquility prevails at Taka.

div.head: ST. HELENS NEWS.
div.p: ST. HELENS NEWS.

PROSECUTIONS BY PRESCOT GUARDIANS.—At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Andrew Benson was committed to gaol for six weeks, at the instance of the Prescot Guar- dians, for non-payment of an order to contribute towares the support of his aged mother; and George Moore was committed a month for a similar offence with regard to the maintenance of his wife, who is a lunatic. AN OYER-CLEVER THIEF AT PRESCOT.—Mary Kelly was, on Tuesday, committed to gaol for 21 days for having stolen five pairs of stockings from the shop-door of John Jones, pawnbroker, Prescot.—The prisoner, who was a stranger to the town, had taken the articles named from the shop-door, and then gone inside to try and pawn them; but they were recognised by a boy in the shop. CIRISTMAS in OAOL.—John Fahey, a lad 17 years of age, was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having stolen a pair of boots, value 7s 61. The boots, it seemed, had been taken from the shop door of Mr. Hulme, Liverpool-road, on the 26th September, but as Fahey had been in gaol till the previous day he could not be dealt with sooner for the theft. He was sent back to gaol for three months' hard labour. SUDDEN DEATH AT Sr. HELENS.—OR Wednesday morn- ing, about seven o'clock, a labourer named John Regan, 45 years of age, who was employed by Messrs. Harris and Sons, builders, fell down and suddenly expired while work- ing at the Cowley Hill Glassworks, belonging to Messrs. Pilkington. Deceased had gone to work as usual at 6-30, apparently in good health. Half an hour before his death, however, be complained of not being well, although he con- tinued to work. THE MESSIAH AT Sr. HELENS.—It will be noticed from our advertising columns that the St. Helens Congregational Church choir, assisted by members of other choirs, are to give a performance of Handel's "Messiah," in the Town Hall, on Thursday evening next. The artistes are Madame Laura Smart, Fraulein Dreier, Miss Alice Wolstenholme, Mr. George Barton, Mr. Fred Gordon, and a band and chorus of about 90 performers. We have every confidence in com- mending the performance to the attention of our readers. AN OBSTINATE PARENT.—Anthony Bannister, fruiterer, was again summoned before the St. Helens magistrates on Friday last, to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for not paving .£1 15s. 6d., arrears of an order made minn hip n to pay per week towards tha rnlintananon nf his son in an induithat sctiool. Bannister has already been committed to gaol several times for non-payment of arrears en this order, which he obstinately refuses to comply with He was again sent to gaol for six weeks. AN ANNOYING PRACTICE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday last, four young men named Patrick Reid, James Scarry, James Riley, and Thomas Davies, were charged with having committed a breach of the peace.— P.C. Barker said the deiendants and a number of others from Greenbank, had been behaving in a disorderly manner in Hall-street, pn the previous Sunday evening, and also rung Mr. Hodgson's door bell.—Mr. Hodgson said that for the last 18. months, his door bell had been rung in this mis- chievous manner on an average of about three times a day. —The Bench, however, decided that they could not convict of a breach of the peace on the evidence given. ASSAULTING A CRIPPLE.--At the St. Helens Police Court on Monday, Richard McCormick, a young man, was charged with having assaulted John Taife on the 13th October. The prisoner had previously been summoned for this offence, but not having appeared he was apprehended on a warrant. Taife, who is a cripple, having only one leg, said the prisoner came up to him en the night in question, knocked him down, and kicked him. Superintendent John- ston said the prisoner had a very vile character, having been convicted several times this year for offences of violence.— He was fined and costs, or one month's imprisonment. STEALING RAISINS AT Sr. HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday, two youths named James Riley and Thomas Davis, were charged with having stolen a box of raisins, valued at 55., the property of Edward Johnson, provision dealer. The box, it seemed, had been missed at Mr. Johnson's warehouse in Tontine-street, and P.C. Cot. tam apprehended the two prisoners on suspicion, and from what they confessed it appeared that they had stolen the raisins, sold them, and divided the proceeds. They both pleaded guilty, and as they had previously been in the hands of the police, Riley was sent to gaol for two months, and Davis for one month.

ITRANSFERS AT PRESCOT.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday. the following transfers were granted :—The Royal Oak, Prescot, from Thomas Edwards to Daniel Robin- son; St. Patrick's, Prescot, from Mary Kenny to John Jas. Saxton ; The White Horse, Prescot, from Joseph Dickenson to Margaret Todd; White Horse, Rainhill, from William Thewell to Mary Kenny; The Queen's Arms, Prescot, from Thomas Deans to Michael Quinn.—Permission to sell :—The Queen's Arms, Huyton, from G. Oscar Mow! to Thomas Edwards; The Commercial Inn, Widnes, from Mark Wright, senr., to Mark Wright, junr. ;The Dog Tavern, Prescot, from Daniel Robinson to Thomas Robinson. GOOD TEMPLARIS3I AT ST. HELENS.—The "Great Heart" Lodge 1.0.G.T, held their usual session on Tues- day evening last, when the "Morning Star" Lodge paid a fraternal visit and entertained the Lodge very well. The following programme was very efficiently gone through : Bro. Joseph Hesketh, W.M., three songs; Sister King, P.W.C.T., reading; Bro. John Hesketh, W.C.T., two songs; Bro. T. Thompson, W.Chap., reading; Sister Rawlinson, W.D.M., reading. A vote of thanks was given to the visitors and responded to. Bro. Brockbank, superintendent of the "Young Great Heart" Juvenile Temple, banded over to the Lodge £2 from the juveniles. A pleasant session.

'STRUGGLE WITH' A POACHER.—George Houghton, from Garston, was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with night poaching on the 14th November.— Idosee White, the keeper for Miss Watts, of Speke Hall, said that about mid-night, on the 11th ult., he was out watch- ing when the defendant fired off a gun at a pheasant within about 30 yards of him. Witness made a rush at Houghton, when the latter held up the gun and told him to "stand back." He however, rushed upon the prisoner, and after scuffing four or five minutes they fell to the ground to- gether, Heughton being uppermost. Witness, however, managed to turn his antagonist over and himself get on the top and shout for assistance. Houghton then said be would go quietly and witness let him get up, and took him in charge.—The prisoner, who had a bad character, pleaded guilty and was sent to gaol for six weeks, and was ordered to afterwards obtain sureties for good behaviour for 12 months, or suffer other cix months' imprisonment. PRESCOT CHURCH SCHOOLS.—These schools have been carried on hitherto as simple elercientary schools. Occa- sionally a government inspector was invited to examine the children, not for the object of earning a grant (as the schools are not under Government) but in order to test the efficiency of the scholars. It is, however, the intention of the managers to place the schools under Govecument inspec- Gon after Christmas, and to meet the requirements of the Ealucation Act the schoole had to undergo certain alterations at a considerable coat. The Vicar, who takes a warm in- terest in the schools, has been most fortunate in raising by subsee;ption the amount which will almost cover the .cost of improvements, Szc., and it is hoped the small sum yet re- quired to complete the work will be forthcoming. On Sun- day last sermons were preached, morning and evening, at the Parish Church, and an appeal made to the congr,gation at the close of each service on behalf of the echools im- provement fund. The sermons, which were excellent and very appropriate, were preached by the Rev. Canon Snail!). Principal of St. Aiden's College, Birkenhead, The collec- tions amounted to £l3 Bs. lid.

FOOTB kLL. RUNCORN TRUE BLUE V. RUNCORN VICTORIAS.—These clubs met on Saturday on the ground of the former. True Blues: One goal, one try, four minor points. Victerias One try, two minor points. WARRINGTON.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the home team by one goal, one try, and four minor points to St. Elphin's one try and one minor point. TEsm). —This match was played at LYMM on Saturday, and remlted in faveur of the Man- cunians by one goal and tw., tries to.one try. The tries were obtained by Clark (2) and Adler (I). NEWTON (2ND) —A match between these clubs was played at Warrington on Batarday before a fair number of spectators. The game (a very noisy and un- pleasant one), ended in a draw in favour of Warrington by 2 touchdowns to I. The play of Boardman and Naylor behind, and of Lennox (forwards for the visitors) is especially worthy of nitice ; as was also that of Speakman, Robinson, and Wright for the home team. RUNCORN V. BIRKENHEAD RANGERS. This fixture was played off at Birkenhead on Saturday, in wretched weather. ,etter to itte editor. GUTENBERG'S INVENTION. Sir,—ls the following worth a place in your columns as ; a companion story to that about the black boy of Mann- U 8 : Young Bertha was a belle. And Fredric roved her well; And often, in the sunny summer weather, They sat npin the seat. Their happiness complete. And lovingly they passed the time tog4her. Upon the bench he put An F and B. well cut, For never yet did any youngster lack knife; There were the letters seen. A skewered heart between. So neatly carved by Fredr:c's ready j telt-knife, His carving to improve, And gratify his love. He thought to add a little lively colour; And cherries from the tree He pressed, as you may see, Until the carven lines could be no fuller. Thither his teacher came. Herr Gutenberg by name, Who then was meditating his inventi-n ; The scapegrace boy he chid, But Fredric's work was hid Bene%th him by the part we need not mention. To all the talk, indeed, Young Fred gave little heed, And thought of nothing but his carving caper. When words gave place to blows, The frightened boy arose, And backward fell upon his teacher's paper. The eld man stood amazed, As at the sheet he gazed, And stared and muttered like a man demented. The letters printed there, Might truly make him star, For thus the art of printing was inventel. The teacher, full of jny, Then carried off the boy, And kept the secret in his own possession; But Bertha sobbed and sighed. While Fredric yelled and cried, Because they used his " form" for each "Impression." It is taken from the libretto to a series of seven humorous plates designed by Mr. B. A. Wikstrom, and published by Mr. J. H. Hamburger, of New York. The story may console those Newtonian lovers who were once upon a time so rudely disturbed by a shower of quoins. Yours, &a., ANGLO SCOTUS.
